stem: A 55-year-old woman is discharged after iron deficiency anemia workup with a new prescription for oral iron. She takes levothyroxine and calcium daily, drinks coffee all morning, and asks about the dark stools she noticed. The nurse's best counseling is:

options: Coordinate an urgent same-day evaluation: fever and increasing redness 4 days after arthroplasty are red flags for surgical site infection that cannot wait for routine follow-up
Reassure her that redness is normal and keep the 2-week appointment
Tell her to apply ice and call back in 3 days
Document the call and take no action
rationale: Fever plus expanding erythema 4 days after joint arthroplasty is a surgical site infection until proven otherwise; urgent same-day evaluation is the standard. Reassurance, ice, and watchful waiting risk progression to a prosthetic joint infection with devastating consequences.
stem: A 70-year-old woman calls 4 days after discharge following a total hip arthroplasty. She reports a temperature of 101.2°F and increasing redness around the incision. Her 2-week follow-up is scheduled. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with instructions to follow up as needed
Home health skilled nursing for ostomy teaching reinforcement, peristomal skin surveillance, hydration monitoring, and coordination of the oncology plan
A home aide for housekeeping only
Outpatient ostomy clinic in 1 month with no interim support
rationale: A new ileostomy with high output, early skin irritation, and a frightened spouse needs skilled nursing: teaching reinforcement, skin surveillance, dehydration monitoring, and oncology coordination. Housekeeping does not address skilled needs, and a 1-month gap without support risks dehydration readmission and skin breakdown.
stem: A 61-year-old man is discharged with a new ileostomy after colectomy for cancer. His output is high, his peristomal skin is irritated, and his wife is frightened of the appliance. The best referral is:

options: Document the plan and discharge
Tell the family to watch him closely
Arrange a 24-hour sitter at the family's expense
Hold discharge and escalate: new delirium with no identified cause in an older adult is not a safe discharge condition; evaluate for underlying causes and ensure a safe, supervised disposition
rationale: New-onset delirium of unclear cause in an older adult is a medical emergency and an absolute bar to safe discharge; the nurse must hold discharge and escalate for workup and a supervised disposition. Documenting, family vigilance without a diagnosis, and a private sitter all leave the underlying cause unaddressed and the patient unsafe.
stem: An 84-year-old man is scheduled for discharge after a hip fracture repair. This morning he is newly confused, does not recognize his daughter, and is picking at the air. No cause has been identified. The family wants to take him home today. The nurse's best action is:

options: Tell her to stop the statin permanently
Reassure her that muscle aches are harmless
Document the symptom and take no action

Report the muscle pain to the prescriber for evaluation of statin-associated muscle symptoms, discuss the risks of stopping without guidance, and arrange timely follow-up rather than unsupervised discontinuation
rationale: New muscle pain on a statin requires prescriber evaluation for statin-associated muscle symptoms versus other causes; unsupervised discontinuation after MI forfeits secondary prevention benefit. Permanent cessation without evaluation is premature, blanket reassurance misses rhabdomyolysis risk, and silent documentation leaves her to stop the drug on her own.
stem: A 66-year-old woman discharged 1 week ago after a myocardial infarction calls: she stopped her atorvastatin 3 days ago because of muscle aches. The nurse's best response is:

options: Coordinate a pre-discharge oncology pharmacist session with a written neutropenic precaution plan, teach-back on fever action thresholds, confirmation of the 48-hour lab and clinic visit, and a 24-hour contact number
Give him a thermometer and the clinic phone number
Tell him to avoid crowds and discharge
Schedule the first lab recheck in 2 weeks
rationale: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia makes fever a medical emergency; a structured pre-discharge bundle — pharmacist teaching, written fever action plan with explicit thresholds, confirmed early labs and visit, and a 24-hour contact — is the standard that prevents delayed presentation and sepsis death. A thermometer without thresholds, vague avoidance advice, and a 2-week lab gap each leave life-threatening holes.
stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged after his first cycle of chemotherapy for lymphoma. His absolute neutrophil count is falling, and he lives 45 minutes from the hospital. He asks what to do if he feels feverish. The most effective discharge bundle is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call if bleeding occurs
Escalate to the prescriber and pharmacist: dual NSAID therapy markedly increases bleeding and renal risk, and one agent should be discontinued with a safer pain plan
Tell her to take the celecoxib in the morning and ibuprofen at night
Document both medications as reconciled
rationale: Concurrent celecoxib and ibuprofen is duplicate NSAID therapy with compounded GI bleeding, renal, and cardiovascular risk; the nurse must escalate for discontinuation of one and a safer pain strategy. Staggering the doses does not reduce the risk, and documenting without action perpetuates a dangerous duplication.
stem: A 69-year-old woman with osteoarthritis is discharged after a knee arthroscopy. Her home celecoxib 200 mg daily was continued, and the discharge list adds ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for postoperative pain. The nurse's priority is:

options: No referral; her daughter's daily visits are enough
A meal delivery service alone
Home health skilled nursing for medication management, depression screening and monitoring, and coordination of the psychiatry follow-up
A friendly visitor volunteer program
rationale: New antidepressant initiation in an isolated older adult with a recent overdose attempt requires skilled monitoring for suicidality, medication adherence, and care coordination — a meal service or visitor program cannot provide clinical surveillance. Daily daughter visits help but do not substitute for skilled assessment, and the psychiatry follow-up needs active coordination, not passive scheduling.
stem: A 74-year-old woman is discharged after a suicide attempt by medication overdose. She lives alone, was started on a new antidepressant, and her daughter visits daily but works full time. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with a standard seizure precaution handout
Tell her employer she had a seizure
Restrict her from all activities for 6 months

Coordinate an epilepsy action plan with teach-back for the patient and a designated coworker or family member, confirm neurology follow-up within 2 weeks, reconcile the new antiepileptic with home medications, and review driving restrictions per state law
rationale: A first seizure with a new antiepileptic in a commercial driver demands a comprehensive bundle: an action plan taught to the patient and a bystander, early neurology follow-up, reconciliation for interactions, and explicit driving restriction counseling given her livelihood. A handout alone, notifying the employer without her consent, and blanket 6-month restriction without legal context are each inadequate or inappropriate.
stem: A 42-year-old woman is discharged after a first generalized seizure. She was started on levetiracetam, works as a commercial driver, and is terrified of losing her license. Her husband was not present for teaching. The most effective discharge plan is:

options: Verify he can perform the exchange procedure with return demonstration, confirm the supply delivery and 24-hour dialysis nurse contact, reconcile the new phosphate binder with his medication list, and schedule the first clinic visit before discharge
Give him the dialysis center's phone number and discharge
Tell him to watch the training video again at home
Schedule the clinic visit for 1 month out
rationale: A new peritoneal dialysis patient needs verified procedural competence (return demonstration), confirmed supplies and 24-hour support, reconciled binders, and a scheduled early visit — the complete readiness bundle for a high-risk home therapy. A phone number, a video, and a 1-month gap each leave critical safety holes that predict technique failure and peritonitis.
stem: A 55-year-old man with end-stage renal disease is discharged to start peritoneal dialysis at home. He completed training but seems hesitant during the exchange procedure. His wife will assist. He was started on sevelamer. The nurse's priority before discharge is:

options: Tell him to take the prednisone only when he feels weak
Escalate to the prescriber: the taper was stopped early, risking adrenal crisis, and the plan needs clarification with stress-dose teaching
Document the early stop as patient nonadherence
Reassure him that stopping early is fine since he feels well
rationale: Abruptly stopping a prednisone taper after prolonged therapy risks adrenal insufficiency and crisis; the nurse must escalate for plan clarification and provide stress-dose teaching. PRN use of steroids for weakness is unsafe, documenting without intervening misses a preventable emergency, and reassurance is false — he may decompensate under stress.
stem: A 63-year-old man is discharged after a COPD exacerbation on a prednisone taper. He calls 3 days later saying he stopped the prednisone because he 'felt fine' and now feels weak and nauseated. The nurse's best action is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the family to hire a private aide
Home health skilled nursing and physical therapy for continued rehabilitation, fall-risk assessment and home safety modifications, medication review, and caregiver respite coordination
A nursing home placement because of the fall history
rationale: Recurrent falls with injury, polypharmacy, and an overwhelmed caregiver require skilled nursing plus PT: rehabilitation, home safety assessment, medication review for fall-risk drugs, and respite coordination. Standard instructions ignore the pattern, a private aide is not skilled care, and nursing home placement is excessive when home services can address the risks.
stem: A 81-year-old man is discharged after his third fall-related injury this year. He takes 9 medications, lives with his wife who is overwhelmed, and the home has stairs and poor lighting. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to return if the bleeding recurs
Tell her to avoid NSAIDs in the future and discharge
Document the transfusion and discharge

Coordinate a gastroenterology follow-up within 1-2 weeks, reconcile the anticoagulant resumption plan with cardiology and gastroenterology, provide bleeding warning-sign teach-back, and confirm she understands when to seek care
rationale: A GI bleed on anticoagulation requires coordinated resumption planning between cardiology (thrombotic risk) and gastroenterology (rebleed risk), plus timely follow-up and warning-sign teaching — the bundle that prevents both clot and rebleed. Vague return precautions, NSAID advice alone, and documentation without coordination each miss the central therapeutic dilemma.
stem: A 72-year-old woman is discharged after a gastrointestinal bleed while on apixaban for atrial fibrillation. She received 2 units of packed red blood cells. The apixaban was held. She asks when she can restart it. The most effective coordination plan is:

options: Hold discharge and escalate: she cannot verbalize the warning signs or demonstrate the device, so she does not meet readiness criteria for a life-sustaining device
Document the teaching as complete since the video was watched
Schedule a device clinic visit in 1 month and discharge
Give her the manufacturer's helpline number
rationale: A left ventricular assist device patient who cannot demonstrate driveline care or verbalize emergency procedures is not safe for discharge — device infection and power emergencies are life-threatening, and readiness requires verified competence. A watched video is not competence, a 1-month gap without skills is dangerous, and a helpline does not substitute for hands-on mastery.
stem: A 59-year-old man is scheduled for discharge with a new left ventricular assist device (LVAD). His wife watched the driveline care video but cannot demonstrate sterile dressing technique, and neither can verbalize what to do during a power alarm. The nurse's best action is:

options: Tell her the rash will fade and discharge
Escalate to the prescriber and pharmacist for evaluation of a possible drug reaction, review the full medication list for the culprit, and hold the suspect agent pending guidance
Advise her to take diphenhydramine and continue all medications
Document the rash as an expected side effect
rationale: A new diffuse rash with pruritus after starting allopurinol raises concern for a hypersensitivity reaction that can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome; the nurse must escalate for evaluation and hold the suspect drug pending guidance. Minimizing it, masking it with antihistamines while continuing the trigger, and normalizing it as expected all risk a life-threatening progression.
stem: A 66-year-old woman started on allopurinol for gout calls 5 days after discharge with a new diffuse rash and itching. She is otherwise well. The nurse's best action is:

options: Discharge with advice to call 911 if chest pain returns
A 7-day cardiology follow-up with medication reconciliation, teach-back on dual antiplatelet adherence and bleeding signs, depression screening, and a 48-hour check-in call
A cardiac rehabilitation referral in 3 months with no interim follow-up
Instructions to resume all normal activities immediately
rationale: Post-MI patients with depression history and a prior missed appointment need intensive transitional care: early cardiology follow-up, reconciled medications, adherence teach-back for dual antiplatelet therapy, depression screening, and early check-in. Vague 911 advice, delayed rehab alone, and immediate unrestricted activity each miss the adherence and mood risks that drive readmission and stent thrombosis.
stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged after a myocardial infarction with a drug-eluting stent. He has a history of depression and missed his last primary care appointment. He is prescribed dual antiplatelet therapy, a statin, and a beta-blocker. The most effective readmission prevention bundle is:

options: Discharge with the standard heart failure handout
Tell her to limit fluids to 2 liters without further teaching
Document that teaching was completed

Coordinate a heart failure clinic visit within 7 days, reconcile the diuretic plan with teach-back on daily weights and the action plan, arrange a scale if needed, and schedule a 48-hour check-in call
rationale: New heart failure with low health literacy and no scale requires the full transitional bundle: early specialty follow-up, reconciled diuretic plan, verified weight and action-plan understanding, a scale, and early check-in. A handout alone is unreadable to her in practical terms, fluid restriction without teaching is incomplete, and documentation without verification is a known failure.
stem: A 62-year-old woman is discharged with a new diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. She has low health literacy, no bathroom scale, and asks, 'How will I know if I am getting worse?' The best coordination plan is:

options: Reconcile with the prescriber: the carbamazepine induces the metabolism of her oral contraceptive, risking contraceptive failure, and alternative contraception or a different antiepileptic should be discussed
Tell her the medications do not interact
Document the list as accurate
Advise her to double the contraceptive dose
rationale: Carbamazepine is a potent enzyme inducer that reduces the effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives, risking unintended pregnancy; this interaction must be reconciled with the prescriber for alternative contraception or antiepileptic selection. Denying the interaction, silent documentation, and doubling the contraceptive dose are all unsafe.
stem: A 29-year-old woman with epilepsy is discharged on carbamazepine. Her home medication list includes a combined oral contraceptive. She tells the nurse she does not want to become pregnant. The nurse's priority is:

options: No referral; he can manage the pump himself
Home health skilled nursing for insulin pump site assessment, hypoglycemia surveillance, and coordination of the endocrinology follow-up
A diabetes education class in 6 weeks
Instructions to call the pump manufacturer with questions
rationale: A new insulin pump in a patient with hypoglycemia unawareness and a recent severe episode requires skilled nursing: site assessment, hypoglycemia surveillance, and endocrinology coordination during the high-risk initiation period. Self-management without support is unsafe given unawareness, a 6-week class is too late, and the manufacturer cannot provide clinical surveillance.
stem: A 47-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is discharged with a new insulin pump. He has hypoglycemia unawareness and had a severe episode last month. He lives alone. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to eat more fiber
Tell her the bloating is expected and will resolve
Document the symptoms as normal
Escalate for evaluation: new abdominal distension, decreased output, and nausea after colostomy creation are red flags for obstruction or ileus that require prompt assessment, not routine follow-up
rationale: New distension with decreased stoma output and nausea after colostomy is a potential obstruction or ileus — a surgical emergency that cannot wait for routine follow-up. Fiber advice, reassurance, and passive documentation risk delayed treatment of a life-threatening complication.
stem: A 64-year-old woman calls 6 days after discharge following a new colostomy. She reports increasing abdominal distension, decreased stoma output, and nausea. Her follow-up is in 1 week. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with a standard medication list
Tell him to avoid salt and discharge
Document the teaching as complete

Coordinate a pre-discharge session with the pharmacist and dietitian: teach-back on the low-sodium diet with culturally familiar foods, daily weight and symptom action plan, medication purpose teach-back, and a 7-day follow-up visit with a 48-hour check-in call
rationale: New heart failure in a patient with language barriers and dietary unfamiliarity requires an interprofessional, culturally adapted bundle: pharmacist and dietitian teaching, verified understanding of weights and the action plan, and early follow-up with check-in. A standard list, vague salt advice, and documentation without verification each leave the transition to fail.
stem: A 55-year-old man is discharged with a new diagnosis of heart failure. He speaks limited English, eats a traditional high-sodium diet, and was started on 4 new medications. The interpreter is available before discharge. The most effective discharge bundle is:

options: Alert the prescriber: reintroducing the full home warfarin dose without an INR check after a supratherapeutic value risks recurrent over-anticoagulation and bleeding
Tell him to resume the full dose since it was his home dose
Have him skip warfarin for 1 week
Document the plan as safe
rationale: Resuming the full home warfarin dose immediately after a supratherapeutic INR of 6.2 without rechecking risks recurrent over-anticoagulation; the prescriber must guide reinitiation dosing and INR monitoring. Home-dose status does not make it safe after a bleeding-risk event, a week-long hold without guidance risks thrombosis, and documenting without questioning perpetuates the hazard.
stem: A 68-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation is discharged after his INR was 6.2 without bleeding. The warfarin was held for 2 days in the hospital. The discharge list resumes his full home dose of 5 mg daily starting tonight. The nurse should:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the clinic if she feels sad
A care conference with the patient, daughter, social worker, and palliative care to clarify goals, code status understanding, and the home support plan before discharge
A hospice referral without family discussion
Documentation of the daughter's request and discharge as planned
rationale: Conflicting goals between a patient wanting comfort and a daughter requesting full resuscitation require a facilitated care conference with social work and palliative care to clarify understanding, code status, and the support plan — not unilateral decisions or silent documentation. A hospice referral without discussion bypasses consent, and discharging into an unresolved conflict guarantees crisis.
stem: A 79-year-old woman with advanced COPD and frequent exacerbations is ready for discharge. She tells the nurse she 'does not want to suffer anymore,' but her daughter insists on full resuscitation and another hospitalization 'if anything happens.' The nurse's best action is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell him to ask his neighbor for help with the dressing
Home health skilled nursing for burn wound assessment and dressing management, pain management support, and coordination of the burn clinic follow-up
Outpatient burn clinic in 3 weeks with no interim support
rationale: Partial-thickness burns of the dominant hand in a patient living alone require skilled nursing for wound assessment, dressing changes, pain support, and burn clinic coordination — a neighbor cannot manage burn wounds. Standard instructions alone are insufficient for burn care, and a 3-week gap without support risks infection and contracture.
stem: A 43-year-old man is discharged after partial-thickness burns to his dominant hand from a cooking accident. He lives alone, needs daily dressing changes, and his pain is 6/10. The best referral is:

options: Reassure her that tingling is normal after surgery
Tell her to take extra calcium on her own
Document the symptom and take no action
Escalate for same-day evaluation: perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm 2 days after thyroidectomy are red flags for hypocalcemia that require prompt calcium assessment and management
rationale: Perioral tingling progressing to carpopedal spasm after thyroidectomy signals hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury — a potentially life-threatening emergency requiring same-day calcium evaluation. Reassurance, unsupervised calcium dosing, and passive documentation risk progression to laryngospasm or seizures.
stem: A 52-year-old woman calls 2 days after discharge following a total thyroidectomy. She reports tingling around her mouth and cramping in her hands. Her follow-up is in 1 week. The nurse's priority is:

options: Verify the steroid taper plan with the prescriber, provide teach-back on the taper schedule and stress-dose rules, confirm the follow-up appointment, and arrange a 48-hour check-in call
Give him the taper prescription and discharge
Tell him to stop the steroids if he feels better
Document the plan as understood
rationale: A prolonged high-dose steroid course for ITP requires a verified taper, stress-dose teaching, confirmed follow-up, and early check-in — abrupt cessation or misunderstanding risks adrenal crisis and platelet collapse. A prescription without teaching, symptom-guided stopping, and documentation without verification each leave dangerous gaps.
stem: A 49-year-old man is discharged after immune thrombocytopenia treated with high-dose steroids. He is on a 6-week prednisone taper, has a history of missing doses, and asks what happens if he stops early. The most reliable discharge plan is:

options: Discharge with instructions to avoid grapefruit juice
Hold the statin and notify the prescriber: simvastatin plus newly started diltiazem raises the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis through CYP3A4 inhibition, and the combination needs review
Tell him the combination is safe
Document the interaction as minor
rationale: Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4, markedly raising simvastatin levels and the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis; the nurse must hold the statin pending prescriber review for a dose adjustment or alternative. Grapefruit advice alone does not address the drug interaction, reassurance is false, and minimizing the interaction in documentation is unsafe.
stem: A 67-year-old man is discharged after atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. His home simvastatin 80 mg daily was continued, and diltiazem was newly started. The nurse recognizes the interaction. The best action is:

options: Discharge with a standard pain medication list
Tell her to take the opioids only when pain is severe
Home health skilled nursing for pain assessment, bowel regimen monitoring, safe medication storage teaching, and coordination of the oncology follow-up
A hospice referral since she has metastatic disease
rationale: A new metastatic cancer patient on escalating opioids with constipation, a teenager in the home, and an overwhelmed spouse needs skilled nursing: pain and bowel assessment, safe storage teaching to protect the adolescent, and oncology coordination. A bare medication list, PRN-only advice, and an undiscussed hospice referral each miss the safety and support needs.
stem: A 56-year-old woman is discharged with newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer. She is on escalating opioids for bone pain, is constipated, and lives with her husband and teenage son. Her husband is overwhelmed. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call if the swelling worsens
Tell him to remove the compression stockings at night and reapply in the morning
Document the symptoms as expected
Escalate for same-day evaluation: new unilateral swelling and warmth in the contralateral leg while on anticoagulation are red flags for a new or extended clot that must be assessed promptly
rationale: New contralateral leg swelling and warmth during anticoagulation for DVT suggests clot extension or a new thrombus, possibly indicating treatment failure; same-day evaluation is required. Reassurance, stocking advice, and passive documentation risk missing a progressive thromboembolic event.
stem: A 61-year-old man calls 1 week after discharge for a deep vein thrombosis treated with apixaban. He reports new swelling and warmth in the opposite leg. The nurse's priority is:

options: Coordinate a pre-discharge teach-back session on the signs of rejection and infection, the critical importance of never missing tacrolimus doses, the drug interaction list, and confirmation of the 48-hour lab and clinic visit
Give him a pill organizer and discharge
Tell him the transplant team will call next week
Document the teaching as complete
rationale: Missing tacrolimus doses can precipitate acute rejection of a transplanted kidney; a pre-discharge bundle with teach-back on rejection and infection signs, absolute adherence emphasis, interaction review, and confirmed early labs is the safety standard. A pill organizer without teaching, deferred team contact, and documentation without verification each leave organ-threatening gaps.
stem: A 45-year-old man is discharged 5 days after a kidney transplant. He is on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. He asks what happens if he misses a dose of 'the anti-rejection pill.' The most effective discharge action is:

options: Discharge with instructions to take the antibiotic with food
Notify the prescriber: ciprofloxacin absorption is markedly reduced by calcium, iron, and multivitamins, and the dosing schedule must be separated or revised
Tell her the interaction is not significant
Document the list as reconciled
rationale: Ciprofloxacin binds divalent cations, and concurrent calcium, iron, and multivitamins can render the antibiotic subtherapeutic, risking treatment failure of the kidney infection; the prescriber must revise the schedule with proper separation. Minimizing the interaction, vague food advice, and silent documentation each leave the infection undertreated.
stem: A 59-year-old woman is discharged with ciprofloxacin for pyelonephritis. Her home list includes calcium, iron, and a multivitamin, all taken together every morning. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell her daughter to visit more often
Home health skilled nursing and physical therapy for gait training, home safety assessment, medication review for fall-risk drugs, and coordination of the neurology follow-up
A walker prescription alone
rationale: Parkinson disease with freezing of gait, recurrent falls, and polypharmacy in a patient living alone requires skilled nursing plus PT: gait training, home safety assessment, medication review, and neurology coordination. Standard instructions and a walker alone do not address freezing episodes or drug-related fall risk, and more daughter visits are not skilled care.
stem: A 76-year-old woman with Parkinson disease is discharged after a fall with a contusion. She has freezing of gait, takes 8 medications, and lives alone with her daughter visiting twice weekly. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to return if she vomits
Tell her the symptoms are from the anesthesia
Document the call and take no action
Escalate for urgent evaluation: intractable vomiting, confusion, and muscle cramps after parathyroidectomy suggest severe hypocalcemia requiring prompt assessment
rationale: Vomiting with confusion and cramps after parathyroidectomy points to severe hypocalcemia, a potentially life-threatening emergency; urgent evaluation with calcium assessment is required. Reassurance, anesthesia attribution, and passive documentation risk progression to seizures or cardiac arrhythmia.
stem: A 58-year-old woman calls 3 days after discharge following a parathyroidectomy. She reports persistent vomiting, confusion, and muscle cramps. The nurse's priority is:

options: Hold discharge and escalate: he cannot state the purpose of the apixaban or the bleeding precautions, so he does not meet medication readiness criteria; arrange teach-back with the pharmacist and confirm understanding
Document the teaching as complete
Give him a wallet card about apixaban and discharge
Schedule a pharmacist call for next week
rationale: A patient who cannot state why he takes apixaban or its bleeding precautions is at high risk for nonadherence or unrecognized bleeding; readiness requires verified understanding before discharge, best achieved with pharmacist-led teach-back. Documentation without verification, a wallet card without comprehension, and a deferred call each leave the gap open during the highest-risk days.
stem: A 73-year-old man is scheduled for discharge after a pulmonary embolism. He is prescribed apixaban but cannot state why he takes it or name any bleeding precautions. He lives alone. The nurse's best action is:

options: Tell her to take the levothyroxine at bedtime instead

Escalate to the prescriber and pharmacist: omeprazole is not the concern, but the evening calcium and iron markedly impair levothyroxine absorption, and the schedule needs revision with morning empty-stomach dosing
Document the schedule as acceptable
Advise her to double the levothyroxine dose
rationale: Calcium and iron taken in the evening still impair levothyroxine absorption if timing overlaps, and the core problem is that she is not taking it on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before food; the schedule needs prescriber and pharmacist revision. Bedtime dosing without proper separation, silent documentation, and doubling the dose are all unsafe.
stem: A 64-year-old woman is discharged after pneumonia. Her discharge list includes levothyroxine, omeprazole, calcium, and iron. She says she takes them all together at bedtime. Her TSH was elevated on admission. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the clinic with questions
A 48-hour post-discharge phone call, a 7-day clinic visit with reconciled medications, teach-back on the action plan, and coordination of transportation
A 1-month follow-up appointment
Instructions to go to the emergency department if she feels worse
rationale: COPD with low health literacy, technique failure, and missed visits needs the full transitional bundle: early phone contact, a 7-day visit with reconciliation, verified technique and action plan, and solved transportation. A 1-month gap misses the high-risk window, emergency department instructions are not follow-up, and vague clinic instructions do not address the barriers.
stem: A 68-year-old woman is discharged after a COPD exacerbation. She has low health literacy, could not demonstrate inhaler technique, and missed her last two appointments due to transportation. The most effective readmission prevention plan is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the wife to call 911 if he falls
Document the plan as safe
Convene the physical therapist, occupational therapist, case manager, and the couple before discharge to reassess the disposition, because the home setup cannot safely support his current function
rationale: A patient who cannot transfer independently being discharged to a spouse who cannot assist, with stairs and no bathroom equipment, is an unsafe disposition; the interprofessional team must reassess before discharge (e.g., rehab placement, equipment, increased support). Standard instructions, 911 advice, and documenting an unsafe plan as safe each fail the patient.
stem: A 78-year-old man is scheduled for discharge after a stroke with significant right-sided weakness. He cannot transfer independently. His wife is frail and cannot assist with transfers. The home has stairs and no bathroom equipment. The nurse's best action is:

options: Question the duplicate therapy with the prescriber: two SSRIs increase the risk of serotonin syndrome, and the regimen needs clarification before discharge
Tell her to take both for better effect
Have her alternate the medications daily
Document the list as reconciled
rationale: Concurrent sertraline and escitalopram is duplicate SSRI therapy with serotonin syndrome risk; the nurse must escalate for clarification of which agent to continue. Taking both, alternating, and silent documentation each perpetuate a dangerous duplication.
stem: A 54-year-old woman with depression is discharged after a fall. Her home sertraline 100 mg daily was continued, and the discharge list adds escitalopram 10 mg daily. She asks if she should take both. The nurse's priority is:

options: No referral; the wife can manage the wound
Home health skilled nursing for surgical site assessment, drain management, lymphedema education, and coordination of the oncology follow-up
Outpatient physical therapy only
A home aide for companionship
rationale: Post-mastectomy with a drain, lymphedema risk, and a working spouse needs skilled nursing: wound and drain surveillance, lymphedema teaching, and oncology coordination. The wife's daytime absence leaves a supervision gap that skilled visits fill; PT alone and companionship do not address the skilled needs.
stem: A 60-year-old woman is discharged after a mastectomy with axillary node dissection. She has a surgical drain, new lymphedema precautions, and her wife works full time. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call if the pain worsens
Tell him the pain is from the surgery and will resolve
Document the call as routine
Escalate for urgent evaluation: severe incisional pain with fever and foul drainage 1 week after colectomy are red flags for anastomotic leak or surgical site infection requiring prompt assessment
rationale: Fever with foul-smelling drainage and severe pain 1 week after colectomy suggests anastomotic leak or deep surgical site infection — a surgical emergency. Reassurance, normalization, and passive documentation risk delayed treatment of a life-threatening complication.
stem: A 57-year-old man calls 1 week after discharge following a colectomy. He reports severe incisional pain, fever of 101.8°F, and foul-smelling drainage. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with a standard low-sodium diet handout
Tell him to weigh himself when he remembers
Document the teaching as complete

Verify teach-back on daily weights, the weight-gain action plan, and sodium restriction; confirm a scale is available; reconcile the diuretic plan; and schedule a 7-day follow-up visit with a 48-hour check-in call
rationale: Heart failure discharge readiness hinges on verified self-monitoring skills: teach-back on weights and the action plan, a confirmed scale, a reconciled diuretic plan, and early follow-up with check-in. A handout, casual weighing, and documentation without verification each leave the readmission drivers unaddressed.
stem: A 66-year-old man is scheduled for discharge after a heart failure exacerbation. He says he understands the low-sodium diet and daily weights. He lives alone and has no scale. The nurse's best readiness verification is:

options: Alert the prescriber and pharmacist: the home NSAID plus new apixaban markedly increases bleeding risk, and the pain plan needs revision to a safer alternative
Tell him to take the ibuprofen with food
Document the combination as acceptable
Advise him to stop the apixaban if he notices bruising
rationale: Ibuprofen plus apixaban compounds bleeding risk without added antithrombotic benefit; the pain plan needs prescriber revision to a safer alternative. Taking it with food does not address the interaction, silent documentation leaves the hazard active, and stopping the anticoagulant for bruising invites stroke.
stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is discharged after a knee arthroscopy. His home ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily was continued, and apixaban was restarted. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the office with questions
Home health skilled nursing for wound assessment, diabetes and medication management, and coordination of the vascular surgery follow-up, plus a social work referral for transportation resources
A wound clinic referral in 1 month with no interim support
Instructions to keep the leg elevated and call if it worsens
rationale: A diabetic foot ulcer with a new dressing, missed-visit history, and transportation barriers needs skilled nursing for wound and diabetes management, vascular coordination, and social work for transportation — the bundle that prevents deterioration. A 1-month gap without support, vague elevation advice, and bare instructions each invite readmission.
stem: A 63-year-old man with diabetes is discharged after debridement of a foot ulcer. He has a new dressing, a history of missed wound clinic visits, and no reliable transportation. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to return if symptoms recur
Tell her to avoid all dairy permanently
Document the plan as complete

Coordinate a dietitian visit before discharge with a lactose-free, culturally adapted meal plan, teach-back on label reading, confirmation of the gastroenterology follow-up, and a 1-week check-in call
rationale: A new lactose intolerance diagnosis with dietary confusion and cultural food practices requires dietitian-led, culturally adapted teaching with teach-back, confirmed follow-up, and early check-in. Vague return precautions, permanent blanket dairy avoidance without teaching, and documentation without verification each leave her without usable guidance.
stem: A 45-year-old woman is discharged after workup for chronic diarrhea revealed lactose intolerance. She eats a traditional dairy-heavy diet, is confused about what she can eat, and asks for a meal plan. The most effective discharge plan is:

options: Reassure him that the interaction is not clinically significant
Tell him to take the antacid 1 hour before the antibiotic
Document the schedule as reconciled
Notify the prescriber: antacids markedly reduce the absorption of the prescribed fluoroquinolone, and the dosing schedule must be separated by several hours or revised
rationale: Antacids containing magnesium, aluminum, or calcium markedly reduce fluoroquinolone absorption, risking treatment failure of the pneumonia; the prescriber must revise the schedule with proper separation of several hours. Reassurance is false, 1 hour of separation is insufficient, and documenting without action leaves the infection undertreated.
stem: A 62-year-old man is discharged with levofloxacin for pneumonia. His home list includes an aluminum/magnesium antacid taken three times daily with meals. He asks if he can take them together. The nurse's priority is:

options: Coordinate a pre-discharge case management review to verify insurance authorization for the skilled nursing stay, confirm the facility received the reconciled medication list and wound care orders, and schedule the follow-up visit
Discharge her directly to the facility with the standard paperwork
Tell the family to arrange transportation themselves
Document the referral as complete
rationale: Transfer to a skilled nursing facility requires verified authorization, transmitted reconciled orders, and a scheduled follow-up — the coordination bundle that prevents rejected admissions and medication errors at handoff. Standard paperwork without verification, family-arranged transport without coordination, and documentation without confirmation each leave transition gaps.
stem: A 78-year-old woman is discharged to a skilled nursing facility after a hip fracture repair with a surgical drain and 9 medications. Her daughter asks what needs to happen before the transfer. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the clinic with questions
Arrange a 48-hour post-discharge phone call, a 7-day follow-up visit with lab recheck, teach-back on bleeding precautions and the procedure action plan, and confirmation of transportation
Schedule a 1-month follow-up visit
Instructions to go to the emergency department for any bleeding
rationale: Post-ERCP with sphincterotomy on a resumed anticoagulant is a high-risk transition: early phone contact, a 7-day visit with labs, verified bleeding-precaution understanding, and solved transportation form the safety net. A 1-month gap misses the bleeding window, emergency department instructions are not follow-up, and vague clinic instructions do not verify understanding.
stem: A 70-year-old man is discharged after ERCP with sphincterotomy for choledocholithiasis. His apixaban was held for the procedure and is to resume in 48 hours. He lives alone and has no transportation. The most effective readmission prevention plan is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell him to take the phosphate binder with meals without further teaching
Home health skilled nursing for medication management, dietary counseling reinforcement, fluid management teaching, and coordination of the dialysis schedule
A dietitian appointment in 2 months
rationale: New hemodialysis with hyperphosphatemia, fluid nonadherence, and dietary confusion requires skilled nursing: medication and diet reinforcement, fluid teaching, and dialysis schedule coordination during the high-risk initiation period. Standard instructions and a deferred dietitian visit do not address the immediate adherence gaps.
stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged to start outpatient hemodialysis. He was started on sevelamer, has a 2-liter fluid restriction he does not follow, and is confused about the renal diet. He missed his first dialysis education session. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to return if the pain worsens
Tell her the pain is from the biopsy and will resolve
Document the call and take no action
Escalate for urgent evaluation: severe flank pain with fever and vomiting 3 days after kidney biopsy are red flags for perinephric bleeding or infection requiring prompt assessment
rationale: Flank pain with fever and vomiting after percutaneous kidney biopsy suggests perinephric hematoma or infection — a potentially life-threatening complication requiring urgent evaluation. Reassurance, normalization, and passive documentation risk delayed treatment of hemorrhage or sepsis.
stem: A 55-year-old woman calls 3 days after discharge following a percutaneous kidney biopsy. She reports severe flank pain, fever of 101.5°F, and vomiting. The nurse's priority is:

options: Verify teach-back on the signs of rejection, infection precautions, the tacrolimus schedule with no missed doses, and confirmation of the 48-hour lab and clinic visit before discharge
Give her a medication list and discharge
Tell her the transplant coordinator will call next week
Document the teaching as complete
rationale: A new liver transplant recipient who cannot name rejection signs or the tacrolimus schedule is not ready for discharge — missed immunosuppression risks acute rejection, and unrecognized infection signs risk sepsis. Verified teach-back plus confirmed early labs and visit are the readiness standard; a list, deferred contact, and documentation without verification each leave organ-threatening gaps.
stem: A 52-year-old woman is scheduled for discharge 6 days after a liver transplant. She is on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. She cannot name any signs of rejection and is unsure when to take the tacrolimus. The nurse's best action is:

options: Tell him the combination is safe at these doses
Escalate to the prescriber and pharmacist: tramadol plus sertraline increases seizure and serotonin syndrome risk, and the pain plan needs revision
Document the combination as acceptable
Advise him to take the tramadol only at night
rationale: Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold and adds serotonergic activity to an SSRI, raising the risk of serotonin syndrome and seizures; the prescriber and pharmacist must revise the pain plan. Reassurance is false, silent documentation perpetuates the hazard, and nighttime-only dosing does not eliminate the interaction.
stem: A 64-year-old man is discharged after a back injury. His home sertraline 150 mg daily was continued, and the discharge list adds tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours as needed. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard heart failure handout
A 7-day heart failure clinic visit with medication reconciliation, teach-back on daily weights and the action plan, home health nursing for monitoring, and a 48-hour check-in call
A 1-month follow-up appointment
Instructions to call 911 for any weight gain
rationale: Heart failure with new atrial fibrillation, polypharmacy, and no scale needs the full transitional bundle: early specialty follow-up, reconciliation, verified self-monitoring, home nursing, and early check-in. A handout alone, a 1-month gap, and 911-only guidance each miss the adherence and monitoring risks that drive readmission.
stem: A 71-year-old woman is discharged after heart failure exacerbation with new-onset atrial fibrillation. She was started on apixaban, has 8 home medications, and no bathroom scale. The most effective readmission prevention plan is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the family to watch her closely
Document the plan as safe
Hold discharge and convene the team: she cannot demonstrate the walker, has uncontrolled pain, and no confirmed ride home — she does not meet readiness criteria
rationale: Inability to demonstrate the walker safely, uncontrolled pain, and no confirmed transportation are three unmet readiness criteria after hip fracture repair; the team must reconvene to revise the plan. Standard instructions, family vigilance without a safe mobility plan, and documenting an unsafe plan as safe each fail the patient.
stem: A 79-year-old woman is scheduled for discharge after a hip fracture repair. She cannot demonstrate safe walker use, her pain is 7/10, and her ride home has not been confirmed. The nurse's best action is:

options: Coordinate a pharmacist-led session with a pill organizer setup, teach-back on each drug's purpose and timing, a written schedule with pictures, and a 48-hour check-in call
Give him a printed medication list and discharge
Tell him to ask his son to sort the pills
Schedule a medication review in 3 months
rationale: A new 9-drug cardiac regimen in a patient with low literacy who sorts by color demands pharmacist-led, teach-back-verified counseling with a visual schedule and early check-in — the standard that prevents post-discharge adverse drug events. A printout, delegating to the son without teaching, and a 3-month review each leave the immediate risks unmanaged.
stem: A 66-year-old man is discharged after a myocardial infarction on 9 medications, 5 of them new. He has low health literacy and sorts pills by color. His son lives nearby. The most effective discharge medication plan is:

options: No referral; she can manage on her own
Home health skilled nursing for wound assessment, negative pressure therapy monitoring, diabetes management, and coordination of the wound clinic follow-up
A wound clinic visit in 1 month with no interim support
Instructions to change the dressing herself
rationale: A diabetic foot ulcer on negative pressure wound therapy with a new device alarm she cannot troubleshoot requires skilled nursing: wound assessment, device monitoring, diabetes management, and wound clinic coordination. Self-management of negative pressure therapy without verified competence is unsafe, and a 1-month gap without support risks infection and device failure.
stem: A 59-year-old woman with diabetes is discharged with negative pressure wound therapy for a foot ulcer. She lives alone, the device alarmed twice in the hospital, and she does not know how to troubleshoot it. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call if she feels worse
Tell her to avoid all physical activity
Document the symptoms as expected
Escalate for same-day evaluation: new unilateral leg swelling and shortness of breath 1 week after knee arthroscopy while on anticoagulation are red flags for DVT or pulmonary embolism
rationale: New unilateral swelling with dyspnea after knee arthroscopy suggests venous thromboembolism despite anticoagulation — possibly treatment failure or nonadherence — requiring same-day evaluation. Reassurance, activity restriction, and passive documentation risk missing a life-threatening pulmonary embolism.
stem: A 62-year-old woman calls 1 week after discharge following a knee arthroscopy. She reports new swelling in the operative leg and shortness of breath when walking. She is taking rivaroxaban as prescribed. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with a standard diet handout
Tell him to avoid alcohol and discharge
Document the teaching as complete

Coordinate a pre-discharge bundle: teach-back on lifelong alcohol abstinence resources with a scheduled addiction follow-up, thiamine and nutrition plan with dietitian input, warning-sign teaching for recurrent pancreatitis, and a 1-week follow-up visit
rationale: Recurrent alcoholic pancreatitis with continued drinking, malnutrition, and missed visits requires a comprehensive bundle: addiction linkage with a scheduled intake, nutritional rehabilitation, warning-sign teaching, and early follow-up. A handout, vague alcohol advice, and documentation without verification each ignore the addiction and nutrition drivers of readmission.
stem: A 48-year-old man is discharged after his third episode of alcoholic pancreatitis. He continues to drink, is malnourished, and missed his last two clinic visits. The most effective discharge plan is:

options: Alert the prescriber: the home dose of glipizide with new poor oral intake and weight loss risks severe hypoglycemia, and the diabetes regimen needs revision before discharge
Continue glipizide since it was a home medication
Tell her to take the glipizide only on days she eats well
Document the plan as safe
rationale: Continuing a full-dose sulfonylurea in a patient with new poor intake and weight loss invites severe hypoglycemia; the prescriber must revise the diabetes regimen for her changed clinical picture. Home-medication status does not make it safe, symptom-guided dosing without orders is unsafe, and silent documentation perpetuates the hazard.
stem: A 74-year-old woman with diabetes is discharged after a prolonged pneumonia admission. She has lost 12 pounds, is eating poorly, and her home glipizide 10 mg twice daily was continued on the discharge list. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Home health skilled nursing and physical therapy for continued rehabilitation, home safety assessment, and coordination of the neurology follow-up, plus a social work referral for caregiver support
A nursing home placement because of the cognitive changes
Outpatient physical therapy in 6 weeks
rationale: Post-stroke with new cognitive deficits, a fall, and an overwhelmed spouse needs skilled nursing plus PT: rehabilitation, home safety assessment, neurology coordination, and caregiver support via social work. Standard instructions ignore the cognitive and fall risks, nursing home placement is excessive, and delayed PT wastes the recovery window.
stem: A 72-year-old man is discharged after a stroke with new mild cognitive deficits. He fell once in the hospital, lives with his wife who is overwhelmed, and has a new walker. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to return if the redness spreads
Tell him to apply warm compresses and call back in 3 days
Document the call as routine
Escalate for urgent evaluation: rapidly spreading redness with fever and severe pain 2 days after discharge for cellulitis are red flags for necrotizing infection requiring prompt assessment
rationale: Rapidly spreading erythema with systemic signs after a cellulitis discharge suggests treatment failure or necrotizing soft tissue infection — a surgical emergency. Watchful waiting, compresses, and passive documentation risk delayed treatment of a life-threatening infection.
stem: A 58-year-old man calls 2 days after discharge for leg cellulitis. He reports rapidly spreading redness, fever of 102°F, and severe pain. He is taking cephalexin as prescribed. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell her to take the iron when she remembers
Document the counseling as complete

Provide teach-back counseling on taking iron on an empty stomach or with vitamin C, separating it from thyroid medication and calcium, and warning signs including black tarry stools versus expected darkening
rationale: Post-gastric bypass iron absorption is already impaired, and concurrent thyroid medication and calcium further reduce it; teach-back on timing, separation, and distinguishing expected stool darkening from melena is essential. Vague adherence advice, casual timing, and documentation without counseling each leave the anemia untreated and bleeding warning signs unrecognized.
stem: A 49-year-old woman is discharged after a gastric bypass revision with a new prescription for oral iron for anemia. She takes levothyroxine and calcium daily, all together in the morning. The nurse's best counseling is:

options: Verify return demonstration of the feeding tube flush and medication administration, confirm the formula delivery and pump operation, reconcile the crushed-medication list with the pharmacist, and schedule the 1-week follow-up before discharge
Give him the home health phone number and discharge
Tell him to watch the training video at home
Schedule the follow-up for 1 month out
rationale: A new gastrostomy tube with a pump, a crushed-medication list, and a nervous spouse requires verified competence (return demonstration), confirmed supplies and equipment, pharmacist reconciliation of crushable drugs, and early follow-up — the readiness bundle for home enteral therapy. A phone number, a video, and a 1-month gap each leave critical safety holes.
stem: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for discharge with a new gastrostomy tube after a stroke with dysphagia. He will receive pump feeds and 6 crushed medications. His wife is nervous about the pump. The nurse's priority before discharge is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the clinic with questions
A 48-hour post-discharge phone call, a 7-day visit with INR and hemoglobin recheck, teach-back on bleeding precautions and the warfarin diet, and confirmation of transportation
A 1-month follow-up appointment
Instructions to go to the emergency department for any bruising
rationale: Restarting warfarin after a GI bleed is a high-risk transition requiring early phone contact, a 7-day visit with INR and hemoglobin surveillance, verified bleeding-precaution understanding, and solved transportation. A 1-month gap misses the rebleed and over-anticoagulation windows, emergency department instructions are not follow-up, and vague clinic instructions do not verify understanding.
stem: A 69-year-old man is discharged after a gastrointestinal bleed. His warfarin for atrial fibrillation was held and is to restart in 1 week. He lives alone and has no transportation. The most effective readmission prevention plan is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the daughter to hire a private caregiver
Home health skilled nursing for behavioral assessment, medication management, caregiver training and respite coordination, and safety planning
A memory care facility placement immediately
rationale: New behavioral disturbances with wandering in dementia, plus a frightened and exhausted daughter, require skilled nursing: behavioral assessment, medication review, caregiver training, respite coordination, and safety planning. Standard instructions and a private caregiver do not provide skilled assessment, and immediate facility placement bypasses less restrictive home supports.
stem: A 82-year-old woman with dementia is discharged after a urinary tract infection. She is newly agitated, wanders at night, and her daughter is frightened and exhausted. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to return if she feels faint
Tell her the dizziness is from the new medication and will resolve
Document the call as routine
Escalate for same-day evaluation: dizziness with a heart rate of 42 on a new beta-blocker after MI is a red flag for symptomatic bradycardia requiring prompt assessment
rationale: Symptomatic bradycardia with a heart rate of 42 on a newly started beta-blocker after MI requires same-day evaluation for dose adjustment or alternative therapy. Reassurance, normalization, and passive documentation risk syncope, falls, or cardiac compromise.
stem: A 67-year-old woman calls 4 days after discharge following a myocardial infarction. She reports dizziness when standing and her home blood pressure cuff shows a heart rate of 42. She was started on metoprolol. The nurse's priority is:

options: Coordinate a palliative care consult for goals-of-care clarification, advance directive completion, and home hospice evaluation before discharge
Discharge with the standard heart failure instructions
Tell the family to decide about hospice after discharge
Document the prognosis discussion as complete
rationale: Advanced heart failure with recurrent hospitalizations, declining function, and conflicting family goals requires inpatient palliative care: goals clarification, advance directives, and hospice evaluation before discharge — not deferred decisions. Standard instructions ignore the goals conflict, deferring the decision abandons the family, and documentation without action resolves nothing.
stem: A 78-year-old man with advanced heart failure is ready for discharge after his fourth hospitalization this year. He is weaker with each admission, and his family disagrees about future hospitalizations. The nurse's best coordination action is:

options: Tell her to take both antihypertensives for better control
Escalate to the prescriber: duplicate ACE inhibitor therapy risks hyperkalemia, hypotension, and renal injury, and one agent must be discontinued
Document the duplication as intentional
Advise her to alternate the medications daily
rationale: Concurrent lisinopril and enalapril is duplicate ACE inhibitor therapy with compounded risks of hyperkalemia, hypotension, and acute kidney injury; the prescriber must discontinue one. Taking both, alternating, and documenting without questioning each perpetuate a dangerous duplication.
stem: A 66-year-old woman with hypertension is discharged after pneumonia. Her home lisinopril 10 mg daily was continued, and the discharge list adds enalapril 5 mg daily. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell him to use the stairs one at a time
Home health skilled nursing and occupational therapy for ADL retraining, adaptive equipment assessment, energy conservation teaching, and coordination of the pulmonology follow-up
A pulmonary rehabilitation referral in 3 months with no interim support
rationale: Severe COPD with new oxygen, ADL dependence, and a small apartment with stairs needs skilled nursing plus OT: ADL retraining, equipment assessment, energy conservation, and pulmonology coordination. Standard instructions and stair advice do not address the functional deficits, and delayed rehab alone misses the immediate transition needs.
stem: A 74-year-old man with severe COPD is discharged on new home oxygen. He needs help with bathing and dressing, lives in a second-floor apartment, and is anxious about managing the oxygen. The best referral is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call if the wound opens
Tell her the drainage is normal and will resolve
Document the call as routine

Escalate for urgent evaluation: wound separation with purulent drainage and fever 10 days after hysterectomy are red flags for surgical site infection or fascial dehiscence requiring prompt assessment
rationale: Wound separation with purulent drainage and fever after hysterectomy suggests deep surgical site infection or fascial dehiscence — a surgical emergency. Reassurance, normalization, and passive documentation risk delayed treatment of a potentially life-threatening complication.
stem: A 54-year-old woman calls 10 days after discharge following an abdominal hysterectomy. She reports the incision has opened slightly with yellow drainage and she has a fever of 101°F. The nurse's priority is:

options: Hold discharge and escalate: she cannot explain the insulin dosing or demonstrate the injection, so she does not meet medication readiness criteria; arrange diabetes educator teach-back and confirm understanding
Document the teaching as complete
Give her a prefilled insulin pen and discharge
Schedule a diabetes class for next month
rationale: A new insulin start without demonstrated dosing understanding or injection technique is not safe for discharge — dosing errors cause hypoglycemia or DKA. Readiness requires diabetes educator teach-back with verified competence; a pen without teaching, documentation without verification, and a deferred class each leave life-threatening gaps.
stem: A 61-year-old woman is scheduled for discharge after a hyperglycemic emergency. She was started on insulin glargine and lispro but cannot explain the dosing schedule or demonstrate an injection. She lives alone. The nurse's best action is:

options: Discharge with instructions to avoid potassium-rich foods
Notify the prescriber: spironolactone plus lisinopril plus potassium supplement with a potassium of 5.6 is a dangerous combination, and the regimen needs urgent revision
Tell him the potassium will normalize on its own
Document the laboratory value and take no action
rationale: A potassium of 5.6 on spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor plus supplementation is a hyperkalemia emergency in the making; the prescriber must urgently revise the regimen. Dietary advice alone is insufficient, spontaneous normalization cannot be assumed, and silent documentation leaves him at risk for a fatal arrhythmia.
stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure is discharged on spironolactone, lisinopril, and a potassium supplement. His discharge potassium is 5.6 mEq/L. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
A 7-day follow-up visit with the reconciled medication list, teach-back on the steroid taper and glucose monitoring, a written sick-day plan, and a 48-hour check-in call
A 1-month follow-up appointment
Instructions to call 911 for high blood sugar
rationale: New diabetes on steroids with low literacy and no monitoring supplies needs early follow-up with reconciliation, verified taper and glucose understanding, a sick-day plan, and early check-in. A 1-month gap misses the steroid and glycemic risks, 911 instructions are not follow-up, and a bare handout does not verify understanding.
stem: A 57-year-old man is discharged after a COPD exacerbation treated with systemic steroids. He was newly diagnosed with diabetes, has low health literacy, and no glucose meter. The most effective readmission prevention plan is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the husband to call 911 if she stops breathing
Document the plan as safe

Verify return demonstration of the suction machine and backup suction, confirm the emergency plan and 24-hour contacts, reconcile the secretion management medications, and coordinate home health nursing with tracheostomy expertise
rationale: A new tracheostomy with thick secretions, a prior mucus plug, and an anxious spouse requires verified suction competence, backup equipment, a clear emergency plan, reconciled medications, and skilled home nursing — the readiness bundle for a high-risk airway. Standard instructions, 911-only guidance, and documenting an unverified plan as safe each leave life-threatening gaps.
stem: A 64-year-old woman is scheduled for discharge with a new tracheostomy after prolonged intubation. She has thick secretions, had a mucus plug in the hospital, and her husband is anxious about suctioning. The nurse's priority before discharge is:

options: Coordinate a case management referral to verify the prior authorization, confirm the specialty pharmacy delivery, reconcile the biologic with her medication list, and schedule the 2-week follow-up before discharge
Give her the prescription and discharge
Tell her to call the insurance company herself
Document the plan as complete
rationale: A new biologic for rheumatoid arthritis requires prior authorization, specialty pharmacy coordination, interaction review, and early follow-up — all arranged before discharge to avoid a therapy gap. A bare prescription, self-navigation of insurance, and documentation without verification each risk a failed start.
stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is discharged with a new prescription for a biologic agent. It requires prior authorization and specialty pharmacy dispensing. She has no follow-up scheduled. The nurse's best action is:

options: Tell him to take the colchicine daily for prevention
Escalate to the prescriber and pharmacist: colchicine plus newly started clarithromycin markedly raises the risk of colchicine toxicity, and the combination needs revision
Document the combination as safe
Advise him to halve the colchicine dose on his own
rationale: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, markedly raising colchicine levels with risk of fatal toxicity including myopathy and bone marrow suppression; the prescriber and pharmacist must revise the combination. Daily colchicine without guidance, silent documentation, and unsupervised dose-halving are all unsafe.
stem: A 68-year-old man with gout is discharged on colchicine. His home list was continued and clarithromycin was newly started for pneumonia. The nurse recognizes the interaction. The priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the family the ICU team will call with updates

A structured handoff using a standardized tool that includes the code status, pending test results, active drips and lines, and the plan of care, with an opportunity for the receiving nurse to ask questions
A brief verbal report at the bedside without documentation
rationale: ICU-to-floor transfers are high-risk transitions; a structured handoff with a standardized tool covering code status, pending results, lines and drips, and the care plan — with read-back and questions — is the evidence-based standard that prevents information loss. Standard discharge instructions do not apply to a unit transfer, deferred ICU calls leave the floor nurse uninformed, and an undocumented brief report invites critical omissions.
stem: A 66-year-old man is transferred from the ICU to the medical-surgical floor after sepsis. He has a central line, is on a norepinephrine wean, and has pending blood cultures. His code status is full. The most effective handoff practice is:

options: Discharge with instructions to follow up as needed
Tell her the emergency department will fax the records
Document the transfer as complete

Ensure the receiving facility gets a complete transfer packet: the reconciled medication list, advance directives, recent labs and imaging, wound and device orders, and a direct nurse-to-nurse handoff call
rationale: Interfacility transfers fail most often on incomplete information; a complete transfer packet with the reconciled list, directives, labs, device orders, and a live nurse-to-nurse handoff is the standard that prevents errors at the receiving facility. Vague follow-up instructions, deferred faxing, and documentation without confirmation each leave the receiving team without critical information.
stem: A 79-year-old woman with dementia is transferred from the emergency department to a skilled nursing facility for a short rehabilitation stay. She has 10 medications, a stage 2 pressure injury, and a urinary catheter. The nurse's priority to ensure information continuity is:

options: Call the primary care physician's office before discharge to transmit the reconciled medication list, pending test results with a follow-up plan, and the 7-day appointment, and document the communication
Give the patient a copy of the discharge summary and assume the physician will receive it
Tell the patient to schedule her own follow-up
Document the discharge as complete
rationale: Closing the loop with the primary care physician before discharge — transmitting the reconciled list, pending results with a plan, and the scheduled visit — is the core of hospital-to-home information continuity. Assuming electronic transmission, delegating scheduling to a complex patient, and documenting without communicating each leave the outpatient team uninformed.
stem: A 72-year-old woman is discharged after heart failure exacerbation. She has pending thyroid labs, 9 medications with 3 changes, and a 7-day follow-up appointment. Her primary care physician is in a different health system. The best action to ensure information continuity is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions

A warm handoff call between the hospital nurse and the home health nurse covering the wound status, the reconciled medication list, pending labs, and the follow-up plan, plus a written summary the patient keeps
A fax of the face sheet to the home health agency
Instructions for the patient to explain her history to the home health nurse
rationale: A new complex wound with a visiting nurse starting in 2 days needs a warm handoff call covering wound status, medications, pending labs, and the plan — plus a written patient-held summary — so the home nurse starts with complete information. Standard instructions, a face-sheet fax, and asking the patient to retell her history each risk critical information loss.
stem: A 68-year-old woman is discharged with a complex abdominal wound requiring packing. Home health nursing starts in 2 days. She has a new antibiotic, pending wound culture results, and a follow-up appointment. The most effective transition practice is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the lab for results
Tell him the results will be posted to the portal

A documented pending-result plan: the ordering provider is notified, the patient receives written instructions on how and when results will be communicated, and the primary care physician is looped in before discharge
Document the pending test and discharge
rationale: Pending biopsy results at discharge require a documented closed-loop plan: provider notification responsibility, written patient instructions on result communication, and PCP linkage — the standard that prevents lost results. Portal-only or lab-call instructions place the burden on the patient, and documenting without a communication plan leaves the result to fall through the cracks.
stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged after a liver biopsy. The pathology results are pending and will take 5 days. He is anxious about the results. The nurse's priority to ensure information continuity is:

options: Give a brief verbal report and leave
Document the handoff in the chart only
Have the oncoming nurse read the chart independently
Use a standardized bedside handoff that includes the patient's goals, pending tasks, abnormal trends, and contingency plans, with the patient and family participating
rationale: Bedside handoff with a standardized structure — goals, pending tasks, trends, contingencies — and patient and family participation is the evidence-based standard that reduces errors and engages the patient. A brief verbal report, chart-only documentation, and independent chart reading each omit the interactive verification and patient voice that make handoffs safe.
stem: A 74-year-old man with heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and diabetes is handed off at shift change. He has pending morning labs, a new insulin regimen, and his daughter is at the bedside. The safest handoff practice is:

options: Ensure the discharge summary explicitly states the indication, target INR range, planned duration, and follow-up monitoring plan, and that the primary care physician receives it before the first post-discharge visit
Give the patient a warfarin education booklet and discharge
Tell the patient to ask his physician about the duration
Document the warfarin order as continued
rationale: Warfarin started for a new DVT requires explicit documentation of indication, INR target, duration, and monitoring in the discharge summary transmitted to the PCP — without it, the outpatient team cannot safely manage the therapy. A booklet alone, delegating the question to the patient, and documentation without transmission each leave the transition incomplete.
stem: A 63-year-old man is discharged on new warfarin therapy for a deep vein thrombosis. His primary care physician will manage the anticoagulation. The nurse's priority to ensure safe information continuity is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions

A structured discharge summary transmitted to the dialysis center within 24 hours covering the infection, the catheter exchange, antibiotic course, and reconciled medication changes, plus a nurse-to-nurse call
A verbal report to the patient to relay to the dialysis center
Instructions for the dialysis center to check the portal
rationale: A hemodialysis patient returning to the center after a catheter infection needs a structured summary transmitted within 24 hours plus a nurse-to-nurse call — the dialysis team must know the infection history, catheter details, antibiotics, and medication changes to safely resume care. Standard instructions, patient-relayed reports, and portal-checking each risk critical gaps in a high-risk handoff.
stem: A 70-year-old man on hemodialysis is discharged after a tunneled catheter exchange for bacteremia. He returns to the dialysis center in 2 days. The most effective information continuity practice is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call 911 for chest pain

A reconciled problem list, the updated medication list with reasons for changes, pending stress test results with a follow-up plan, and the cardiology appointment transmitted to the primary care physician before discharge
A copy of the discharge instructions for the patient only
Instructions for the patient to summarize the hospitalization for her physician
rationale: A complex cardiac admission with medication changes and pending tests needs the full information package transmitted to the PCP before discharge: reconciled problem list, medication changes with rationales, pending results with a plan, and the scheduled appointment. 911-only guidance, patient-only copies, and asking the patient to summarize each leave the outpatient team without the clinical detail needed for safe follow-up.
stem: A 66-year-old woman is discharged after a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction. She has 4 medication changes, a pending outpatient stress test, and a cardiology appointment in 2 weeks. Her primary care physician needs the full picture. The best transition practice is:

options: Give a quick verbal update at the nurses' station
Document the transfer note and leave
Have the floor nurse review the chart on arrival

Perform a structured handoff at the bedside including the airway plan, sedation wean status, lines and drains, pending results, and family communication preferences, with read-back from the receiving nurse
rationale: Post-ICU transfers after prolonged ventilation carry airway, sedation, line, and communication complexities that demand a structured bedside handoff with read-back — the standard that prevents information loss during high-acuity transitions. A quick verbal update, chart-only documentation, and independent chart review each omit the interactive verification that catches critical details.
stem: A 58-year-old man is transferred from the ICU to the step-down unit after prolonged mechanical ventilation for ARDS. He has a tracheostomy, is weaning from sedation, and has multiple lines. The safest handoff practice is:

options: Confirm the receiving nurse gets a complete report including the insulin pump settings, the hypoglycemia action plan, pending labs, and the endocrinology follow-up, with an opportunity for questions
Send the patient with the chart and assume the report is sufficient
Give a brief verbal report without the pump details
Document the transfer as complete
rationale: An insulin pump patient transferring units needs a complete report with pump settings, the hypoglycemia plan, pending labs, and follow-up — pump details are safety-critical and cannot be assumed from the chart. A chart-only transfer, a report omitting pump settings, and documentation without confirmation each risk a dangerous dosing error.
stem: A 47-year-old man with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump is transferred from the emergency department to the medical-surgical floor for cellulitis treatment. The most effective handoff practice is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions

A complete device handoff packet for the home health nurse: the wound VAC settings, dressing change schedule, alarm troubleshooting guide, the reconciled medication list, and a nurse-to-nurse call before the first visit
A verbal report to the patient about the device
Instructions for the home health nurse to read the manual
