rationale: A wound VAC at home requires a complete device handoff: settings, schedule, troubleshooting, medications, and a nurse-to-nurse call before the first visit — the standard that ensures the home nurse can safely manage the technology. Standard instructions, patient-relayed device details, and manual-reading each leave the home nurse unprepared for a complex device.
stem: A 61-year-old man is discharged with a wound VAC for a sacral pressure injury. Home health nursing starts the next day. The nurse has never managed this patient's device. The best transition practice is:

options: Discharge with instructions to call the clinic with questions
Tell the patient the oncologist will receive the records automatically
A transmitted treatment summary including the chemotherapy regimen, cycle dates, nadir precautions, the reconciled medication list, and the oncology follow-up plan, with confirmation of receipt
A copy of the discharge summary for the patient only
rationale: A patient discharged mid-chemotherapy needs a transmitted treatment summary — regimen, cycle dates, nadir precautions, medications, follow-up — with confirmed receipt by the outpatient oncology team. Assuming automatic transmission, patient-only copies, and vague clinic instructions each risk a gap in a therapy where timing and toxicity monitoring are critical.
stem: A 55-year-old woman is discharged between chemotherapy cycles for breast cancer. She had neutropenic fever during this admission. Her outpatient oncologist needs the full treatment picture. The most effective information continuity practice is:

options: Give a brief report and return to the unit
Document the handoff and leave
Have the PACU nurse read the operative note independently
Perform a structured handoff including the anesthesia course, airway status, pain management plan, lines and drains, pending labs, and the surgeon's postoperative orders, with read-back
rationale: PACU-to-floor transfers after major surgery require a structured handoff covering anesthesia, airway, pain plan, lines, drains, labs, and orders with read-back — the standard that prevents postoperative information loss. A brief report, chart-only documentation, and independent note-reading each omit the interactive verification that catches critical postoperative details.
stem: A 69-year-old woman is transferred from the PACU to the surgical floor after an open colectomy. She has an epidural, a Jackson-Pratt drain, and pending hemoglobin results. The safest handoff practice is:

options: Verify the skilled nursing facility receives the reconciled medication list, the fall-risk assessment, the therapy recommendations, and the follow-up appointments, with a nurse-to-nurse handoff call
Send the patient with a copy of the discharge instructions
Tell the facility to call with questions
Document the transfer as complete
rationale: A post-hip-fracture transfer to skilled nursing needs verified transmission of the reconciled list, fall-risk assessment, therapy plan, and appointments plus a live handoff call — the bundle that prevents the medication errors and missed therapy that plague facility transitions. A patient-carried copy, deferred questions, and documentation without confirmation each leave the receiving team under-informed.
stem: A 80-year-old man is transferred to a skilled nursing facility after a hip fracture repair. He has 8 medications, is a high fall risk, and needs continued physical therapy. The best practice to ensure information continuity is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions

A structured sign-out to the covering provider that includes the patient's active issues, pending morning labs and imaging, contingency plans for the chest pain workup, and code status, with an opportunity for questions
A brief text message with the room numbers
Instructions for the covering provider to read the charts
rationale: Night-shift coverage of a chest pain workup with pending troponins requires a structured sign-out: active issues, pending studies, contingency plans, and code status with interactive questions — the standard that prevents overnight errors. Standard instructions do not apply, a room-number text omits clinical content, and chart-reading alone misses the contingency thinking.
stem: A 62-year-old man admitted with chest pain has pending serial troponins overnight. The day nurse signs out to the night covering provider. The safest handoff practice is:

options: Discharge with instructions to follow up as needed
Tell the family the records will be sent eventually

A complete transfer summary transmitted before transport: the reconciled medication list, code status and goals-of-care notes, recent labs and imaging, device and wound orders, and a nurse-to-nurse handoff call
A copy of the face sheet sent with the patient
rationale: An interfacility transfer of a ventilated, multi-device patient requires a complete summary transmitted before transport plus a live handoff call — the standard that ensures the LTACH team can safely assume care on arrival. Vague follow-up instructions, deferred records, and a face sheet alone each leave the receiving team without life-sustaining details.
stem: A 71-year-old man with a tracheostomy, gastrostomy tube, and wound VAC is transferred to a long-term acute care hospital. The most effective information continuity practice is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the patient to bring all pill bottles to the visit
Document the medication list as final

Perform a complete medication reconciliation at the first post-discharge visit: compare the discharge list against what the patient is actually taking, resolve discrepancies with the pharmacist, and update the primary care record
rationale: The first post-discharge visit is the critical safety checkpoint where the discharge list meets reality — comparing it against actual home use with pharmacist support catches the duplications, omissions, and misunderstandings that drive readmissions. Standard instructions, bottle-bringing without a structured review, and treating the discharge list as final each miss the reconciliation opportunity.
stem: A 75-year-old woman is seen in clinic 1 week after discharge for pneumonia. She brings 12 pill bottles, some of which do not match the discharge list. The most effective continuity practice at this visit is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions

A closed-loop pending-result workflow: the responsible provider is named, the patient gets written instructions on result timing and contact, the primary care physician is notified, and receipt is documented
A verbal promise to call the patient with results
Instructions for the patient to check the portal daily
rationale: A pending lung nodule biopsy at discharge needs a closed-loop workflow: a named responsible provider, written patient instructions, PCP notification, and documented receipt — the standard that prevents lost critical results. A verbal promise, portal-only checking, and standard instructions each leave the result vulnerable to falling through the cracks.
stem: A 64-year-old man is discharged after a lung nodule biopsy. The pathology results are pending for 7 days. He is anxious and asks how he will learn the results. The nurse's priority is:

options: Discharge with the standard printed instructions
Tell the home health nurse to call with questions
A nurse-to-nurse handoff call covering the peritoneal dialysis prescription, the exit-site status, the reconciled medication list, and the clinic follow-up, plus a written summary for the patient
A fax of the dialysis orders to the agency
rationale: A new peritoneal dialysis patient starting home health needs a nurse-to-nurse handoff covering the dialysis prescription, exit-site status, medications, and follow-up plus a patient-held written summary — the standard that ensures the home nurse starts with complete, accurate information. Standard instructions, deferred questions, and a faxed order sheet alone each risk technique errors and infection.
stem: A 55-year-old man is discharged to start peritoneal dialysis at home with home health nursing support. The home health nurse has not cared for this patient before. The most effective transition practice is:

options: Skilled nursing facility for short-term rehabilitation
Inpatient rehabilitation facility for 3 hours of daily therapy
Home with home health aide visits twice weekly
Long-term acute care hospital for continued medical management
rationale: SNF is appropriate: she needs daily skilled nursing/PT but not physician-level daily management or the 3-hour therapy intensity of IRF. IRF requires the ability to tolerate intensive therapy and a qualifying diagnosis; home with an aide alone is unsafe given stairs, cognition, and dependence. LTAC is for prolonged medically complex care, not rehab.
stem: A 78-year-old woman post ORIF of a left hip fracture is medically stable on postoperative day 3. She lives alone in a two-story home with 14 steps to the bathroom, has mild cognitive impairment, and can bear weight as tolerated but cannot yet transfer independently. She needs daily physical therapy and wound checks for 2 more weeks. Which discharge destination best matches her needs?

options: Skilled nursing facility for wound care and rehabilitation
Inpatient rehabilitation facility for ventilator weaning
Home with home health nursing for IV antibiotics
Long-term acute care hospital for prolonged complex medical management
rationale: LTAC is designed for medically complex patients needing an average stay of 25+ days with daily physician oversight, such as prolonged ventilator weaning, complex wounds, and extended IV antibiotics. SNFs cannot manage ongoing ventilator weaning with tracheostomy at this acuity, IRF focuses on intensive rehabilitation rather than prolonged medical management, and home health cannot support ventilator weaning.
stem: A 64-year-old man is on day 12 of a medical-surgical unit stay with ventilator weaning in progress via tracheostomy, stage 4 sacral pressure injury requiring daily dressing changes, and IV antibiotics for osteomyelitis expected for 4 more weeks. He is hemodynamically stable but will need weeks of continued skilled medical care. Which setting is the most appropriate next level of care?

options: She has Medicare coverage that requires a 3-day qualifying hospital stay
She can tolerate 3 hours of therapy per day across at least two disciplines
She needs only wound care and medication management
She prefers a facility closer to her home
rationale: IRF admission requires the patient to tolerate an intensive therapy program, generally 3 hours/day across at least two disciplines, with a need for daily physician oversight and a coordinated multidisciplinary team. Insurance rules and preference are not clinical criteria; needing only wound care/meds points to SNF, not IRF. Motivation and potential for improvement support IRF candidacy.
stem: A 59-year-old woman post left middle cerebral artery stroke has right-sided hemiparesis, moderate expressive aphasia, and requires moderate assistance with transfers. She was previously independent, is highly motivated, and her family can support her. She needs intensive multidisciplinary therapy. Which criterion makes her a strong candidate for inpatient rehabilitation facility admission rather than SNF?

options: The patient's room number and the names of her visitors
A reconciled medication list with the reason each drug was started, changed, or stopped
The hospital's visiting hours and cafeteria location
The patient's preferred television channels
rationale: Medication reconciliation with start/change/stop rationales is a core continuity element that prevents errors during transitions; it is a leading source of post-discharge harm. Room numbers, visitor names, visiting hours, and TV preferences do not affect clinical safety at the receiving facility.
stem: A nurse is giving a warm handoff report to the receiving SNF nurse for a patient with heart failure, a stage 3 heel ulcer, and a new PICC for IV diuretics. Which element is most essential to include for information continuity across this transition?

options: He is homebound, requiring considerable effort to leave home, and needs intermittent skilled nursing
He has a willing family caregiver available 24 hours a day
He owns his home and has reliable transportation
He prefers home visits over clinic visits
rationale: Medicare home health requires the patient to be homebound and need intermittent skilled nursing or therapy. A 24-hour caregiver, home ownership, transportation, or preference alone do not establish eligibility; homebound status plus skilled need does.
stem: A 71-year-old man with COPD is discharged after an exacerbation. He lives with his wife, is short of breath with minimal exertion, and needs nursing visits for medication teaching, pulse oximetry monitoring, and coordination of a home oxygen delivery that was delayed. He is reluctant to leave the house. Which criterion supports home health rather than outpatient follow-up?

options: Provide a printed diet handout at discharge
Schedule a follow-up appointment within 7 days and use teach-back for daily weights and red-flag symptoms
Recommend over-the-counter supplements for energy
Advise him to call 911 only if chest pain occurs
rationale: Early follow-up within 7 days combined with teach-back on self-monitoring and red flags is the evidence-based bundle that most reduces readmissions. A handout alone without comprehension checks, supplements, and incomplete red-flag guidance (HF warning signs include rapid weight gain, dyspnea, edema) are inadequate.
stem: During discharge planning for a 66-year-old man with newly diagnosed heart failure, low health literacy, and no primary care follow-up scheduled, the nurse identifies the highest-yield intervention to reduce 30-day readmission. Which action should the nurse prioritize?

options: Discharge as planned since family is the best caregiver option
Assess the daughter's willingness and ability, and arrange caregiver training plus home health nursing support
Ask the daughter to hire a private aide without assessing her capacity
Delay discharge indefinitely until the daughter quits her job
rationale: Assessing caregiver readiness and arranging training plus skilled home health support addresses the identified gap safely. Assuming family can manage, delegating without assessment, or demanding the caregiver quit work are inappropriate; the nurse must verify capability and build support into the plan.
stem: An 82-year-old man with dementia is being discharged to his daughter's home. The daughter works full-time, has never managed medications, and says, 'I'll figure it out.' The patient needs twice-daily insulin and wound care. What is the nurse's priority before discharge?

options: Assume the SNF will sort out the discrepancies on admission
Document the hold history and restart date clearly in the transfer summary and verbally highlight it in handoff
Omit the apixaban from the list since it was held
Tell the patient to remind the SNF nurse about the hold
rationale: Anticoagulant holds and restarts are high-risk transitions; the nurse must explicitly document and verbally hand off the hold history to prevent duplicate or missed dosing. Assuming the SNF will catch it, omitting the drug, or relying on the patient are all unsafe.
stem: A patient being transferred to a SNF takes 14 medications including apixaban, metoprolol, and insulin. The MAR shows the apixaban was held for 2 days pre-procedure and restarted yesterday. The SNF admission orders list all home medications without noting the hold. What should the transferring nurse do?

options: Hospice referral for comfort-focused care at home
Another cycle of inpatient chemotherapy
LTAC admission for continued aggressive treatment
SNF placement for rehabilitation
rationale: Her goals (comfort, home), prognosis, and pattern of recurrent hospitalizations make hospice the appropriate transition; it provides symptom management and support at home. Further chemotherapy, LTAC, or SNF rehab contradict her stated goals and prognosis.
stem: A 74-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has had three hospitalizations in 2 months for pain crises and bowel obstruction. She says she is tired of hospitals and wants to be comfortable at home. Her oncologist estimates prognosis of weeks to months. Which transition best aligns with her goals?

options: The patient's age, diagnosis, and surgical date
That the home nurse should assess the sternal wound, monitor for amiodarone side effects, and reinforce the weight-monitoring plan at the first visit
The patient's insurance policy number
A list of all hospital staff who cared for the patient
rationale: The Recommendation component states what the receiver should do — specific assessments and actions for the first visit. Age/diagnosis/surgical date belong in Background, insurance in administrative data, and staff names are irrelevant to the plan of care.
stem: A nurse calls the home health agency to initiate services for a post-CABG patient with a sternal wound, new-onset atrial fibrillation on amiodarone, and a 10-pound weight gain limit. Using a structured handoff, which information belongs in the 'Recommendation' portion?

options: Medicare covers SNF only after a 3-day qualifying inpatient stay, which he meets, and he needs daily skilled care
Medicare never covers SNF stays for pneumonia
Coverage depends only on his age, not the hospital stay
He must pay privately because antibiotics can be given at home
rationale: Medicare SNF coverage requires a 3-day qualifying inpatient stay (not observation) plus a need for daily skilled nursing or rehabilitation; his 4-day inpatient stay qualifies. Pneumonia is not an exclusion, age alone does not determine coverage, and medical need — not whether home administration is theoretically possible — drives the decision.
stem: A 70-year-old man was admitted as hospital inpatient for 4 days for pneumonia, then needs SNF care for deconditioning and continued IV antibiotics. His daughter asks whether Medicare will cover the SNF stay. What is the nurse's best response?

options: Schedule the next visit for the following week
Reinforce diuretic adherence, assess for worsening heart failure, and coordinate same-day provider contact
Tell her to double the furosemide dose on her own
Document the nonadherence and wait for the provider to notice
rationale: A 6-pound gain in 3 days with edema signals acute decompensation; the transitional care nurse must intervene now — reinforce adherence, assess severity, and arrange urgent provider contact. Waiting a week, unsupervised dose changes, or passive documentation risk hospitalization.
stem: A transitional care nurse follows a 68-year-old woman with diabetes and heart failure for 30 days post-discharge. At the first home visit, the patient has gained 6 pounds in 3 days, has 2+ pitting edema, and admits she stopped taking furosemide because it made her urinate too often. What is the transitional care nurse's priority action?

options: Assisted living facility with medication management services
Long-term acute care hospital
Inpatient rehabilitation facility
Acute inpatient hospice unit
rationale: Assisted living provides housing plus help with ADLs and medication reminders for patients who do not need daily skilled care. LTAC, IRF, and inpatient hospice all require skilled medical needs or intensive therapy she does not have.
stem: An 85-year-old woman with mild dementia, stable on medications, needs help with bathing, dressing, and medication reminders but no skilled nursing or daily therapy. Her family asks about placement options. Which setting fits?

options: The patient's meal preferences at the hospital
Ostomy self-care competency, recent output trends, and the warfarin indication with target INR
The name of the surgeon who performed the operation
The hospital unit's phone number
rationale: Without knowing what ostomy teaching was completed, output trends, and the warfarin indication/INR target, the SNF cannot safely continue either therapy — both carry high harm potential. Meal preferences, surgeon name, and unit phone number are secondary to clinical continuity.
stem: A patient with a new ileostomy, on warfarin, is transferred from the surgical unit to a SNF. The transfer packet includes orders and a medication list but no information about ostomy teaching completed, output trends, or warfarin indication and INR goal. What is the most important gap for the receiving nurse to close?

options: Praise him for stopping an unnecessary medication
Explain the taper prevents adrenal crisis and rebound flare, assess symptoms, and arrange provider guidance on completing or adjusting the taper
Tell him to restart the full dose immediately without assessment
Document his decision and end the call
rationale: Abruptly stopping a prednisone taper risks adrenal insufficiency and rebound exacerbation; the nurse must explain why the taper matters, assess current symptoms, and coordinate with the provider. Praising discontinuation, ordering an unsupervised restart, or passive documentation all miss the safety issue.
stem: A nurse makes a 48-hour post-discharge call to a 62-year-old man sent home after a COPD exacerbation with a new inhaler, prednisone taper, and smoking cessation counseling. He says he feels better and stopped the prednisone because 'steroids are bad.' What is the nurse's best response?

options: Whether the SNF has an arrangement for on-site or coordinated dialysis transportation
The color scheme of the facility rooms
Whether the facility allows visitors after 8 PM
The facility's cafeteria menu variety
rationale: Dialysis-dependent patients can only be placed where dialysis access is coordinated — either in-house or via reliable transport — or the placement fails. Room aesthetics, visiting hours, and menus are irrelevant to placement feasibility.
stem: A 58-year-old man on thrice-weekly hemodialysis is recovering from a below-knee amputation and needs wound care, prosthesis training, and continued dialysis. His home is 60 miles from the dialysis center and he cannot drive. Which placement consideration is most critical?

options: The patient states, 'I will take apixaban twice daily, seek care for unusual bleeding, and tell all my doctors and dentist I take a blood thinner'
The patient says, 'I understand everything, don't worry'
The patient repeats the drug name correctly
The patient nods while the nurse explains the medication
rationale: True teach-back requires the patient to explain back in his own words the dosing, warning signs, and precautions — not merely repeat a name, nod, or offer reassurance. Only the first option demonstrates comprehension of the critical safety points.
stem: Before discharging a 55-year-old man with new-onset atrial fibrillation on apixaban, the nurse uses teach-back. Which patient response demonstrates adequate understanding?

options: That the patient likes the SNF's visiting policy
That the SNF has the correct VAC unit, canisters, and dressing supplies available on admission day, with orders matching current settings
That the patient's family has toured the SNF
That the hospital bed is cleaned
rationale: Wound VAC continuity fails if supplies or matching orders are not ready at admission; verifying equipment, supplies, and orders prevents therapy interruption and infection risk. Visiting policy, family tours, and bed cleaning do not affect clinical continuity.
stem: A patient with an abdominal wound VAC set to 125 mmHg continuous suction is transferring to a SNF. The SNF confirms it can manage wound VACs. What must the hospital nurse verify before transfer?

options: Discharge with a 90-day supply and no follow-up
Coordinate a 7-day follow-up with psychiatry and primary care, provide a blister-packed medication organizer, and confirm the sister's understanding of the plan
Tell him to return to the ED if he feels unwell
Give him a pamphlet on diabetes
rationale: Early psychiatric and medical follow-up, adherence supports (blister packing), and confirmed caregiver understanding directly target his known pattern of discontinuation. A 90-day supply without follow-up, ED-only safety netting, or a pamphlet do not ensure continuity.
stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia and newly diagnosed diabetes is medically stable for discharge. He has a history of stopping antipsychotics when he feels better, and his sister will supervise medications. What is the most important transitional care intervention?

options: Schedule another pulmonary function test in 6 months
Refer to hospice, as his trajectory, prognosis, and goals align with hospice eligibility
Admit to LTAC for pulmonary rehabilitation
Increase his bronchodilator and discharge home
rationale: Recurrent hospitalizations, severe obstruction, weight loss, and a clear preference for no further hospitalization and dying at home meet hospice referral criteria. More testing, LTAC rehab, or routine discharge ignore his goals and prognosis.
stem: A 69-year-old man with end-stage COPD on 4L home oxygen has been followed by inpatient palliative care during three admissions this year. He now says he wants no more hospitalizations and to die at home. His FEV1 is 22% predicted and he has lost 15 pounds in 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step?

options: Home health nursing for intermittent skilled wound care with caregiver teaching
LTAC admission for wound management
Inpatient rehabilitation for ADL training
SNF placement for 24-hour supervision
rationale: Intermittent skilled need (dressing changes 3x/week) in an otherwise independent patient with a willing caregiver is the classic home health scenario. LTAC, IRF, and SNF all require daily skilled needs or intensive therapy she does not have.
stem: A 63-year-old woman post colectomy has a healing surgical incision, needs dressing changes three times weekly, and is otherwise independent in ADLs. She lives with her husband who is willing to learn. Which option best fits?

options: After the physical therapist clears him for discharge
On admission, with early assessment of home situation, support, and post-acute needs
The morning of discharge
Only if the patient requests it
rationale: Discharge planning begins on admission — early assessment of function, home environment, and support prevents delays and unsafe discharges. Waiting until therapy clearance, the morning of discharge, or patient request compresses planning and increases readmission risk.
stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted with a hip fracture requiring surgery. When should discharge planning begin?

options: Send her by private car to save time
Complete EMTALA-compliant transfer: stabilize to the extent possible, obtain accepting physician and facility agreement, and send records with qualified transport personnel
Transfer without records since the receiving team can start fresh
Have the family drive her to avoid ambulance cost
rationale: EMTALA requires appropriate screening, stabilization within capability, acceptance by the receiving physician/facility, medical records, and qualified personnel/equipment during transport. Private car or family transport and omitting records violate transfer requirements and endanger the patient.
stem: A 50-year-old woman with necrotizing fasciitis needs transfer from a rural hospital to a tertiary center for surgical debridement and ICU care. Which action is required for a safe, compliant transfer?

options: Whether her favorite nurse works at the SNF
Whether her stay was inpatient or observation, because observation days do not count toward the 3-day qualifying inpatient stay
What her room number was
Whether she liked the hospital food
rationale: Only inpatient days count toward Medicare's 3-day qualifying stay; observation status does not qualify, which directly determines SNF coverage. Nurse preference, room number, and food are irrelevant to coverage.
stem: A 67-year-old woman has been in the hospital 2 nights under observation status for chest pain, now ruled out. She needs SNF rehabilitation for deconditioning. What must the nurse clarify with the care team before promising Medicare SNF coverage?

options: Discharge to the street with prescriptions and standard instructions
Coordinate with social work for medical respite or shelter placement, simplify the regimen, and provide a written plan with a follow-up location
Keep him inpatient indefinitely until housing is found
Give him IV antibiotics to take with him
rationale: Social work coordination for medical respite/shelter, regimen simplification, and concrete follow-up addresses the barriers that would otherwise guarantee treatment failure. Street discharge with standard instructions, indefinite hospitalization, or sending IV antibiotics home are inappropriate or unsafe.
stem: A 54-year-old man experiencing homelessness is being discharged after cellulitis treatment requiring 5 more days of oral antibiotics. He has no phone and no reliable shelter. What is the most appropriate discharge coordination?

options: Transfer all records and assume he will adapt
Use a structured transition program: assess self-management skills, provide skills coaching, and overlap pediatric and adult teams with a warm handoff
Discharge him from pediatric care without a plan
Tell his parents to continue managing everything indefinitely
rationale: Structured transition with skills assessment, coaching, and overlapping teams prevents the well-documented drop-off in care during pediatric-to-adult transfer. Abrupt transfer, no plan, or indefinite parental management do not build the self-management he needs.
stem: A 21-year-old with cystic fibrosis and diabetes is transitioning from pediatric to adult care. He has never scheduled his own appointments or refilled prescriptions. What is the transitional care priority?

options: Keep her in the acute hospital for 6 weeks
Discharge to a SNF that can administer IV vancomycin with drug-level monitoring
Stop antibiotics since she feels better
Send her home with oral antibiotics instead
rationale: A SNF can provide daily skilled IV antibiotic administration with vancomycin trough monitoring at far lower cost than a 6-week acute stay. Stopping therapy risks relapse; substituting oral antibiotics without an order or susceptibility basis is unsafe.
stem: A 60-year-old woman needs 6 weeks of IV vancomycin for MRSA bacteremia via PICC, is otherwise stable, and walks independently. Her insurance denies home infusion. Which setting is most appropriate?

options: The POLST and goals-of-care documentation must accompany him and be reviewed with the SNF team and health care proxy
The POLST can stay in the hospital chart since the SNF will ask about code status later
His code status should be upgraded to full code for the transfer
Goals of care only matter in the ICU
rationale: POLST and goals-of-care documents must travel with the patient and be actively reviewed with the receiving team and proxy; otherwise unwanted intubation or hospitalization can occur. Leaving the POLST behind, changing code status for convenience, or limiting goals discussions to the ICU all break continuity of his wishes.
stem: A 76-year-old man with advanced dementia, admitted for aspiration pneumonia, has a POLST indicating comfort-focused measures and no intubation. He is transferring to a SNF. What is critical for continuity?

options: SNF for continued skilled nursing and gradual therapy progression
IRF for 3 hours of daily intensive therapy
Outpatient therapy three times a week
Home with no services
rationale: He needs 24-hour supervision and skilled care but cannot tolerate IRF-intensity therapy, making SNF the right level. IRF requires 3-hour tolerance, outpatient is unsafe given total dependence, and no services is unsafe.
stem: A 62-year-old man post ischemic stroke has dense left hemiplegia, requires total assistance for transfers, has new dysphagia on a modified diet, and needs 24-hour supervision. He cannot yet tolerate more than 30 minutes of therapy at a time. Which setting is most appropriate?

options: Tell her to skip the medications until she can afford them
Connect her with social work or pharmacy for prior authorization, patient assistance programs, or lower-cost alternatives, and notify the provider
Advise her to borrow medications from a neighbor
Document the cost barrier and take no further action
rationale: Cost-related nonadherence requires active intervention: social work/pharmacy can pursue prior authorization, assistance programs, or therapeutic alternatives, and the provider must know. Advising her to skip doses, borrow medications, or passive documentation all leave her unprotected from stroke and hyperglycemia.
stem: A patient is discharged on apixaban, atorvastatin, and a new insulin regimen. At the 72-hour follow-up call, she has not filled any prescriptions, saying the pharmacy quoted $340 and she cannot afford it. What should the nurse do?

options: The hospital cafeteria menu she preferred
The DKA precipitating factors, insulin regimen rationale, medication changes, new CKD diagnosis, and recommended follow-up labs and timing
The names of her hospital roommates
Her preferred appointment day of the week
rationale: The PCP needs the clinical narrative: DKA triggers, why insulin was started, what changed and why, the new CKD diagnosis, and what follow-up is needed — this closes the loop. Menus, roommates, and scheduling preferences do not support clinical continuity.
stem: A 58-year-old woman is discharged after DKA with new insulin, a changed metformin dose, and new CKD stage 3 noted on labs. Which information is most important to transmit to her primary care provider?

options: Her age alone determines she cannot benefit from rehab
An assessment of rehab potential, goals of care, and prognosis — considering whether skilled rehab can meaningfully improve function versus a palliative approach
Insurance authorization status is the only factor
Family preference alone determines the plan
rationale: Placement decisions must weigh realistic rehab potential, the patient's goals, and prognosis — not age alone, insurance alone, or family preference alone. With progressive disease and recurrent aspiration, the team must honestly assess whether rehab can help or whether palliative-focused care better serves her.
stem: A 90-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson disease, severe dysphagia requiring thickened liquids, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and progressive weight loss is being considered for SNF rehabilitation after her third admission in 2 months. Her son asks about aggressive rehab. What should guide the team's recommendation?

options: Document the missed appointment and wait for her to reschedule
Arrange a same-day telehealth or urgent clinic visit, connect her with transportation resources, and reinforce daily weight monitoring
Tell her to go to the ED for every weight gain
Discharge her from the practice for nonadherence
rationale: The nurse should solve the barrier — arrange timely clinical contact, link transportation resources, and reinforce self-monitoring — rather than passively document, overuse the ED, or punish the patient for a structural barrier.
stem: A 64-year-old woman with heart failure misses her 1-week post-discharge appointment because her car broke down and she has no other transport. Her weight is up 4 pounds. What is the best transitional care response?

options: Accept the placement since the SNF said it can handle wounds
Verify specific capability: NPWT experience, certified wound nurse availability, and supply access — and seek an alternative SNF if these are absent
Send the patient home with the wound VAC and no support
Remove the wound VAC before transfer
rationale: Vague assurance is not capability; the planner must verify NPWT experience, certified expertise, and supplies, or find a facility that has them. Accepting on assurance alone, discharging home unsupported, or discontinuing ordered therapy are all unsafe.
stem: A patient with a stage 4 pressure injury with tunneling, on negative-pressure wound therapy, needs SNF placement. The first SNF offered says it 'can handle wounds' but has no wound-certified nurse and has never managed NPWT. What should the discharge planner do?

options: Tell the SNF the summary will be dictated sometime next week
Provide a verbal summary now covering diagnoses, hospital course, pending tests, and follow-up plan, and expedite the written summary
Refuse to discuss the patient due to HIPAA
Ask the patient to explain his hospital course to the SNF
rationale: Care continuity requires timely information; a verbal summary of course, pending results, and plan plus an expedited written summary bridges the gap. Delaying a week, citing HIPAA for treatment-related communication (which is permitted), or relying on the patient are all inappropriate.
stem: A patient discharged Friday evening to a SNF arrives without a discharge summary; the SNF has only the transfer form. The SNF nurse calls the hospital Saturday morning. What is the best response?

options: Discharge him home on room air for 3 days
Delay discharge until oxygen is in the home or arrange an interim supply, verifying delivery before he leaves
Send him home and hope his breathing stays stable
Cancel the oxygen order since he looks comfortable
rationale: Discharging a patient who desaturates to 84% on room air without oxygen in place is unsafe; discharge must wait for confirmed delivery or an interim supply. Hoping for stability or canceling the order ignores objective hypoxemia.
stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD exacerbation is discharged on 2L home oxygen. The DME company says delivery will take 3 days. His SpO2 on 2L is 91%; on room air it drops to 84%. What should the nurse arrange?

options: Provide English-only written instructions since her son can translate
Use a qualified medical interpreter for discharge teaching, provide translated materials, and confirm understanding with teach-back through the interpreter
Skip detailed teaching to save time
Have the son sign that he understands without teaching
rationale: Qualified interpreters plus translated materials and teach-back ensure accurate comprehension; relying on family interpreters risks errors and omissions. English-only materials, skipping teaching, or a signature without teaching are unsafe.
stem: A 70-year-old Vietnamese-speaking woman is discharged after a stroke with new medications, a modified diet, and follow-up appointments. Her son interprets at home. What best supports a safe transition?

options: ED-to-SNF admission is never allowed
Whether she meets SNF medical-necessity criteria and payer requirements, and that a safe plan cannot be achieved with home services
Her favorite television shows
Whether the ED staff like the SNF
rationale: Direct ED-to-SNF placement is permissible when medical necessity and payer criteria are met and home discharge is unsafe; the decision rests on clinical need and coverage, not on prohibitions or preferences. Note Medicare typically requires a qualifying inpatient stay, so payer verification is essential.
stem: A 79-year-old woman is evaluated in the ED for a fall with no fracture, but she is newly unable to bear weight due to pain and deconditioning, lives alone, and cannot safely return home. The team considers direct ED-to-SNF admission. What is the key consideration?

options: Assume the culture will be negative
Assign clear ownership: who will check the result, the timeframe, and how the patient will be contacted with plan changes
Tell the patient cultures are rarely important
Wait for the patient to call with symptoms
rationale: Pending tests at discharge are a classic failure point; the safeguard is explicit ownership, timeframe, and a contact plan. Assuming negativity, minimizing importance, or waiting for symptoms all risk missed bacteremia.
stem: A patient is discharged to home with a pending blood culture that was drawn for fever on the day of discharge. The culture may grow an organism requiring antibiotic change. What is the most important transitional safeguard?

options: Increased number of consults ordered during admission
Reduced 30-day readmissions and improved patient-reported continuity of care
Longer lengths of stay
Higher patient satisfaction with hospital food
rationale: The Transitional Care Model targets readmission reduction and continuity for high-risk elders; those are its validated outcomes. More consults, longer stays, and food satisfaction are not model endpoints.
stem: A hospital implements the Transitional Care Model for high-risk older adults, with an advanced practice nurse following patients from admission through 30 days post-discharge. Which outcome best demonstrates the model's effectiveness?

options: LTAC admission for ongoing dialysis and medical management
SNF admission where dialysis can be coordinated, after confirming the facility accepts patients on thrice-weekly hemodialysis
Home discharge with outpatient dialysis and no nursing support
IRF admission for intensive amputation rehabilitation
rationale: She is medically stable and ambulatory with stable grafts, so she does not need LTAC-level medical management or IRF-intensity therapy. The correct SNF choice explicitly includes confirming dialysis coordination — the known placement barrier. Home discharge without support is unsafe given wound care needs and new medication regimen.
stem: A 66-year-old woman on thrice-weekly hemodialysis is discharged after a 5-day admission for hyperkalemia, now resolved. Her fistula is mature and stable, she walks independently, and her medications were significantly adjusted. She lives alone 25 miles from the dialysis center. Which discharge plan best balances her needs?

options: Teach the wife insulin injection technique, hypoglycemia recognition, and sick-day rules, confirming return demonstration
Give the wife a printed insulin sliding scale only
Tell the wife to ask the pharmacist later
Defer all teaching to the home health nurse
rationale: Insulin initiation requires hands-on teaching with return demonstration, hypoglycemia recognition, and sick-day rules before discharge; written scale alone is insufficient. Deferring to the pharmacist or home nurse delays essential safety knowledge, and printing alone does not verify learning.
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is discharged on a new basal-bolus insulin regimen after his first DKA episode. His wife will manage injections. What is the most important pre-discharge nursing action?

options: His COPD severity alone
His age and race
The combination of high-risk medication changes, low health literacy, limited support, and prior ED use
His preferred pharmacy location
rationale: Readmission risk is multifactorial: complex medication changes, low health literacy, living alone, and prior ED utilization together predict post-discharge failure. Single factors like COPD severity, age/race, or pharmacy choice do not capture transition risk as well as the composite.
stem: A case manager screens a 71-year-old man with COPD, heart failure, and diabetes for intensive transitional care follow-up. He lives alone, has low health literacy, was started on 6 new medications, and visited the ED twice last month. Which factor most strongly indicates he needs high-intensity transitional follow-up?

options: Repeat the instructions louder in English
Provide written instructions in Spanish, use a professional interpreter, and confirm understanding with teach-back
Ask a bilingual visitor in the hallway to translate
Discharge him since the medications are simple
rationale: Language-concordant discharge requires a professional interpreter, written materials in the patient's language, and teach-back; ad hoc hallway interpreters are unreliable and unsafe. Louder English, casual translators, or skipping teaching all risk misunderstanding of a new anticoagulant.
stem: A 63-year-old Spanish-speaking man is discharged on apixaban and atorvastatin after a TIA. He nods politely but cannot read the English discharge papers. What is the best approach to ensure safe transition?

options: Continue current plan since walking is the only metric that matters
Notify the provider: new purulent drainage and odor suggest surgical site infection requiring evaluation before or coordinated with placement
Apply more gauze and send him to the SNF
Remove the sutures at the bedside
rationale: New purulent drainage with odor is a red flag for surgical site infection; the plan must change to urgent evaluation rather than routine SNF transfer. More gauze, bedside suture removal, or ignoring the finding all miss a potentially limb- or life-threatening complication.
stem: A 70-year-old man is scheduled for SNF transfer after knee arthroplasty. During final assessment, the nurse notes new purulent drainage with odor from the incision, though he is afebrile and walking well. What should the nurse do?

options: A warm handoff: the hospital nurse calls the receiving home health nurse, reviews the plan, and the patient introduces his concerns directly
Mailing the discharge summary the following week
Assuming the home health agency will read the chart
Having the patient memorize his medication list
rationale: A warm handoff — direct nurse-to-nurse communication with patient participation — is the evidence-based standard for information continuity. Mailing later, assuming chart review, or relying on patient memory are passive and error-prone.
stem: A 75-year-old man with heart failure and CKD is discharged home with home health nursing. His daughter worries that 'nobody talks to each other.' What is the most effective way to ensure continuity between hospital and home health teams?

options: The number of visitors he had
The patient's functional status, equipment needs, caregiver capacity, and home safety assessment
The brand of his hospital bed
His meal tray preferences
rationale: Safe home discharge of a ventilated patient hinges on function, equipment readiness, trained caregivers, and home safety — the elements that determine whether the plan can actually be executed. Visitors, bed brands, and meals are irrelevant.
stem: A 55-year-old man with ALS on nocturnal BiPAP is transitioning home after respiratory optimization. He lives with his wife and adult son, both trained on the equipment. Which information is most important for the discharge plan?

options: Discharge as scheduled; anxiety does not affect safety
Assess specific fears, provide targeted education and coping strategies, and involve the spouse in the plan
Sedate the patient before discharge
Cancel the surgery
rationale: Pre-discharge anxiety about self-care should be explored and addressed with targeted teaching and support — it predicts poor adherence. Dismissing anxiety, sedating, or canceling surgery do not resolve the underlying readiness gap.
stem: A 60-year-old woman scheduled for discharge with a new colostomy tearfully says she is terrified to go home and 'cannot do this alone.' Her husband is willing to help. What is the best nursing response?

options: Increase his pain medication dose at home
Confirm a hospice or palliative home program is in place with 24-hour on-call support, and review the comfort medication kit
Tell the family to call 911 for uncontrolled pain
Discharge without a pain plan since hospice will handle everything
rationale: Transitioning a patient with uncontrolled cancer pain requires an active palliative/hospice plan with 24-hour support and a pre-stocked comfort kit before discharge. Simply increasing doses without a plan, defaulting to 911, or assuming hospice 'handles everything' without confirming setup are unsafe.
stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer has pain poorly controlled on oral opioids. He wishes to die at home. What is the most important element of his discharge plan?

options: Home health nursing for skilled wound assessment, dressing changes, and teaching
LTAC admission for hyperbaric oxygen therapy
IRF admission for gait training
Weekly ED visits for wound checks
rationale: She needs intermittent skilled nursing — exactly what home health provides — and she is otherwise independent. LTAC, IRF, and ED visits are inappropriate levels of care for an intermittent wound need.
stem: A 59-year-old woman with a diabetic foot ulcer needs offloading, dressing changes twice weekly, and diabetes teaching. She lives with her husband, walks with a cane, and her wound is not infected. Which service best meets her needs?

options: His insurance card number
A complete reconciled medication list, pending lab results with follow-up plan, and 7-day supply of critical medications
The name of the hospital CEO
A list of nearby restaurants
rationale: Interstate or rural transitions fail without medication continuity and pending-test follow-up; these are the core clinical handoff elements. Insurance numbers, executive names, and restaurants do not prevent post-transfer harm.
stem: A 72-year-old man is transferred from a critical access hospital to a tertiary center 200 miles away for urgent cardiac surgery. What is the most important information to send with him?

options: Tell her to stop the antihypertensives until she sees the doctor
Reinforce which medications to continue, explain the risks of stopping them, arrange early provider follow-up, and use teach-back
Agree that fewer medications are always better
Document her plan without intervening
rationale: Stopping antihypertensives and statins after MI risks rebound hypertension and recurrent events; the nurse must reinforce continuation, explain risks, and secure early follow-up. Agreeing with discontinuation or passive documentation endorses an unsafe plan.
stem: A 61-year-old woman discharged after MI says she plans to stop her metoprolol and atorvastatin because she 'feels fine and hates pills.' What is the nurse's best response?

options: The patient's favorite foods
The patient's baseline cognition, delirium risk, mobility level, fall history, and successful de-escalation strategies
The hospital's parking validation policy
The patient's preferred wake-up time
rationale: Behavioral continuity — baseline cognition, triggers, and what calms the patient — is what the SNF needs to prevent delirium, falls, and behavioral crises. Food preferences and logistics are secondary to safety-relevant behavioral information.
stem: An 84-year-old man with dementia and a history of sundowning is transferred to a SNF after hip fracture repair. He becomes agitated with unfamiliar routines. What information is most important in the handoff?

options: SNF placement for 24-hour skilled supervision and structured medication management
Independent living with a weekly pill organizer
Home with no services and a family visit on weekends
Assisted living without nursing oversight
rationale: Daily skilled needs (wound care, insulin, CHF monitoring) plus inability to manage medications independently require SNF-level care. Independent or assisted settings without skilled oversight cannot meet these needs safely.
stem: An 81-year-old man with CHF, insulin-dependent diabetes, and a stage 2 pressure injury lives alone, cannot manage his 12 medications, and was readmitted twice in 60 days for medication errors. What placement is most appropriate?

options: Only the diagnosis and procedure codes
A problem list with active issues, reconciled medications, allergies, functional status, pending tests, follow-up appointments, and patient goals
Only the operative report
Only the final vital signs
rationale: An interoperable CCD must carry the full clinical picture — problems, meds, allergies, function, pending tests, follow-ups, and goals — to support continuity. Codes, operative reports, or vitals alone are fragments.
stem: A hospital adopts a Continuity of Care Document (CCD) to transmit to the patient's accountable care organization at discharge. Which data set best supports care continuity?

options: Schedule the appointment in 6 weeks
Call the primary care office for a 2-3 day urgent slot, reconcile the new medications, and confirm the patient can get there
Tell him to walk in to the ED if concerned
Fax the discharge summary and take no further action
rationale: A 2-week-old stroke on new dual antiplatelet therapy with a missed appointment needs urgent primary care contact, medication reconciliation, and access confirmation. Six-week scheduling, ED walk-in advice, or passive faxing all leave gaps.
stem: A 66-year-old man discharged after ischemic stroke on aspirin and clopidogrel missed his primary care appointment. The care coordinator learns he has no transportation and is unsure which pills are 'the blood thinners.' What is the best action?

options: Cancel the SNF transfer and keep him in the ED
Verify the SNF can manage a new tracheostomy: staff competency, suction equipment, humidification, and emergency backup plan — and only proceed if confirmed
Send him to the SNF with a note saying 'trach care as needed'
Have the family perform all trach care at the SNF
rationale: New tracheostomies require verified staff competency, equipment, and emergency planning at the receiving facility; a vague note or family-provided care is unsafe. Keeping him in the ED is not a disposition, and proceeding without verification risks airway catastrophe.
stem: A 62-year-old man with a new tracheostomy after prolonged intubation is medically stable and ready for SNF transfer for weaning and rehab. The accepting SNF has not managed a new tracheostomy in over a year. What should the discharge planner do?

options: Home with home health: intermittent skilled nursing for teaching and monitoring is sufficient
SNF placement for daily skilled care
LTAC admission for continued monitoring
Keeping him inpatient for another week
rationale: He is hemodynamically stable, independent in ADLs, and needs only intermittent teaching and monitoring — the definition of a home health candidate. SNF, LTAC, and extended inpatient stay exceed his needs and waste resources.
stem: A 58-year-old man is discharged 3 days after uncomplicated MI with new metoprolol, atorvastatin, and dual antiplatelet therapy. He is independent, lives with his wife, and needs teaching on medications, activity progression, and cardiac rehab referral. Which is the least restrictive appropriate setting?

options: The patient's religion
The specific ADL deficits, cognitive status, home layout barriers, and caregiver availability — matched against SNF, home health, and assisted living criteria
The patient's occupation 20 years ago
The hospital's average length of stay
rationale: Level-of-care decisions require matching assessed needs — function, cognition, environment, support — against setting criteria. Religion, past occupation, and LOS statistics do not determine the appropriate setting.
stem: A social worker asks the nurse for input on discharge destination for a 77-year-old woman post pneumonia with new oxygen needs, walker dependence, and mild confusion. What assessment data best informs the decision?

options: Tell him Medicare covers unlimited SNF days
Explain the benefit: up to 100 days per benefit period with cost-sharing after day 20, requiring continued skilled need and physician certification
Advise him to switch to private insurance
Promise coverage will be approved
rationale: Accurate counseling requires the real benefit structure: 100 days per benefit period, copay after day 20, and continued skilled need with certification. Promising unlimited days or guaranteed approval misleads the family.
stem: A family asks how long Medicare will cover their father's SNF stay after his stroke. He is making progress in therapy. What should the nurse explain?

options: Send the referral and assume the agency will call
Call the agency to confirm acceptance and first-visit date, give the patient the agency's name and phone number in writing, and confirm a working phone number
Tell the patient to find an agency himself
Document 'home health ordered' and end involvement
rationale: Closed-loop referral — confirming acceptance, visit date, and contact information with the patient — prevents the common failure of referrals that never become visits. Passive ordering without confirmation leaves the patient unsupported.
stem: A 69-year-old woman is discharged with a home health referral for wound care and diabetes teaching. She lives alone and is hard of hearing. What is the most important step to ensure the referral succeeds?

options: Immediate SNF transfer as originally planned
Reassess goals of care with the patient and family: with hours-to-days prognosis, transition to inpatient hospice or home hospice rather than rehabilitative SNF care
Increase the physical therapy frequency
Order more diagnostic tests to find a reversible cause
rationale: A hours-to-days prognosis with goals of comfort makes SNF rehab and more diagnostics inappropriate; reassessing goals and transitioning to hospice aligns care with reality. The original plan is obsolete once prognosis changes.
stem: A 78-year-old woman awaiting SNF transfer for deconditioning deteriorates: she is now minimally responsive, with mottling and irregular respirations. The palliative team estimates hours to days. Her family says, 'We just want her comfortable.' What is the best next step?

options: The patient's shoe size
Verification that the receiving facility's pharmacy can dispense and the nursing staff can administer the specific chemotherapy regimen, with oncology backup available
The patient's favorite TV programs
The distance to the nearest shopping mall
rationale: Chemotherapy continuity requires pharmacy capability, administration competency, and oncology backup at the receiving facility; without verification, treatment is interrupted or given unsafely. Shoe size, TV, and mall distance are irrelevant.
stem: A 60-year-old man receiving a 5-day outpatient chemotherapy cycle needs SNF placement mid-cycle for a hip fracture. What must be verified before transfer?

options: Discharge him with standard heart failure instructions
Involve social work and community resources: confirm a working phone, arrange transportation, simplify the regimen, and schedule close follow-up
Tell him to buy a phone before his appointment
Keep him hospitalized until he gets a phone
rationale: The nurse must actively bridge the gaps — phone access, transportation, regimen simplification, and close follow-up — rather than discharge with standard instructions that assume resources he lacks. Indefinite hospitalization is not a solution, and demanding he buy a phone ignores his means.
stem: A 55-year-old man with heart failure is discharged to a rural home 40 miles from the clinic. He has no cell phone, no car, and his prescriptions were changed at discharge. What is the most important transitional intervention?

options: Let the daughter decide alone without input
Facilitate a family meeting with the interdisciplinary team to review prognosis, the patient's known wishes, and SNF versus hospice options
Tell the family hospice is mandatory
Avoid discussing prognosis to prevent distress
rationale: A facilitated family meeting with the team aligns the decision with prognosis and the patient's values. Leaving the daughter to decide alone, mandating hospice, or avoiding prognosis discussion all fail shared decision-making.
stem: The daughter of an 82-year-old man with advanced dementia, recurrent aspiration, and 15-pound weight loss asks whether SNF rehab or hospice is 'the right thing.' He never completed advance directives. What is the nurse's best action?

options: SNF placement near the daughter with a plan for wound care, rehab, and clear follow-up
LTAC admission in the home state
Keeping her in the current hospital indefinitely
Discharge to the home state with no services
rationale: SNF near family support with a defined clinical plan addresses both medical and psychosocial needs. LTAC is not indicated for stable rehab needs, indefinite hospitalization is inappropriate, and unsupported discharge is unsafe.
stem: A 73-year-old woman from out of state is hospitalized while visiting her daughter. She needs 2 weeks of wound care and rehab after a fall. She is stable for transfer. What is the best transition plan?

options: Only the admitting diagnosis
The reconciled medication list, code status, allergies, isolation status, functional baseline, and pending results
Only the patient's name and age
Only the insurance information
rationale: Safe interhospital transfer requires meds, code status, allergies, isolation, function, and pending results — the elements that prevent immediate harm at arrival. Name/age, diagnosis alone, or insurance alone are dangerously incomplete.
stem: A patient with MRSA bacteremia on contact precautions is transferred between hospitals for a higher level of care. What information must accompany the patient?

options: Assume he will improve with time
Screen for delirium, reconcile medications for deliriogenic drugs, and communicate the change to the team and family
Restrain him to prevent falls
Sedate him for the transfer
rationale: New confusion in an older adult suggests delirium — screen, review medications, and communicate; do not assume improvement, restrain, or sedate, which worsen delirium and risk harm during transfer.
stem: An 80-year-old man being transferred to a SNF becomes newly confused and agitated the morning of transfer. He was at baseline yesterday. What should the nurse do before transfer?

options: Tell her the SNF will figure out the dosing
Verify the SNF can perform INR monitoring with timely result reporting and dose adjustment per protocol, and include the warfarin indication and target INR in the transfer orders
Discontinue warfarin before transfer
Switch her to aspirin without an order
rationale: Warfarin transitions require confirmed INR monitoring capability and explicit indication/target in orders; otherwise bleeding or clotting risk goes unmanaged. Assuming the SNF will figure it out, stopping anticoagulation, or switching agents without orders are all unsafe.
stem: A 74-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (target INR 2-3) is transferring to a SNF. Her last INR was 2.4. What is the most important safety step?

options: Routine SNF placement for strengthening
Urgent evaluation for safe discharge planning: assess decision-making capacity, involve social work and APS if criteria are met, and do not discharge to an unsafe environment
Discharge him home with a pamphlet on fall prevention
Ask the neighbor to check in weekly
rationale: Suspected self-neglect with impaired capacity and an unsafe environment triggers urgent evaluation, social work, and possible APS referral — not routine placement or discharge to the same unsafe setting. A weekly neighbor check is inadequate.
stem: A 79-year-old man found on the floor after 2 days is admitted for dehydration and rhabdomyolysis. He lives alone, the home has no utilities, he is confused, and he insists on returning home 'where I belong.' What is the priority?

options: The patient's preferred pharmacy only
Medication reconciliation with start/stop/change rationale, pending labs, functional status, diet orders, and follow-up appointments
The patient's employment history
The names of all consulting physicians
rationale: The receiving facility needs the full transition bundle — reconciled meds with rationales, pending labs, function, diet, and follow-ups. Pharmacy preference, employment history, and consultant names do not drive the care plan.
stem: A patient with ESRD, diabetes, and heart failure is discharged to a SNF. Which information set is most essential in the transfer packet?

options: Begin discharge planning after the first failed weaning trial
Involve palliative care and the family early to explore goals, values, and acceptable outcomes alongside ongoing weaning efforts
Wait until the patient codes to discuss goals
Tell the family that weaning will definitely succeed
rationale: Prolonged ventilation with uncertain weaning demands early concurrent palliative involvement for goals exploration — not waiting for crisis or promising success. Starting planning only after failure or at code time misses the window for values-aligned decisions.
stem: A 70-year-old man has failed 3 ventilator weaning trials after pneumonia. His family asks about 'what happens if he can't come off the machine.' What is the best transitional care approach?

options: Home with family and no professional support
Inpatient hospice unit for intensive symptom management with a plan to transition home with hospice when stable
LTAC for continued aggressive care
Another round of inpatient chemotherapy
rationale: Uncontrolled terminal restlessness and secretions need inpatient hospice stabilization first, then home hospice when symptoms allow — matching his wish to die at home. Family-only care is unsafe with uncontrolled symptoms; LTAC and chemo contradict his goals.
stem: An 82-year-old man with end-stage ALS has uncontrolled secretions and terminal restlessness. He wants to die at home but his symptoms are not controlled on current medications. What is the best transition?

options: Discharge home with standard instructions
Arrange a 48-72 hour post-discharge phone call, reconcile the antibiotic change explicitly, and confirm follow-up
Tell her to finish the antibiotics and she will be fine
Schedule routine follow-up in 3 months
rationale: A new antibiotic at discharge with a changed regimen warrants early phone follow-up, explicit reconciliation of the change, and confirmed follow-up — the window when confusion and adverse effects emerge. Standard instructions or 3-month follow-up miss this risk period.
stem: A 64-year-old woman is discharged after pyelonephritis with a new oral antibiotic she has never taken, replacing the IV regimen. She lives alone. What is the best transitional safeguard?

options: The color of the discharge folder
Confirmation that the SNF dietitian received the renal diet order, fluid restriction, and potassium/phosphorus limits
The patient's favorite snacks
Whether the patient liked the hospital meals
rationale: Diet continuity for ESRD — renal diet, fluid restriction, K/Phos limits — must be explicitly confirmed with the receiving dietitian; missed restrictions cause hyperkalemia and overload. Folder color, snacks, and meal preferences are irrelevant.
stem: A 61-year-old man with ESRD on hemodialysis, on a 1.5L fluid restriction and renal diet, is transferred to a SNF. What is the most important dietary handoff element?

options: Require him to demonstrate walking 200 feet before discharge
Assess home stairs and bathroom access, arrange for a walker and raised toilet seat, and confirm home health PT evaluation
Tell him to avoid stairs completely
Discharge him without equipment since he is young
rationale: Safe discharge requires matching the home environment to his current function: assess barriers, provide equipment, and arrange PT follow-up. Arbitrary walking distances, total stair avoidance without a plan, or no equipment all leave him unsafe.
stem: A 52-year-old man post total knee arthroplasty is discharged home on postoperative day 2. He lives in a split-level home with 8 stairs to the bedroom. What is the most important discharge preparation?

options: Give him the number for a taxi service
Verify insurance authorization for non-emergency medical transport, schedule recurring rides aligned with dialysis days, and confirm a backup plan
Tell him to ask other patients for rides
Document the barrier and discharge him
rationale: Dialysis is life-sustaining and thrice-weekly; the plan must verify NEMT authorization, align rides with treatment days, and include backup. Taxi numbers, informal rides, or passive documentation do not guarantee he reaches treatment.
stem: A 57-year-old man starting outpatient hemodialysis has no car and no family nearby. He missed his first two sessions due to transportation. What should the discharge team arrange?

options: The patient repeats back the red-flag symptoms, medication changes, and follow-up plan in her own words
The patient signs the discharge paperwork
The patient says she feels ready to go home
The nurse documents that teaching was completed
rationale: Teach-back is validated only by the patient's own-words explanation of red flags, medication changes, and follow-up — not by signatures, stated readiness, or documentation of teaching delivered.
stem: A nurse uses teach-back with a 70-year-old woman discharged after heart failure exacerbation. Which finding confirms the teaching was effective?

options: Her age
The new oxygen requirement, activity tolerance, home safety, and caregiver support — matching needs to home health versus SNF criteria
Her marital status
The day of the week she was admitted
rationale: The decision rests on oxygen needs, tolerance, home safety, and support matched to setting criteria — not demographics or admission day. Her new O2 need and limited support may push toward SNF or home health with close monitoring.
stem: A 77-year-old woman is discharged after COPD exacerbation with new home oxygen, a walker, and lives alone. Her neighbor checks in daily. Which assessment best determines home health versus SNF?

options: Discharge him tonight to free the bed
Escalate: reassess now, notify the provider of the trend, and hold the SNF transfer until stability is confirmed
Give an extra dose of metoprolol and proceed
Document the vitals and proceed with transfer
rationale: A deteriorating trend — rising HR, falling SBP, dropping SpO2 — before transfer demands escalation and holding the transfer; masking it with an extra beta-blocker dose or proceeding risks collapse at the SNF. Bed availability never justifies unsafe transfer.
stem: On the morning of SNF transfer, a 68-year-old man's vitals trend worse: HR 118, BP 92/58, SpO2 89% on 2L. Yesterday he was stable. The transport van is waiting. What should the nurse do?

options: Speech therapy for swallowing evaluation
Occupational therapy for energy conservation
Physical therapy for gait training, strengthening, and fall-risk reduction
Social work for placement
rationale: PT addresses gait instability, deconditioning, and fall risk through strengthening and balance training — the priority safety issue. Speech therapy is not indicated without dysphagia, OT's energy conservation is secondary to preventing the next fall, and social work placement is premature before rehab potential is addressed.
stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted after a fall at home. He has bilateral knee osteoarthritis, walks with an unsteady wide-based gait, and has fallen twice this month. He wants to remain independent at home. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for lower-extremity strengthening
Occupational therapy for ADL retraining, adaptive equipment, and home safety assessment
Speech therapy for memory strategies
Nutrition for a high-protein diet
rationale: OT specializes in ADLs, adaptive equipment, and home safety — exactly her deficits with bathing, dressing, and meal prep. PT targets mobility rather than ADL tasks, speech therapy is not indicated for this presentation, and nutrition alone does not restore function.
stem: A 68-year-old woman post right-hemisphere stroke has left-hand weakness and cannot button her blouse, bathe independently, or prepare meals safely. She walks with supervision. Which consult best addresses her primary deficits?

options: Speech-language pathology for a clinical swallow evaluation
Physical therapy for core strengthening
Occupational therapy for feeding adaptations
Nutrition for thickened liquids prescription
rationale: New coughing with liquids after stroke is a red flag for aspiration; SLP performs the clinical swallow evaluation and recommends diet modifications or instrumental assessment. PT and OT do not evaluate swallowing, and dietitians do not prescribe swallow precautions — they implement SLP recommendations.
stem: A 71-year-old man, day 2 post left-hemisphere stroke, begins coughing when drinking thin liquids and has a wet vocal quality. He is otherwise stable. Which consult should the nurse request first?

options: Physical therapy for ambulation
Speech therapy for word-finding
Registered dietitian for malnutrition assessment and a refeeding-risk nutrition plan
Social work for meal delivery
rationale: With 12% weight loss, low albumin, and refeeding risk after prolonged poor intake, the dietitian must assess malnutrition and design a safe refeeding plan — the immediate life-threatening concern. PT, speech, and meal delivery are secondary to safe nutritional rehabilitation.
stem: A 64-year-old man with COPD exacerbation has lost 12% of body weight in 3 months, has temporal wasting, albumin 2.8 g/dL, and has eaten poorly for a week. He is started on enteral nutrition. Which consult is most urgent?

options: Chaplaincy for spiritual support
Physical therapy for deconditioning
Pharmacy for comprehensive medication review and renal dose adjustment
Nutrition for sodium restriction teaching
rationale: Fourteen medications with dizziness and a fall in a patient with CKD stage 3 demand pharmacist review for polypharmacy, drug interactions, and renal dosing — the likely cause of her symptoms. Chaplaincy, PT, and nutrition teaching do not address the probable medication-related cause.
stem: An 82-year-old woman with CKD stage 3 takes 14 medications, reports dizziness on standing, and fell last week. Her daughter brings a bag of pill bottles with several duplicates. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for endurance training
Palliative care for goals-of-care discussion, symptom burden assessment, and advance care planning
Occupational therapy for ADL training
Wound care for pressure injury prevention
rationale: Recurrent admissions, progressive disease, and the patient's own statement that he is 'tired of fighting' signal a need for palliative care to explore goals, relieve symptoms, and plan ahead. PT, OT, and wound prevention do not address the core issue of aligning care with his values.
stem: A 74-year-old man with end-stage heart failure has had 4 admissions in 5 months, is dyspneic at rest despite optimal therapy, and tells the nurse he is 'tired of fighting.' His wife asks what else can be done. Which consult best serves him?

options: Social work for discharge barrier assessment, insurance navigation, and community resource linkage
Physical therapy for strengthening
Speech therapy for cognition
Pharmacy for medication teaching
rationale: Homelessness, no insurance, and no phone are social determinants blocking discharge — social work's domain: benefits, shelter, medication access programs. PT, speech, and pharmacy teaching cannot proceed until these foundational barriers are addressed.
stem: A 52-year-old man with cellulitis is medically ready for discharge but is homeless, uninsured, has no phone, and cannot afford the prescribed antibiotics. Which consult is most urgent for a safe discharge?

options: Occupational therapy for wheelchair positioning
Speech therapy for communication
Physical therapy for transfer training
Wound/ostomy nurse for pressure injury staging, treatment plan, and prevention strategies
rationale: A stage 3 pressure injury with undermining requires a certified wound nurse for accurate staging, debridement decisions, dressing selection, and a prevention plan. OT, speech, and PT do not manage wound treatment, though PT/OT support offloading.
stem: A 70-year-old immobile man develops a stage 3 sacral pressure injury with undermining during a prolonged hospitalization. The bedside nurse is unsure about dressing selection. Which consult is indicated?

options: Speech therapy for swallowing
Occupational therapy for upper-extremity dressing
Physical therapy for prosthetic gait training and residual limb conditioning
Nutrition for weight loss
rationale: Post transtibial amputation, PT leads residual-limb shaping, strengthening, balance, and prosthetic gait training. Speech is not indicated, OT addresses ADLs secondarily, and weight loss is not the priority.
stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetes undergoes transtibial (below-knee) amputation. His residual limb is healing well and he is motivated to walk again. Which consult is the priority for his rehabilitation?

options: Physical therapy for swallowing exercises
Speech-language pathology for aphasia assessment and communication strategies
Occupational therapy for cooking
Social work for disability paperwork
rationale: Fluent but nonsensical speech with poor comprehension after left-hemisphere stroke indicates Wernicke-type aphasia — SLP's domain for assessment and communication strategies. PT does not treat language, OT cooking is unsafe given comprehension deficits, and paperwork is secondary.
stem: A 66-year-old woman post left-hemisphere stroke speaks fluently but her speech is nonsensical, and she cannot follow simple commands. Her family is frustrated they cannot communicate with her. Which consult is indicated?

options: Pharmacy for anticoagulation education, interaction screening, and adherence planning
Physical therapy for fall prevention
Nutrition for vitamin K teaching
Social work for transportation
rationale: New warfarin initiation in an older adult on multiple medications demands pharmacist-led education, interaction review, and adherence planning — the highest-risk element. PT, nutrition, and social work are supportive but secondary to safe anticoagulation initiation.
stem: A 79-year-old man with new atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin. He takes 9 other medications, lives alone, and has mild cognitive impairment. Which consult best ensures safe anticoagulation?

options: Physical therapy for walking
Speech therapy for voice
Occupational therapy for energy conservation, ADL adaptation, and durable medical equipment
Nutrition for calorie counts
rationale: Severe COPD with ADL dependence needs OT for energy conservation techniques, task adaptation, and equipment (shower chair, reachers). PT addresses ambulation but not the ADL burden; speech and calorie counts are secondary.
stem: A 72-year-old woman with severe COPD becomes exhausted bathing and dressing, and has stopped cooking because standing tires her. She wants to stay home. Which consult best addresses her functional goals?

options: Social work for nursing home placement
Palliative care for refractory dyspnea, goals clarification, and family support alongside ongoing treatment
Physical therapy for reconditioning
Chaplaincy alone for comfort
rationale: Refractory dyspnea despite maximal therapy with recurrent admissions calls for palliative care's symptom expertise and goals clarification — concurrent with, not replacing, disease treatment. Placement, PT, and chaplaincy alone do not address the symptom crisis or decision needs.
stem: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has dyspnea refractory to opioids and oxygen, and her family is distressed. She is still receiving chemotherapy. Which consult is most appropriate?

options: Physical therapy for gait
Registered dietitian for a carbohydrate-consistent meal plan, medication-food timing, and hypoglycemia prevention
Speech therapy for diet texture
Social work for food pantry referral only
