rationale: New insulin with recurrent hypoglycemia requires dietitian expertise in carbohydrate consistency, meal timing with insulin, and hypoglycemia prevention. PT, speech, and a pantry referral alone do not address the knowledge deficit driving the hypoglycemia.
stem: A 60-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes started on basal-bolus insulin has had two hypoglycemic episodes at home. He eats irregularly and does not understand carbohydrate counting. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy to improve walking endurance
Occupational therapy for a home safety evaluation and adaptive equipment before discharge
Speech therapy for medication management
Nutrition for a cardiac diet handout
rationale: Two falls in a cluttered home with a loose rug point to environmental hazards — OT's home safety evaluation and adaptive equipment directly target the cause. PT endurance, speech, and diet handouts do not fix the home hazards.
stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted after her second fall in a month. She lives alone in a cluttered apartment with loose rugs and no bathroom grab bars. Which consult best prevents the next fall?

options: Nutrition for thickened liquids
Physical therapy for posture
Speech-language pathology for voice assessment and therapy
Social work for communication devices
rationale: New hoarseness after prolonged intubation suggests vocal cord dysfunction — SLP evaluates voice and provides therapy. Nutrition and PT do not assess the larynx, and devices are premature before evaluation.
stem: A 55-year-old man is extubated after 9 days of mechanical ventilation. He is hoarse, his voice fatigues quickly, and he is anxious about returning to his teaching job. Which consult is indicated?

options: Tell him bruising is normal and take no action
Pharmacy for antiplatelet interaction review, bleeding-risk assessment, and coordination with the surgical team
Physical therapy for the knee
Nutrition for iron supplementation
rationale: Bruising on dual antiplatelet therapy after a fall with head strike needs pharmacist review of bleeding risk and coordination with surgery/cardiology on perioperative management — the urgent safety issue. Dismissing bruising, PT, and iron do not address the immediate risk.
stem: A 70-year-old man on aspirin and clopidogrel after recent drug-eluting stent placement falls and strikes his head. He needs urgent hip fracture surgery and has new bruising. Which consult is most urgent?

options: Physical therapy for range of motion
Wound/ostomy/continence nurse for stoma site marking, pouching education, and complication prevention
Nutrition for a low-residue diet only
Social work for emotional support only
rationale: Preoperative stoma site marking by a certified WOC nurse reduces pouching problems and improves quality of life; postoperative pouching education is also their expertise. PT, diet-only, and emotional support alone miss the technical stoma needs.
stem: A 62-year-old man is scheduled for an APR with permanent colostomy for rectal cancer in 3 days. He is anxious about managing the ostomy. Which consult should occur before surgery?

options: Social work for suspected elder neglect assessment, safety planning, and APS referral coordination
Physical therapy for the fracture
Nutrition for weight gain
Pharmacy for pain medication review
rationale: The pattern — delayed care, fearfulness, poor hygiene, missed appointments — raises concern for elder neglect, which social work must assess with safety planning and possible APS referral. Treating only the fracture, nutrition, or pain misses the underlying safety threat.
stem: An 84-year-old woman is admitted with a hip fracture after a fall 3 days ago. She is unkempt, fearful when her son speaks, and has missed 4 clinic appointments. Her son says she 'refuses help.' Which consult is the priority?

options: Speech therapy for chewing
Physical therapy for mobility
Registered dietitian for enteral formula selection, rate advancement, and tolerance monitoring
Social work for tube-feeding supplies
rationale: New PEG feeding requires dietitian expertise in formula selection, initiation rates, and tolerance monitoring to avoid refeeding and GI complications. Speech, PT, and supply logistics are secondary to safe feeding prescription.
stem: A 76-year-old man with advanced dementia and dysphagia has a new PEG tube placed per family request. He is malnourished with albumin 2.9 g/dL. Which consult is most important for safe initiation of feeds?

options: Occupational therapy for dressing
Physical therapy for progressive mobilization, ventilator-associated deconditioning, and ICU-acquired weakness rehabilitation
Speech therapy for communication board
Nutrition for calorie counts
rationale: Twenty-one days of ventilation produces profound deconditioning and ICU-acquired weakness; PT leads progressive mobilization and weakness rehabilitation. OT, speech, and calorie counts are supportive but secondary to restoring basic mobility.
stem: A 63-year-old man is being liberated from mechanical ventilation after 21 days for ARDS. He cannot lift his arms against gravity and cannot sit at the edge of the bed. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for swallowing
Speech-language pathology for cognitive-communication assessment and compensatory strategies
Occupational therapy for cooking independently
Pharmacy for memory medications
rationale: Mild cognitive deficits affecting medication management and finances after TBI fall under SLP's cognitive-communication scope for assessment and compensatory strategies. PT does not treat cognition, independent cooking is unsafe, and medications are not first-line.
stem: A 45-year-old man post moderate TBI has difficulty with short-term memory, problem-solving, and managing his medications and finances. He is otherwise physically intact. Which consult best addresses his deficits?

options: Palliative care for goals-of-care exploration given recurrent admissions, limited prognosis, and the patient's values
Cardiology for another revascularization
Physical therapy for cardiac rehab
Nutrition for a stricter diet
rationale: Four admissions in 6 months, progressive decline, and his stated preference for home over hospital signal that goals-of-care exploration is the priority — palliative care's role. Another procedure, rehab, or stricter diet do not address the trajectory or his values.
stem: An 80-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF 20%) has had 4 heart failure admissions in 6 months. He tells the team he 'doesn't want to keep coming back to the hospital' but his daughter wants 'everything done.' Which consult best helps navigate this?

options: Physical therapy for transfer training
Occupational therapy for ADL retraining
Speech-language pathology for safe swallowing strategies and diet recommendations
Nutrition for supplement drinks
rationale: Coughing on thin liquids after extubation indicates possible aspiration; SLP must evaluate swallowing and recommend diet modifications before supplements or training proceed. PT, OT, and supplements do not address the airway safety issue.
stem: A 69-year-old woman is extubated after 5 days of ventilation for pneumonia. On her first sips of water she coughs repeatedly and her voice sounds gurgly. Which consult is the priority before advancing her diet?

options: Nutrition for a renal diet handout
Social work for insurance issues
Pharmacy for hyperkalemia risk review, binder education, and renal dosing of his medications
Physical therapy for cramps
rationale: K+ 5.8 on an ACE inhibitor with CKD stage 4 is a medication-safety emergency; pharmacy review of hyperkalemia contributors, binder counseling, and renal dosing is the priority. A diet handout, insurance help, and PT do not address the immediate danger.
stem: A 67-year-old man with CKD stage 4 has potassium 5.8 mEq/L, takes lisinopril and spironolactone, and reports muscle cramps. He was just prescribed a potassium binder but does not understand it. Which consult is most urgent?

options: Physical therapy for back strengthening
Occupational therapy for joint protection, energy conservation, and adaptive equipment for hand function
Speech therapy for pain communication
Nutrition for an anti-inflammatory diet
rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis with hand deformities limiting ADLs calls for OT's joint protection, energy conservation, and adaptive equipment expertise. PT, speech, and diet do not address the hand-function deficits.
stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has ulnar deviation and cannot open jars, turn keys, or fasten buttons. She is independent in walking. Which consult best addresses her limitations?

options: Registered dietitian for a low-sodium, fluid-appropriate meal plan tailored to his preferences and literacy level
Physical therapy for exercise prescription
Speech therapy for salt craving counseling
Social work for grocery delivery
rationale: Recurrent HF admissions from dietary indiscretion in a patient who 'doesn't understand' the diet require dietitian-led, literacy-appropriate meal planning — the direct cause of his readmissions. Exercise, speech, and grocery delivery alone do not fix the knowledge gap.
stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure has been admitted 3 times in 4 months for volume overload. He eats canned soups and processed meats daily and says he 'doesn't understand the salt thing.' Which consult is the priority?

options: Occupational therapy for handwriting
Physical therapy for vestibular rehabilitation and gait/balance retraining
Speech therapy for hearing
Nutrition for dizziness diet
rationale: BPPV with gait unsteadiness is treated with vestibular rehabilitation — PT's domain — including canalith repositioning and balance retraining. OT, speech, and nutrition do not treat the vestibular disorder.
stem: A 72-year-old woman with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo has severe dizziness with head movements and an unsteady gait. She is afraid to walk alone. Which consult is indicated?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Speech-language pathology for instrumental swallow assessment and aspiration precautions
Occupational therapy for self-feeding
Social work for feeding tube decisions
rationale: Recurrent aspiration pneumonia with weight loss in Parkinson disease requires SLP instrumental assessment (e.g., videofluoroscopy) and aspiration precautions to determine safe diet or feeding route. PT, OT, and placement discussions are secondary to diagnosing the swallowing impairment.
stem: A 78-year-old man with Parkinson disease has had 2 aspiration pneumonias in 3 months and ongoing weight loss. He coughs with meals. Which consult is the priority?

options: Nutrition for protein shakes
Wound/ostomy/continence nurse for fistula pouching, skin protection, and output management
Physical therapy for mobility
Social work for body image counseling
rationale: An enterocutaneous fistula with caustic output destroying periwound skin needs WOC expertise in pouching systems, skin barriers, and output measurement. Protein shakes, PT, and counseling alone do not solve the technical wound problem.
stem: A 60-year-old man post bowel surgery develops an enterocutaneous fistula with high caustic output excoriating the surrounding skin. Standard dressings fail within hours. Which consult is indicated?

options: Social work for caregiver support resources, respite options, and advance directive facilitation
Physical therapy for the patient
Speech therapy for the patient
Nutrition for the caregiver's meals
rationale: Caregiver burnout with health decline and no advance directives is social work's domain: respite, support resources, and advance care planning facilitation. Treating only the patient or the caregiver's meals misses the dyad's needs.
stem: The wife of an 83-year-old man with advanced dementia is exhausted, tearful, and reports her own health is declining. There are no advance directives and she feels guilty considering placement. Which consult best supports this family?

options: Physical therapy for deconditioning
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Palliative care for refractory symptoms, prognosis discussion, and hospice transition planning
Nutrition for appetite stimulants
rationale: Metastatic disease with refractory pain, anorexia, and weeks-to-months prognosis needs palliative care for symptom control and hospice transition planning — not rehab or appetite stimulants. The trajectory has shifted from restorative to comfort-focused care.
stem: A 71-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer has worsening pain despite escalating opioids, progressive anorexia, and a prognosis of weeks to months. She asks what the focus of her care should be now. Which consult is most appropriate?

options: Tell her to take the pills at whatever time she remembers
Pharmacy for a simplified regimen review, adherence packaging options, and teach-back counseling
Physical therapy for medication timing with exercise
Nutrition for pill-swallowing techniques
rationale: Missing doses of 11 medications requires pharmacist-led regimen simplification, adherence packaging (e.g., blister packs), and teach-back — the direct fix. Accepting random timing, PT, and nutrition do not address adherence.
stem: A 75-year-old woman takes 11 medications but admits she misses doses 'all the time' and cannot explain what half of them are for. Her blood pressure is uncontrolled. Which consult best addresses this?

options: Physical therapy for walking practice
Occupational therapy for wheelchair skills, transfer training, and home accessibility assessment
Speech therapy for breathing
Nutrition for weight management
rationale: New paraplegia requires OT for wheelchair skills, transfer techniques, and home accessibility — the foundation of his independence. PT addresses lower-extremity function secondarily, speech is not indicated, and weight management is not the priority.
stem: A 34-year-old man with new T12 paraplegia after a motor vehicle crash is preparing for discharge to a one-story home. He needs to learn wheelchair mobility and transfers. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for chest physiotherapy
Speech-language pathology for laryngectomy communication rehabilitation and alaryngeal speech options
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Nutrition for tube feeding
rationale: Total laryngectomy removes the voice; SLP provides communication rehabilitation including electrolarynx training and other alaryngeal speech options. PT, OT, and tube feeding do not address his primary loss — communication.
stem: A 62-year-old man undergoes total laryngectomy for laryngeal cancer. Postoperatively he is aphonic and communicates by writing, which frustrates him. Which consult is the priority?

options: Speech therapy for meal supervision
Physical therapy for fall risk
Registered dietitian for pressure injury nutrition support: protein, calorie, vitamin C, and zinc assessment
Social work for placement
rationale: Stage 4 pressure injury healing demands dietitian assessment of protein, calories, and micronutrients (vitamin C, zinc) — nutrition is a cornerstone of wound healing. Speech, PT, and placement do not address the nutritional deficit impairing healing.
stem: A 68-year-old man with a stage 4 sacral pressure injury is malnourished with albumin 2.6 g/dL and poor intake. The wound has not improved in 3 weeks. Which consult best supports healing?

options: Occupational therapy for fine motor skills
Physical therapy for progressive ambulation, endurance, and activity tolerance
Speech therapy for breath support
Social work for oxygen funding
rationale: Post-PE deconditioning with exertional dyspnea and fear of activity needs PT-led progressive ambulation and endurance building to restore tolerance safely. OT, speech, and funding help are secondary to rebuilding activity capacity.
stem: A 59-year-old man is recovering from a large pulmonary embolism on anticoagulation. He is deconditioned, dyspneic with minimal exertion, and afraid to move. Which consult best restores his function?

options: Physical therapy for neck exercises
Speech-language pathology for instrumental swallowing assessment given his high aspiration risk
Occupational therapy for feeding
Nutrition for pureed diet order
rationale: Head and neck radiation causes progressive dysphagia with silent aspiration risk; SLP instrumental assessment determines safe diet and strategies. PT, OT feeding, and ordering puree without assessment are inadequate or unsafe.
stem: A 64-year-old man receiving radiation for base-of-tongue cancer develops progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, and a 10-pound weight loss. He has no cough with swallowing. Which consult is most urgent?

options: Palliative care for goals-of-care discussion: aligning further chemotherapy with his prognosis, values, and quality of life
Oncology for a fourth-line regimen
Physical therapy for fatigue
Nutrition for appetite
rationale: With disease progression through 3 lines of therapy and a prognosis of months, palliative care helps align the fourth-line decision with his values and quality of life — the central question. More chemo by default, PT, and appetite measures avoid the decision he is actually facing.
stem: A 66-year-old man with metastatic gastric cancer has progressed through 3 lines of chemotherapy. His oncologist offers a fourth line with low response rates. He asks the nurse, 'Is it worth it?' Which consult best helps him decide?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Occupational therapy for self-care
Pharmacy for anticholinergic burden review, renal dosing, and safer alternatives for urinary symptoms
Nutrition for fluid restriction
rationale: New confusion and urinary retention in an older man on oxybutynin point to anticholinergic toxicity; pharmacy review of anticholinergic burden, renal dosing, and safer alternatives is the priority. PT, OT, and fluid restriction do not address the drug-induced cause.
stem: An 80-year-old man with BPH on oxybutynin develops new confusion and urinary retention. He takes 8 other medications and has CKD stage 3. Which consult is most urgent?

options: Physical therapy for gait
Speech therapy for swallowing
Occupational therapy for one-handed ADL techniques, adaptive equipment, and upper-extremity splinting
Nutrition for healing diet
rationale: A flail dominant arm after brachial plexus injury requires OT for one-handed techniques, adaptive equipment, and splinting to preserve function. PT, speech, and diet do not address the upper-extremity functional loss.
stem: A 29-year-old man has a flail right (dominant) arm after a brachial plexus injury from a motorcycle crash. He cannot use the arm at all. Which consult best restores his independence?

options: Physical therapy for endurance
Speech-language pathology for tracheostomy speaking valve evaluation and communication
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Nutrition for swallowing diet
rationale: A new tracheostomy with inability to vocalize needs SLP evaluation for speaking valve candidacy and alternative communication — restoring his voice is the priority. PT, OT, and diet changes are secondary.
stem: A 57-year-old man with a new tracheostomy after prolonged intubation cannot vocalize and is becoming withdrawn and depressed. He is otherwise stable. Which consult is the priority?

options: Respiratory therapy for inhaler technique teaching and COPD action plan reinforcement
Physical therapy for walking
Speech therapy for cough
Social work for smoking cessation resources
rationale: Recurrent exacerbations from poor inhaler technique and no action plan are respiratory therapy's domain: device teaching and written action plans directly prevent the next admission. PT, speech, and cessation resources alone do not fix the technique deficit.
stem: A 65-year-old woman with COPD has had 3 exacerbations this year. She uses her inhalers incorrectly and has no written action plan. Which consult best prevents the next exacerbation?

options: Physical therapy for strengthening
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for cognition
Social work for SNF placement against his wishes
rationale: Wanting to die at home with uncontrolled symptoms and an overwhelmed caregiver is a hospice-appropriate scenario; social work facilitates the hospice referral, caregiver support, and planning. PT, OT, and speech do not address the end-of-life transition need.
stem: A 77-year-old man with end-stage liver disease has refractory ascites, encephalopathy episodes, and a prognosis of weeks. He says he wants to die at home but his wife is overwhelmed. Which consult best facilitates his wish?

options: Occupational therapy for dressing
Physical therapy for progressive mobilization and airway clearance techniques
Speech therapy for intubation communication
Nutrition for ventilator calories
rationale: Post-lobectomy with atelectasis and retained secretions needs PT for progressive mobilization and airway clearance — the direct treatment for his pulmonary complications. OT, speech, and calorie planning are secondary.
stem: A 63-year-old man post right upper lobectomy for lung cancer has atelectasis, retained secretions, and is reluctant to move or cough due to pain. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for gait training
Occupational therapy for ADL retraining
Speech therapy for word-finding exercises
Case management for care coordination across the stroke team, discharge planning, and community resource linkage
rationale: With multiple new deficits, a worried spouse, and complex follow-up needs, case management coordinates the interdisciplinary team, discharge plan, and resources — the overarching need. Individual discipline consults address fragments but not the coordination gap the wife is describing.
stem: A 70-year-old man post stroke has new hemiparesis, dysphagia, and aphasia. His wife is overwhelmed by appointments, therapy schedules, and equipment needs. Multiple specialists are involved but no one is coordinating. Which referral best addresses the family's core problem?

options: Social work for placement
Physical therapy for progressive mobility, safe transfer training, and caregiver instruction on assisting without injury
Speech therapy for communication
Nutrition for calorie needs
rationale: The immediate safety issue is the wife's unsafe lifting and his fall; PT provides transfer training and teaches the caregiver safe assist techniques. Placement, speech, and nutrition do not address the imminent injury risk.
stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease fell when his wife tried to lift him from the floor. She has back pain now and is afraid to help him move. He needs moderate assistance with transfers. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for swallowing
Occupational therapy for mealtime setup, adaptive utensils, and positioning to support safe self-feeding
Speech therapy for aspiration precautions
Nutrition for supplement selection
rationale: Once SLP sets the diet, OT optimizes the mealtime itself — positioning, adaptive utensils, and setup for safe self-feeding in a patient with tremor and weakness. PT does not address feeding, speech already defined the diet, and supplements alone do not enable safe eating.
stem: An 82-year-old woman with Parkinson disease, on a SLP-recommended mechanical soft diet with chin-tuck strategy, spills food, cannot hold utensils steadily, and tires during meals. Which consult best improves her mealtime safety and independence?

options: Speech-language pathology for a formal capacity assessment of decision-making regarding the feeding tube
Physical therapy for appetite stimulation
Occupational therapy for feeding trials
Nutrition for tube formula
rationale: The team disagrees about whether he understands the consequences — a formal SLP (or neuropsychology) capacity assessment of his decision-making about the feeding tube is the indicated step before proceeding. PT, OT, and formula selection presume a decision that has not been validly made.
stem: A 78-year-old man with moderate dementia and dysphagia sometimes refuses the recommended feeding tube and sometimes agrees. The team disagrees about whether he understands the decision. Which consult is most appropriate?

options: Physical therapy for exercise
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for cognition
Pharmacy for a fall-risk medication review: sedatives, anticholinergics, and orthostatic contributors
rationale: Two recent falls in a patient on sedating and anticholinergic medications point to a medication review for fall-risk drugs — the modifiable cause. PT, OT, and speech address function but not the pharmacologic driver.
stem: An 85-year-old man has fallen twice this month. He takes diphenhydramine nightly for sleep, oxybutynin, and metoprolol. He is orthostatic on exam. Which consult best identifies the modifiable cause?

options: Nutrition for a diabetic diet handout
Social work for SNF placement
Palliative care for goals-of-care discussion: prognosis, treatment burden, and the patient's values regarding dialysis
Physical therapy for dialysis fatigue
rationale: At 88 with progressive decline asking 'how much longer,' the central need is a goals-of-care conversation about prognosis and whether dialysis still serves his values — palliative care's role. A diet handout, placement, and PT avoid the question he is asking.
stem: An 88-year-old man on hemodialysis for 6 years has progressive frailty, recurrent hospitalizations, and asks the nurse 'how much longer do I have to do this?' Which consult best serves him?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Registered dietitian for a potassium- and phosphorus-restricted meal plan within his food preferences and budget
Speech therapy for chewing
Social work for food stamps only
rationale: Hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia in ESRD require dietitian-crafted restriction plans tailored to preferences and budget — the direct intervention. PT, speech, and benefits assistance alone do not correct the dietary cause.
stem: A 60-year-old man with ESRD on hemodialysis has potassium 6.0 and phosphorus 7.2. He eats bananas, oranges, and processed cheese daily and says 'nobody told me what I can eat.' Which consult is the priority?

options: Wound/ostomy nurse for peristomal skin assessment, pouching system refit, and leakage troubleshooting
Physical therapy for core strength
Nutrition for output thickening
Social work for supply costs
rationale: Frequent leakage with skin excoriation is a pouching-fit problem requiring WOC expertise in peristomal assessment and system refit. Core strength, diet changes, and cost help are secondary to fixing the seal.
stem: A 66-year-old woman with a new ileostomy has frequent pouch leakage with peristomal skin excoriation. She is changing the pouch twice daily and is distressed. Which consult is indicated?

options: Physical therapy for gait
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for language
Social work for intimate partner violence screening, safety planning, and resource linkage
rationale: The injury pattern inconsistent with the story plus fearfulness raises concern for intimate partner violence — social work must screen privately, safety-plan, and link resources. PT, OT, and speech treat injuries while missing the cause and ongoing danger.
stem: A 42-year-old woman is admitted with a forearm fracture and facial bruising. She says she 'tripped,' but the injuries do not match the story, and she appears fearful when her partner visits. Which consult is the priority?

options: Occupational therapy for ADLs
Physical therapy for early mobilization, sternal precautions education, and progressive activity
Speech therapy for intubation effects
Nutrition for cardiac diet
rationale: Post-CABG day 2 with reluctance to move needs PT for early mobilization within sternal precautions and progressive activity — preventing atelectasis and deconditioning. OT, speech, and diet teaching are secondary to mobilization.
stem: A 68-year-old man is post-op day 2 after CABG. He is reluctant to get out of bed, has diminished breath sounds at the bases, and is anxious about 'popping' his sternum. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for walking
Speech-language pathology for cognitive-linguistic assessment and return-to-work planning
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Social work for disability forms
rationale: Word-finding difficulty and trouble following conversations after concussion indicate cognitive-linguistic deficits; SLP assesses and plans cognitive rehabilitation for return to work. PT, OT ADLs, and forms do not address the cognitive barrier to his job.
stem: A 38-year-old accountant post concussion has persistent word-finding difficulty and trouble following conversations 6 weeks later. He cannot return to work. Which consult best addresses his barrier?

options: Chaplaincy for spiritual distress assessment and support
Physical therapy for weakness
Speech therapy for prayer
Social work for funeral planning
rationale: Anger at God and questioning faith during terminal illness is spiritual distress — chaplaincy's domain for assessment and support. PT, speech, and funeral planning do not address the spiritual suffering he is expressing.
stem: A 72-year-old man with terminal pancreatic cancer tells the nurse he is angry at God and feels his faith is 'gone.' He is not interested in talking to family about it. Which consult is most appropriate?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Occupational therapy for energy conservation
Speech therapy for swallowing
Pharmacy for chemotherapy-induced nausea regimen optimization and interaction review
rationale: Uncontrolled CINV despite first-line agents needs pharmacist optimization of the antiemetic regimen and interaction review — the direct fix. PT, OT, and speech do not address the pharmacologic failure.
stem: A 58-year-old woman receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy has refractory nausea and vomiting despite ondansetron. She is dehydrated and considering stopping treatment. Which consult best addresses her symptom?

options: Nutrition for weight gain shakes
Social work for nursing home placement
Palliative care for advance care planning, dyspnea management, and aligning care with her stated wish to avoid the ICU
Physical therapy for reconditioning
rationale: Severe COPD with 3 ICU admissions, 35-pound weight loss, and her explicit wish to avoid the ICU call for palliative advance care planning and dyspnea management. Shakes, placement, and PT do not address her stated goal.
stem: A 70-year-old woman with severe COPD, 3 ICU admissions this year, and 35-pound weight loss says she 'never wants to go back to the ICU.' Which consult best honors her goal?

options: Physical therapy for leg strength
Registered dietitian for a heart-healthy, sodium-aware meal plan adapted to Filipino foods and cooking methods
Speech therapy for chewing
Social work for grocery shopping
rationale: Dietary counseling only works if adapted to his actual foods; a dietitian can build a sodium-aware plan around Filipino dishes and cooking methods. Generic PT, speech, and shopping help do not address the cultural dietary pattern driving his admissions.
stem: A 62-year-old Filipino man with heart failure eats traditional dishes high in sodium (patis, tuyo, processed meats) and has had 2 admissions for overload. He says 'just tell me what to eat.' Which consult is most effective?

options: Physical therapy for transfer training
Occupational therapy for toilet transfer techniques, raised seat and grab bar recommendations, and a home bathroom safety plan
Speech therapy for continence
Nutrition for fiber
rationale: Falls in the bathroom from a low toilet without grab bars need OT's toilet-transfer training and bathroom modification recommendations. PT transfer training is generic, speech is not indicated, and fiber does not prevent falls.
stem: A 79-year-old woman fell twice getting up from her low toilet; her bathroom has no grab bars. She is afraid to use the bathroom alone now. Which consult best addresses this specific problem?

options: Physical therapy for posture
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for hoarseness
Social work for disability benefits
rationale: New hoarseness in a smoker with a neck mass raises concern for laryngeal pathology — but among the options, none diagnose; the question asks which team member role fits. Actually the priority is ENT evaluation; of the listed disciplines, speech therapy's voice assessment is the relevant consult. The distractors do not address the voice symptom.
stem: A 60-year-old man who smokes presents with 3 weeks of hoarseness and a neck mass. He is referred to ENT, but the nurse is asked which supportive discipline should also evaluate his voice symptom now. Which is most appropriate?

options: Tell her the confusion is expected and observe
Pharmacy for deliriogenic medication review and safer pain-control alternatives
Physical therapy for mobilization
Nutrition for protein intake
rationale: New confusion after starting diphenhydramine and with oxycodone on board suggests deliriogenic medications; pharmacy review for safer alternatives is the priority. Observing, PT, and nutrition do not address the drug-induced cause.
stem: A 76-year-old woman post hip fracture repair becomes acutely confused on day 2. She takes oxycodone and was started on diphenhydramine for itching last night. Which consult best identifies the likely cause?

options: Physical therapy for gait
Wound/ostomy/continence nurse for a structured incontinence assessment, skin protection plan, and containment product selection
Speech therapy for toileting communication
Nutrition for fluid restriction
rationale: New incontinence with skin breakdown needs WOC continence assessment: cause evaluation, skin protection, and appropriate containment. PT, speech, and fluid restriction do not address the skin injury or product needs.
stem: An 80-year-old woman develops new urinary incontinence after a stroke, with perineal skin breakdown from prolonged moisture exposure. Which consult is indicated?

options: Social work for a psychosocial assessment: depression screening, substance use, support systems, and linkage to counseling and community resources
Physical therapy for fatigue
Speech therapy for motivation
Nutrition for appetite
rationale: New depression with alcohol use, isolation, and poor follow-through in heart failure is a psychosocial crisis affecting outcomes — social work's assessment and linkage role. PT, speech, and appetite measures do not address the underlying depression and substance use.
stem: A 54-year-old man with heart failure is readmitted for the third time. He appears depressed, admits to drinking alcohol daily, lives alone, and has stopped seeing his friends. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for endurance
Occupational therapy for ADL retraining
Speech therapy for cognition
Palliative care for refractory angina symptom management and goals-of-care alignment
rationale: Refractory angina despite maximal therapy with declining function and his question about 'how much more' signal a need for palliative symptom expertise and goals alignment — not more rehab or cognitive work.
stem: A 78-year-old man with refractory angina despite maximal medical therapy has declining function and asks 'how much more of this can there be?' Which consult best addresses his suffering?

options: Occupational therapy for ADLs
Physical therapy for progressive resistance training, balance, and a home exercise program
Speech therapy for encouragement
Nutrition for protein timing
rationale: Sarcopenia with slow gait and difficulty rising from a chair responds to PT-led progressive resistance training and balance work with a home program. OT, speech, and protein timing alone do not rebuild strength.
stem: A 81-year-old man has sarcopenia, slow gait speed, and difficulty rising from a chair. He wants to avoid a nursing home. Which consult best preserves his independence?

options: Physical therapy for walking
Speech-language pathology for a modified barium swallow study to define the safest diet and strategies
Occupational therapy for feeding
Nutrition for thickened liquids
rationale: Silent aspiration risk after stroke requires instrumental assessment — the modified barium swallow study defines safe diet and compensatory strategies. PT, OT feeding, and ordering thickened liquids without assessment are inadequate or presumptive.
stem: A 73-year-old man post right-hemisphere stroke pockets food, has a weak cough, and developed a fever on day 3. The team suspects silent aspiration. Which consult is most urgent?

options: The physical therapist, who leads gait and transfer training
The occupational therapist, who leads ADL retraining and discharge equipment planning
The speech therapist, who leads all discharge planning
The dietitian, who prescribes therapy minutes
rationale: Role clarity matters: PT leads gait/transfers, OT leads ADLs and equipment, SLP leads communication/swallowing — not global discharge planning — and dietitians do not prescribe therapy minutes. The question tests knowing each discipline's scope.
stem: A new nurse asks which team member typically leads gait and transfer training versus ADL retraining and discharge equipment planning for a stroke patient. What is the correct distinction?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Occupational therapy for self-care
Speech therapy for swallowing
Pharmacy for a comprehensive geriatric medication review with deprescribing recommendations
rationale: Eighteen medications with dizziness, confusion, and a fall demand pharmacist-led comprehensive review with deprescribing — the highest-yield safety intervention. Individual discipline therapies do not address the polypharmacy driving her decline.
stem: A 86-year-old woman takes 18 medications prescribed by 5 different providers. She is dizzy, intermittently confused, and fell last week. No single provider has reviewed the full list in a year. Which consult is the priority?

options: Nutrition for a low-salt diet
Social work for placement
Palliative care for goals-of-care discussion given inotrope dependence, recurrent ICU stays, and limited prognosis
Physical therapy for cardiac rehab
rationale: Inotrope-dependent heart failure with recurrent ICU admissions and months-long prognosis needs palliative goals-of-care discussion about the trajectory and acceptable interventions. Diet, placement, and rehab do not address the central decision.
stem: A 64-year-old man with end-stage heart failure is on continuous milrinone, has had 3 ICU admissions in 4 months, and his cardiologist says prognosis is months. His family asks about a transplant evaluation. Which consult best helps the family understand the situation?

options: Physical therapy for strengthening
Registered dietitian for a low-residue, lactose-aware nutrition plan during the flare and repletion afterward
Speech therapy for chewing
Social work for bathroom access advocacy
rationale: A Crohn's flare with 15-pound weight loss needs dietitian-guided low-residue nutrition during inflammation and repletion planning — the direct nutritional intervention. PT, speech, and advocacy do not address the malnutrition.
stem: A 34-year-old woman with Crohn's disease is admitted with a flare, has lost 15 pounds in 2 months, and fears eating because it causes pain. Which consult best addresses her nutritional decline?

options: Physical therapy for gait and endurance
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for communication
Respiratory therapy for airway clearance techniques and breathing retraining
rationale: Bronchiectasis with copious sputum and recurrent exacerbations needs respiratory therapy for airway clearance techniques (huff coughing, PEP devices) and breathing retraining — the direct disease management. PT, OT, and speech are secondary.
stem: A 58-year-old woman with bronchiectasis produces copious sputum daily and has had 4 exacerbations this year. She does not know any airway clearance techniques. Which consult is the priority?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for swallowing
Social work for a home safety and caregiver capacity assessment with APS referral if neglect criteria are met
rationale: Repeated burns from unsafe heating in a cognitively impaired elder living alone suggest self-neglect/unsafe environment — social work assessment with possible APS referral is the priority. Treating burns alone without addressing the environment guarantees recurrence.
stem: A 83-year-old man with mild dementia lives alone and is admitted with second-degree burns from a space heater — his third burn injury this year. Which consult is most urgent for his safety?

options: Occupational therapy for ADLs
Physical therapy for lymphedema complete decongestive therapy: manual drainage, compression, and exercise
Speech therapy for arm use
Nutrition for salt restriction
rationale: Post-mastectomy arm lymphedema is treated with complete decongestive therapy — a PT specialty including manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging, and exercise. OT, speech, and diet do not provide this specialized treatment.
stem: A 55-year-old woman post left mastectomy with axillary node dissection develops progressive left arm swelling. Her arm feels heavy and tight. Which consult is indicated?

options: Physical therapy for gait
Speech-language pathology for stuttering assessment and fluency therapy
Occupational therapy for work tasks
Social work for bullying resources
rationale: New-onset stuttering after head injury (neurogenic stuttering) requires SLP assessment and fluency therapy. PT, OT, and anti-bullying resources do not treat the fluency disorder.
stem: A 16-year-old boy develops new-onset stuttering after a skateboard head injury. He is embarrassed to speak at school. Which consult is indicated?

options: Palliative care for a family meeting to explore goals, prognosis understanding, and acceptable interventions
Intensivist for more aggressive measures
Physical therapy for mobilization
Nutrition for calorie support
rationale: The conflict between the daughter's 'do everything' and his comfort-focused advance directive requires a facilitated palliative family meeting to explore goals and prognosis understanding. More aggressive measures, PT, and calories do not resolve the values conflict.
stem: A 79-year-old man with multisystem organ failure has an advance directive specifying comfort-focused care, but his daughter demands 'do everything.' The team is divided. Which consult best navigates this conflict?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for cognition
Pharmacy for QTc-prolonging drug interaction review and electrolyte monitoring plan
rationale: New QTc prolongation on amiodarone plus ondansetron and hypokalemia is a torsades risk; pharmacy review of QTc-prolonging interactions and electrolyte monitoring is the urgent safety action. PT, OT, and speech are irrelevant to the arrhythmia risk.
stem: A 68-year-old man on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops QTc prolongation to 520 ms. He also takes ondansetron and has potassium 3.1 mEq/L. Which consult is most urgent?

options: Nutrition for a diabetic diet
Social work for insurance
Palliative care for goals-of-care and symptom planning given his prognosis and stated preference against intubation
Physical therapy for reconditioning
rationale: Metastatic cancer with months prognosis, recurrent admissions, and his stated wish to avoid intubation call for palliative goals-of-care and dyspnea planning — not more reconditioning. Diet and insurance do not address the central decision.
stem: A 72-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma has malignant pleural effusions, dyspnea at rest, and a prognosis of months. He says he does not want to be intubated. Which consult best ensures his wishes guide care?

options: Physical therapy for leg exercises
Registered dietitian for a high-protein, high-calorie repletion plan with small frequent meals
Speech therapy for appetite
Social work for meal delivery only
rationale: Fifteen percent weight loss with muscle wasting after prolonged NPO needs dietitian-led repletion: protein/calorie targets and small frequent meals. Leg exercises, speech, and meal delivery alone do not constitute a repletion plan.
stem: A 66-year-old man was NPO for 12 days during a prolonged ileus workup. He has lost 15% of body weight and has visible muscle wasting. He is now cleared for diet. Which consult best guides his nutritional recovery?

options: Physical therapy for deconditioning
Occupational therapy for a pre-discharge home assessment visit to identify hazards and equipment needs
Speech therapy for medication names
Nutrition for a discharge diet
rationale: An OT pre-discharge home visit directly identifies the hazards that caused his prior falls and specifies equipment — the highest-yield prevention. Generic PT, speech, and diet teaching do not assess his specific environment.
stem: A 77-year-old man is being discharged after his third fall-related admission. His home has stairs, poor lighting, and no bathroom modifications. Which consult best prevents the next admission?

options: Physical therapy for jaw exercises
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Nutrition for soft diet
Speech-language pathology for temporomandibular and swallowing assessment after prolonged intubation
rationale: Jaw stiffness and difficulty opening the mouth after prolonged intubation can signal TMJ dysfunction or trismus affecting swallowing safety — SLP assessment is indicated. PT jaw exercises without assessment, OT, and a soft diet presume the diagnosis.
stem: A 61-year-old woman is extubated after 12 days of intubation. She reports jaw stiffness, difficulty opening her mouth, and pain when swallowing. Which consult is indicated?

options: Tell him to stop the metformin on his own
Pharmacy for lactic acidosis risk assessment, renal function review, and coordination with the provider on metformin management
Physical therapy for fatigue
Nutrition for hydration
rationale: Metformin with eGFR 28 raises lactic acidosis risk; pharmacy assessment of renal function and coordination with the provider on whether to hold or adjust metformin is the safety priority. Advising him to stop on his own, PT, and hydration advice do not address the prescribing decision.
stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin is found to have eGFR 28 mL/min. He is fatigued but otherwise stable. Which consult best ensures medication safety?

options: Physical therapy for wound healing
Wound/ostomy nurse for negative-pressure wound therapy evaluation, dressing selection, and healing trajectory monitoring
Speech therapy for nutrition
Social work for wound supplies
rationale: A large dehisced abdominal wound with heavy exudate needs WOC evaluation for NPWT candidacy, dressing selection, and trajectory monitoring. PT, speech, and supply logistics do not determine the wound treatment plan.
stem: A 64-year-old man post laparotomy has a dehisced abdominal wound, 8 cm wide, with heavy exudate. Standard wet-to-dry dressings are not keeping up. Which consult is indicated?

options: Social work for benefits counseling, prior authorization assistance, and patient assistance programs for the biologic
Physical therapy for joint protection
Speech therapy for fatigue
Nutrition for anti-inflammatory foods
rationale: The barrier is cost and access to a $4,000/month biologic — social work's benefits counseling, prior authorization help, and patient assistance programs directly address it. PT, speech, and diet do not solve the access problem.
stem: A 45-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis cannot afford her $4,000/month biologic and her prior authorization was denied. She is flaring. Which consult best addresses the access barrier?

options: Physical therapy for mobility
Occupational therapy for ADLs
Speech therapy for swallowing
Palliative care for existential distress, legacy work, and family anticipatory grief support
rationale: Her statement about meaning, purpose, and her children's future is existential and anticipatory-grief distress — palliative care's domain including legacy work and family support. PT, OT, and speech do not address this suffering.
stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer tells the nurse she is 'not afraid of dying, but of being forgotten' and worries about her young children. Which consult best addresses her distress?

options: Occupational therapy for ADLs
Physical therapy for a supervised progressive walking program with claudication pain management strategies
Speech therapy for circulation
Nutrition for cholesterol diet
rationale: Intermittent claudication is treated with supervised exercise therapy — PT's domain — using walk-rest-walk progression to extend pain-free distance. OT, speech, and diet alone do not provide the exercise prescription.
stem: A 68-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has calf pain after walking one block, forcing him to stop. He wants to avoid surgery. Which consult best improves his walking distance?

options: Physical therapy for tongue exercises
Speech-language pathology for tongue strength, range of motion, and swallowing safety assessment
Occupational therapy for eating
Nutrition for pureed foods
rationale: Post-glossectomy tongue dysfunction affecting speech and swallowing needs SLP assessment of tongue strength, ROM, and swallowing safety with rehabilitation. PT tongue exercises without assessment, OT, and presumptive puree orders are inadequate.
stem: A 59-year-old man post partial glossectomy for tongue cancer has difficulty moving food in his mouth and slurred speech. Which consult is the priority?

options: The nurse's role is to carry out each discipline's orders without questioning
The nurse coordinates the plan: synthesizing assessments, identifying conflicting recommendations, facilitating team communication, and ensuring the patient and family voice guides decisions
The nurse defers all decisions to the physician
The nurse documents only her own assessments
rationale: The medical-surgical nurse is the interprofessional coordinator: synthesizing inputs, catching conflicts (e.g., PT mobility goals vs. nursing fall precautions), facilitating communication, and centering patient/family voice. Passive order execution, total deference, or siloed documentation abdicate this role.
stem: A charge nurse orients a new RN to the interprofessional team caring for a complex stroke patient with PT, OT, speech, nutrition, pharmacy, and social work involved. What best describes the RN's role on this team?

options: Physical therapy for strengthening
Occupational therapy for ADL adaptation
Speech therapy for communication

The full interprofessional team: PT for mobility, OT for ADLs and home setup, SLP for swallowing and communication, dietitian for nutrition, pharmacy for polypharmacy review, and social work for caregiver support and resources
rationale: His deficits span every discipline — mobility, ADLs, swallowing, communication, nutrition, medications, and caregiver burden — so the correct answer is the coordinated full-team approach. Any single-discipline answer addresses only a fragment of his needs.
stem: A 75-year-old man post severe stroke has hemiplegia, dysphagia, aphasia, malnutrition, 12 medications, and an overwhelmed spouse. The nurse recognizes no single consult will suffice. What is the best plan?

options: Arrange the cardiology consult as ordered since heart failure optimization is the admission diagnosis
Request a dietitian consult for cardiac diet education before the cardiology visit
Advocate to prioritize an urgent gastroenterology consult and hold warfarin pending evaluation of the active bleed
Ask pharmacy to bridge warfarin to a heparin infusion immediately
rationale: An active GI bleed with hemodynamic instability and anemia takes precedence over routine heart failure optimization; the nurse should advocate for urgent GI evaluation and holding anticoagulation. Cardiology optimization can follow once bleeding is controlled. Bridging to heparin during an active bleed is dangerous and should not be initiated without GI and cardiology input.
stem: A 68-year-old with HFrEF (EF 30%) on warfarin is admitted with melena, heart rate 118, blood pressure 96/60, and hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL. The admitting provider orders a cardiology consult for heart failure optimization. The patient is actively passing dark stools. What is the nurse's best action?

options: Keep the patient NPO and request a stat speech therapy swallow evaluation before any oral intake
Offer thickened liquids since the patient is only coughing on thin water
Allow small sips of water with close supervision
Order a videofluoroscopic swallow study directly
rationale: New stroke with drooling and cough on water signals high aspiration risk; the patient must remain NPO until speech therapy completes a bedside swallow evaluation. Nurses cannot independently order radiology studies, and offering any oral intake before evaluation risks aspiration pneumonia. Thickened liquids still require a formal swallow assessment first.
stem: A 72-year-old admitted with acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS 8) is drooling and coughing when given sips of water. The daughter asks the nurse to order a breakfast tray because her mother is hungry. What is the best nursing action?

options: Ask the surgeon to cancel physical therapy until the patient feels ready
Report to the team that the patient is noncompliant with therapy
Defer all discussion to the physical therapist since mobilization is their domain
Present current pain control, functional status, and barriers using SBAR so the team can adjust the pain plan and re-attempt mobilization
rationale: The nurse's role in rounds is to synthesize bedside data, voice patient barriers, and drive coordinated plan adjustments using structured communication. Labeling the patient noncompliant or canceling therapy abandons the mobilization goal, and deferring entirely wastes the nurse's unique 24-hour perspective on pain patterns and readiness.
stem: A 74-year-old is post-op day 1 after total hip arthroplasty. Physical therapy documents that the patient refused to get out of bed due to pain. During interdisciplinary rounds, what is the nurse's most effective contribution?

options: Endocrine, to optimize glucose control before any procedures
Infectious disease, to coordinate bone biopsy and pathogen-directed therapy for suspected osteomyelitis
Vascular surgery, for immediate revascularization regardless of infection status
All three consults are equally urgent and sequencing does not matter
rationale: Suspected osteomyelitis with systemic signs threatens limb and life; infectious disease input guides timely bone biopsy and targeted antibiotics, ideally before definitive surgical planning. Glucose control and perfusion assessment remain important, but uncontrolled infection takes priority in sequencing, and revascularization of an actively infected foot without an antibiotic plan risks seeding.
stem: A 59-year-old with diabetes and CKD stage 3b is admitted with a plantar foot ulcer probing to bone, erythema, and fever. Orders are pending for endocrine, vascular surgery, and infectious disease consults. Which consult should the nurse advocate arranging first?

options: Hire a private sitter to keep the patient safe
Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the surgical lines
Request pharmacy and geriatrics consults for anticholinergic medication review and a delirium workup while implementing nonpharmacologic measures
Increase the lorazepam dose to control agitation
rationale: New postoperative delirium in an older adult on highly anticholinergic medications warrants a structured delirium workup and medication review by pharmacy and geriatrics rather than restraints or sedation, which worsen delirium. Nonpharmacologic measures (reorientation, sleep hygiene, mobilization) are first-line. Benzodiazepines can precipitate or prolong delirium except in alcohol withdrawal.
stem: An 81-year-old is post-op day 2 after bowel resection with new confusion, picking at lines, and agitation. Home medications continued include diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, and nightly lorazepam. The family asks for a sitter. What is the best initial interprofessional action?

options: Request respiratory therapy to optimize BiPAP fit and settings and coach breathing technique before pursuing a psychiatry consult
Obtain the psychiatry consult immediately for the anxiety
Administer PRN lorazepam to reduce anxiety
Remove the BiPAP since the patient finds it distressing
rationale: Anxiety and tachypnea on BiPAP are most often driven by poor mask fit and dyssynchrony, which respiratory therapy can correct at the bedside; treating the reversible cause takes priority over a psychiatry consult. Sedating a hypercapnic COPD patient is dangerous, and removing BiPAP during an exacerbation risks respiratory failure.
stem: A 66-year-old with COPD exacerbation is tachypneic and anxious on BiPAP, with frequent mask air leaks. The family requests a psychiatry consult for anxiety. What should the nurse do first?

options: Prosthetist, so limb fitting is not delayed
Outpatient physical therapy for gait training
A peer support group for new amputees
Social work and case management to establish coverage options and coordinate the sequence of referrals
rationale: Without coverage, none of the downstream referrals are actionable; social work and case management must first address insurance, charity care, and benefits so wound care, therapy, and prosthesis referrals can actually be completed. Prosthesis fitting cannot precede wound healing and coverage anyway, and support groups, while valuable, do not unblock the discharge plan.
stem: A 54-year-old uninsured patient with a new below-knee amputation needs wound care, physical therapy, prosthesis fitting, and diabetes management. Discharge is planned in 3 days. Which referral should the nurse prioritize first?

options: Cardiology consult during each admission for diuretic titration
Referral to a multidisciplinary heart failure clinic with an NP, pharmacist, dietitian, and social worker
A home health aide for light housekeeping only
A repeat echocardiogram to recheck ejection fraction
rationale: Recurrent HF admissions driven by medication nonadherence and diet knowledge gaps require coordinated education, medication reconciliation, and barrier assessment that a multidisciplinary HF team provides. Serial cardiology consults alone do not address adherence, a housekeeping aide does not provide skilled teaching, and another echo will not change management driven by volume status.
stem: A 66-year-old with HFrEF (EF 25%) has had 3 admissions in 4 months for volume overload. He misses furosemide doses, eats high-sodium foods, and cannot explain his low-salt diet. Which interprofessional intervention best reduces readmission risk?

options: Schedule wound care to evaluate the incision later today
Wait for the surgeon to round tomorrow morning
Notify the surgeon immediately and facilitate an infectious disease consult for deep sternal wound infection workup
Apply topical antibiotic ointment and continue to observe
rationale: Purulent sternal drainage with fever after CABG suggests deep sternal wound infection or mediastinitis, a surgical emergency; the nurse must escalate immediately and engage infectious disease for cultures and targeted therapy. Waiting for routine rounds or relying on topical treatment delays definitive management of a potentially fatal complication.
stem: A 62-year-old is post-op day 5 after CABG with increasing sternal erythema, purulent drainage, and temperature 38.6 C. The surgeon is in the operating room. What is the nurse's priority action?

options: Request pharmacy for nephrotoxic medication review and vancomycin dosing adjustment, and notify the provider of the acute kidney injury
Consult nephrology alone and continue all antibiotics unchanged
Continue current antibiotics since treating pneumonia takes priority over creatinine
Consult urology for the creatinine rise
rationale: Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam is a known nephrotoxic combination; pharmacy can immediately optimize dosing, check levels, and suggest less nephrotoxic alternatives while the provider is notified. Continuing unchanged risks progressive AKI, and urology is not indicated without obstruction. Nephrology may be needed if AKI worsens, but pharmacy review is the fastest corrective step.
stem: A 70-year-old with pneumonia on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam has a creatinine rise from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL over 48 hours. Which is the best initial consultative action?

options: Further increase opioids without additional assessment
Request a radiology consult for the pain
Plan discharge home with current medications
Request a palliative care consult for comprehensive symptom management and goals-of-care discussion
rationale: Refractory pain, significant weight loss, and existential distress in metastatic cancer are classic triggers for palliative care, which addresses symptoms and goals alongside disease-directed therapy. Simply escalating opioids ignores the multidimensional nature of cancer pain, and palliative care does not require stopping chemotherapy.
stem: A 58-year-old with metastatic pancreatic cancer reports pain 8/10 despite escalating opioids, has lost 12 pounds this month, and is anxious about the future. The oncology team is focused on the next chemotherapy cycle. What is the best next step?

options: Have the health care proxy sign the surgical consent immediately
Request a psychiatry liaison consult for decision-making capacity assessment and notify the surgeon of the concern
Proceed with the family's verbal consent since they know him best
Document the refusal and arrange discharge
rationale: Fluctuating cognition raises legitimate doubt about decision-making capacity, which must be formally assessed before a refusal is accepted or a surrogate decides; psychiatry liaison performs this evaluation. Family cannot override a capable patient's refusal, and discharging a patient with an untreated surgical obstruction without clarifying capacity is unsafe.
stem: A 74-year-old with a small bowel obstruction is refusing recommended surgery. His children state he is not himself and has been confused at home. The surgeon asks the nurse to have the family sign the consent. What is the best action?

options: Report vital signs only, since falls are a therapy issue
Suggest wrist restraints to prevent another fall
Present the fall history and sedating medications, and request physical therapy and pharmacy consults for gait assessment and medication review
Recommend immediate discharge to avoid a hospital fall
rationale: The nurse adds value in rounds by connecting the fall history with modifiable risks like sedating polypharmacy and deconditioning, then requesting the right disciplines. Restraints increase injury risk and deconditioning, vitals-only reporting wastes the nursing assessment, and discharge without addressing fall risk invites readmission.
stem: A 79-year-old admitted after a fall is on 9 medications including diphenhydramine and temazepam, and has fallen twice at home this month. During interdisciplinary rounds, what is the nurse's best contribution?
topic: Nurse's role in rounds - fall risk

options: Consult the certified wound ostomy nurse for pouching system revision and a structured teaching plan
Keep reapplying the same pouching system and hope the skin adapts
Restrict oral fluids to reduce ostomy output
Consult psychiatry for body image concerns before addressing the leak
rationale: A leaking system in a skin crease requires expert pouching assessment, possibly convex products or barrier modifications, which the WOCN provides along with staged patient education. Repeated leaks cause moisture-associated skin damage, fluid restriction does not fix the seal, and psychosocial support complements rather than precedes a functional pouching system.
stem: A 62-year-old is post-op day 2 with a new colostomy that was not marked preoperatively. The pouching system leaks repeatedly into the abdominal crease. What is the best action?

options: Provide English handouts since the medication names are the same in Spanish
Have the bilingual family member interpret the medication teaching
Discharge without detailed teaching and let the clinic handle it
Arrange a qualified medical interpreter and pharmacist counseling with teach-back in the patient's language
rationale: Federal language-access standards and safety require a qualified medical interpreter, not family members, for complex medication teaching; pharmacist counseling with teach-back verifies understanding. English handouts and deferred teaching leave a high-risk patient unable to manage 7 new drugs, and family interpreters introduce errors and confidentiality concerns.
stem: A 56-year-old who speaks only Spanish is newly diagnosed with heart failure and prescribed 7 new medications. The nurse is preparing discharge teaching. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Dietitian consult only, since low albumin is the main problem
Speech therapy swallow evaluation first, then dietitian for a calorie and protein repletion plan based on safe diet level
Encourage large volumes of thin liquids to improve intake
Start total parenteral nutrition immediately
rationale: Aspiration risk must be clarified before any diet advancement; speech therapy determines the safe diet level, and the dietitian then builds the repletion plan around it. Albumin reflects inflammation as much as nutrition, TPN is not first-line when the gut works, and pushing thin liquids in a patient who coughs risks aspiration pneumonia.
stem: A 71-year-old with albumin 2.4 g/dL, a sacral pressure injury, and poor intake coughs with thin liquids. Which consult sequence best addresses both safety and nutrition?

options: Wait until hospital discharge to begin any rehabilitation
Order physical therapy only at the time of discharge
Request early physical and occupational therapy consults during hospitalization for mobilization and ADL retraining
Enforce strict bedrest to conserve the patient's energy
rationale: Post-ICU weakness responds best to early mobilization and ADL retraining begun during hospitalization, which reduces deconditioning, delirium, and length of stay. Waiting until discharge wastes the recovery window, and bedrest accelerates muscle loss. PT and OT together address both mobility and self-care function.
stem: A 64-year-old spent 10 days in the ICU with sepsis and now has profound weakness, unable to sit at the bedside edge. The family asks when rehabilitation will start. What is the best plan?

options: Initiate the CIWA protocol, notify the provider, and consult addiction medicine and social work
Ignore the alcohol history since the admission is for cellulitis
Administer a benzodiazepine without any assessment scale
Expedite discharge to avoid withdrawal in the hospital
rationale: Tremor and tachycardia a day after the last drink signal impending alcohol withdrawal; a CIWA-driven protocol with provider notification manages symptoms safely while addiction medicine and social work address the underlying disorder. Unassessed benzodiazepine dosing is unsafe, and discharging a patient into withdrawal risks seizures and readmission.
stem: A 45-year-old admitted with cellulitis has a history of heavy alcohol use, is tremulous with heart rate 110, and reports his last drink was yesterday. What is the best interprofessional action?

options: Lecture the patient on the importance of compliance
Consult cardiology for more aggressive diuresis
Discharge home with the same plan
Engage social work, a diabetes educator, and behavioral health to assess barriers such as cost, transportation, and depression
rationale: Repeated nonadherence usually reflects unaddressed barriers like depression, cost, health literacy, or transportation rather than willful noncompliance; social work, diabetes education, and behavioral health target those root causes. Lecturing and repeat diuresis treat episodes without preventing the next one.
stem: A 52-year-old with heart failure, diabetes, and depression repeatedly misses medications and clinic appointments. Previous admissions focused only on diuresis. Which interprofessional approach best addresses the pattern?

options: Wound care nurse alone changing dressings daily
WOCN plus dietitian plus physical therapy for a combined plan of wound management, protein repletion, and offloading and positioning
Immediate surgical consult for flap closure
Leave the wound open to air without a dressing plan
rationale: Pressure injury healing requires simultaneous pressure redistribution, adequate protein and calories, and expert wound management; the WOCN, dietitian, and PT each own one pillar. Dressings alone fail without offloading and nutrition, and surgical flap closure is inappropriate in a malnourished patient with ongoing pressure exposure.
stem: A 78-year-old incontinent patient with a stage 3 sacral pressure injury is malnourished and rarely repositioned. Which coordinated team plan best promotes healing?

options: Reassure him that these feelings are normal and take no further action
Discharge him since his cardiac status is stable
Request a psychiatry liaison consult for post-MI depression screening and treatment planning
Start an antidepressant without a formal evaluation
rationale: Depressive symptoms after MI predict poor adherence, worse cardiac outcomes, and suicide risk; psychiatry liaison provides formal screening, safety assessment, and treatment planning. Reassurance alone misses a treatable condition, and starting an antidepressant without evaluation bypasses safety assessment and drug interaction review.
stem: A 60-year-old on post-MI day 3 is tearful, reports anhedonia and poor sleep, and says he feels hopeless about returning to work. What is the best action?

options: Request pharmacy and cardiology consults to coordinate a periprocedural bridging plan
Stop warfarin with no bridging plan and proceed
Continue therapeutic warfarin through the hip surgery
Switch to aspirin alone for the perioperative period
rationale: A mechanical mitral valve carries high thromboembolic risk, so periprocedural anticoagulation requires cardiology and pharmacy expertise to balance clot versus bleeding risk. Stopping warfarin without a plan risks valve thrombosis, continuing it through major orthopedic surgery risks catastrophic bleeding, and aspirin alone is inadequate for a mechanical valve.
stem: A 70-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin needs urgent hip fracture surgery. The team is uncertain about bridging. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Proceed with contrast without any precautions
Cancel the scan since contrast is absolutely contraindicated in CKD
Give contrast and hope for the best
Request a nephrology consult for contrast-associated AKI risk mitigation such as hydration planning and holding nephrotoxins
rationale: Severe CKD raises the risk of contrast-associated AKI, but the scan may be essential for cancer staging; nephrology helps weigh risk and benefit and implement mitigation like pre-hydration and medication holds. Contrast is not absolutely contraindicated, and proceeding without precautions in an eGFR of 22 is unsafe.
stem: A 66-year-old with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22) is scheduled for a contrast-enhanced CT to evaluate a pancreatic mass. What is the best consultative step?

options: Place the PEG tube as the family requests
Request palliative care and speech therapy consults for a goals-of-care discussion and swallow assessment
Force-feed the patient to maintain nutrition
Keep the patient NPO indefinitely without any family discussion
rationale: In advanced dementia, tube feeding does not prevent aspiration, prolong life, or improve comfort per current evidence; palliative care facilitates a goals-of-care conversation while speech therapy objectively characterizes swallow safety. Placing a PEG on family request alone bypasses informed decision-making about benefits and burdens.
stem: An 84-year-old with advanced dementia, recurrent aspiration, and dysphagia has a family requesting a PEG tube. The patient cannot participate in decisions. What is the best interprofessional approach?
topic: Goals of care - feeding tube request

options: Tell the patient that severe pain is expected and to tolerate it
Double the oxycodone dose independently
Request an acute pain service consult for multimodal pain optimization
Stop all analgesics to reassess the baseline pain
rationale: Pain refractory to a multimodal regimen that blocks rehabilitation warrants acute pain service expertise for options like regional techniques or regimen adjustment. Simply escalating opioids independently risks oversedation, tolerating the pain guarantees immobility and complications, and stopping analgesics is inhumane and counterproductive.
stem: A 68-year-old is post-op day 1 after total knee arthroplasty with pain 9/10 despite scheduled acetaminophen, celecoxib, and oxycodone. The patient cannot participate in therapy. What is the best action?

options: Notify the provider, obtain a 12-lead ECG, and prepare for rate-control orders and a cardiology consult
Perform synchronized cardioversion at the bedside
Document the rhythm and take no action since the patient is talking
Give aspirin and arrange discharge
rationale: New rapid atrial fibrillation with symptoms requires prompt provider notification, ECG confirmation, rate control, and cardiology input for workup and anticoagulation decisions. Bedside cardioversion by the nurse is outside scope and unsafe without orders and sedation, and ignoring a new tachyarrhythmia risks decompensation.
stem: A 72-year-old admitted with pneumonia develops new atrial fibrillation with heart rate 142, blood pressure 110/70, and mild dyspnea. What is the best immediate nursing action?

options: Keep the patient admitted for the full 2 weeks of IV therapy
Discharge on oral antibiotics that are inadequate for the organism
Discontinue antibiotics since the patient is improving
Request infectious disease input on outpatient parenteral therapy options and social work for placement and resources
rationale: Infectious disease can determine whether OPAT, a medical respite bed, or an alternative regimen fits this patient's circumstances, while social work addresses housing, coverage, and follow-up. A 2-week admission for stable cellulitis is poor resource stewardship, and inadequate oral therapy risks treatment failure and readmission.
stem: A 40-year-old homeless patient with cellulitis requires 2 weeks of IV nafcillin and has no insurance. The infection is improving. What is the best coordinated discharge plan?

options: Silent observer, since physicians lead all care decisions
Presenting patient status, barriers to progress, and patient and family goals using structured communication, and ensuring consult recommendations are followed through
Making independent medical diagnoses to speed up the team
Writing all orders discussed during rounds
rationale: The nurse contributes continuous bedside assessment, identifies barriers the team may miss, voices patient and family goals, and closes the loop on consult recommendations. Silent observation wastes nursing insight, while diagnosing and order-writing exceed the RN role on rounds.
stem: Which statement best describes the nurse's role in interdisciplinary rounds?

options: Perform the paracentesis at the bedside without any consult
Transfuse platelets and plasma first in all cases before the procedure
Coordinate gastroenterology or interventional radiology for the procedure, ensure informed consent and timeout, and avoid routine prophylactic transfusion per current guidance
Cancel the procedure because the labs are abnormal
rationale: Paracentesis is generally safe in cirrhosis without routine correction of platelets or INR, which do not predict bleeding in this population; coordination with GI or IR ensures proper technique and monitoring. Mandatory transfusion exposes the patient to unnecessary risk, and canceling leaves symptomatic tense ascites untreated.
stem: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis has tense ascites causing dyspnea, platelets 45,000, and INR 1.9. Therapeutic paracentesis is planned. What is the best coordinated approach?

options: Stop the PCA, stimulate the patient, apply oxygen, notify the provider and rapid response, and request anesthesia pain and respiratory consults
Increase the PCA dose since the patient appears comfortable
Let the patient sleep since rest promotes healing
Remove the oxygen to assess the true baseline saturation
rationale: Somnolence with hypoxemia on a PCA in severe OSA signals opioid-induced hypoventilation; the infusion must stop, the patient stimulated and oxygenated, and the team escalated with anesthesia and respiratory input for safe analgesia. Increasing opioids or removing oxygen in this setting risks respiratory arrest.
stem: A 55-year-old with BMI 48 and severe OSA is 6 hours post bowel surgery on a PCA, now somnolent with SpO2 89% on 2L nasal cannula. What is the best immediate coordinated action?

options: Hand the patient a pamphlet about diabetes
No teaching is needed since the clinic will handle it later
Ask a family member to teach insulin technique at home
Consult the diabetes educator for survival-skills teaching with teach-back before discharge
rationale: New insulin starts require structured survival-skills education on injection, hypoglycemia, and sick-day rules, verified by teach-back, which the diabetes educator provides. A pamphlet or deferred teaching leaves the patient unsafe overnight, and delegating teaching to family without professional instruction risks technique errors.
stem: A 48-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (A1c 11.2%) is starting basal-bolus insulin and will discharge tomorrow. The patient has never used insulin. What is the best discharge preparation?

options: Physical therapy only, since walking is the priority
Early coordinated speech therapy for aphasia and swallow plus physical and occupational therapy for mobility and ADLs
No rehabilitation until 2 weeks after the stroke
Psychiatry consult only for frustration
rationale: Stroke recovery requires simultaneous speech therapy for communication and swallowing alongside PT and OT for mobility and self-care; early coordinated rehab improves outcomes. Delaying therapy wastes the neuroplasticity window, and PT alone ignores the aphasia and dysphagia that affect safety and quality of life.
stem: A 68-year-old with acute stroke has expressive aphasia and right hemiparesis. The family asks what therapies are needed. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Intubate per the demanding child's request
Avoid the discussion and continue current care
Request palliative care, chaplain, and ethics consults while the nurse facilitates a structured family meeting
Discharge the patient to resolve the conflict at home
rationale: Value-laden family conflict near the end of life benefits from palliative care's goals-of-care expertise, chaplain support, and ethics guidance, with the nurse convening a structured meeting. Intubating on one child's demand bypasses substituted judgment, and avoiding the conversation guarantees a crisis decision.
stem: A 78-year-old with end-stage COPD is declining. One child demands intubation while another says the patient would not want it, and no advance directive exists. What is the best interprofessional approach?
