topic: Family conflict - palliative and ethics consults

options: Hold the next dose, notify the provider, and request pharmacy for dosing and monitoring guidance
Continue vancomycin unchanged since the infection is serious
Switch to oral vancomycin for the systemic infection
Stop all antibiotics immediately
rationale: A supratherapeutic trough with rising creatinine indicates vancomycin-associated kidney injury; holding the dose, notifying the provider, and engaging pharmacy for AUC-guided dosing prevents further harm. Oral vancomycin is not absorbed systemically, and stopping all antibiotics abandons infection treatment.
stem: A 64-year-old on vancomycin has a trough of 32 mcg/mL with creatinine rising from 1.0 to 1.8 mg/dL. What is the best action?

options: Opioids alone around the clock
Reassure the patient that the pain is imagined and will pass
Schedule a revision amputation
Acute pain service plus physical therapy for mirror therapy and desensitization plus behavioral health for coping strategies
rationale: Phantom limb pain responds best to multimodal care combining neuropathic agents via pain service expertise, PT techniques like mirror therapy and desensitization, and behavioral coping strategies. Opioids alone are often ineffective for neuropathic pain, dismissing the pain destroys trust, and re-amputation does not treat the central mechanism.
stem: A 60-year-old with a recent below-knee amputation reports burning phantom limb pain 7/10 that disrupts sleep. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Add more medications to cover all conditions
Request a pharmacist-led medication reconciliation and de-prescribing review with the provider
Stop all medications to simplify the regimen
Skip the review since the list was accurate on admission
rationale: Recurrent hypoglycemia and hypotension in polypharmacy signal high-risk prescribing; a pharmacist-led review identifies de-prescribing opportunities, interactions, and renal dosing issues in partnership with the provider. Stopping everything is unsafe, adding more worsens the problem, and admission accuracy does not equal appropriateness.
stem: A 78-year-old on 12 medications had 2 recent admissions for hypoglycemia and hypotension. Before discharge, what is the best medication safety intervention?

options: General surgery consult first for possible operative management
Discharge home once vitals stabilize
Urgent gastroenterology consult for endoscopy and variceal management plus hepatology input
Observe without endoscopy since bleeding appears to have slowed
rationale: Suspected variceal bleeding requires urgent endoscopy, ideally within 12 hours, for band ligation and secondary prophylaxis planning, with hepatology guiding liver-specific care. Surgery is rarely first-line for variceal bleeding, and observation alone misses the window for definitive therapy and rebleed prevention.
stem: A 55-year-old with cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. After resuscitation, vitals are stable and hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL. What is the best consult sequencing?

options: Notify the surgeon, keep the patient NPO with NG decompression, and consider a nutrition consult if ileus is prolonged
Advance to a regular diet to stimulate bowel function
Administer a laxative without an order
Discharge home with instructions to eat lightly
rationale: Postoperative ileus requires continued bowel rest with decompression and surgeon notification; early nutrition consult planning matters if ileus persists beyond several days. Advancing diet or unsupervised laxatives risk worsening distension or anastomotic complications, and discharge with an unresolved ileus is unsafe.
stem: A 70-year-old is post-op day 3 after laparotomy with no flatus, abdominal distension, and nausea, currently NPO with an NG tube. What is the best management?

options: No referrals; deconditioning resolves on its own
Physical therapy only for weakness
Direct nursing home placement without evaluation
Physical and occupational therapy plus cognitive screening with speech or neuropsychology plus case management for rehabilitation placement
rationale: Post-sepsis syndrome combines physical deconditioning with cognitive impairment affecting safety and independence; PT and OT address function while cognitive screening characterizes deficits and case management matches placement to needs. PT alone ignores the cognitive component, and placement without evaluation may be unnecessarily restrictive.
stem: A 66-year-old sepsis survivor is deconditioned and the family notes new forgetfulness and difficulty managing bills. What is the best referral set?

options: Cardiology and neurosurgery consults
Physical therapy for fall risk, wound ostomy nursing for skin breakdown, and dietitian for a positive malnutrition screen
Interventional radiology and electrophysiology
Anesthesia for elective procedures
rationale: Nurse-driven protocols commonly authorize referrals triggered by nursing assessments, such as PT for fall risk, WOCN for skin issues, and dietitian for malnutrition screens, because they are low-risk and assessment-based. Cardiology, neurosurgery, IR, and anesthesia consults require physician judgment about medical necessity and procedural risk.
stem: The hospital allows nurse-driven consult protocols for certain referrals. Which set of consults can the nurse typically initiate without waiting for a physician order?

options: Apply wrist restraints each evening
Administer a high-dose sedative at bedtime
Request geriatrics and pharmacy consults for delirium evaluation and de-prescribing, with nonpharmacologic measures first
Hire a private sitter as the sole intervention
rationale: Evening agitation in an older adult warrants evaluation for delirium and review of sedating or anticholinergic medications by geriatrics and pharmacy, paired with nonpharmacologic strategies like daylight exposure and toileting. Restraints and sedatives worsen delirium and fall risk, and a sitter alone does not address the underlying cause.
stem: An 82-year-old with sundowning pulls at his IV each evening. The family asks for someone to watch him overnight. What is the best interprofessional approach?

options: Vascular surgery to confirm adequate perfusion, then plastic surgery for coverage planning, with infectious disease as needed
Infectious disease alone since the wound is open
Immediate below-knee amputation
Dress the wound and discharge without consults
rationale: Exposed tendon requires confirmed perfusion before coverage planning, so vascular assessment comes first, followed by plastic surgery for definitive closure; ID joins if infection develops. Amputation is premature with palpable pulses and no infection, and discharge leaves exposed tendon at high risk of desiccation and infection.
stem: A 50-year-old with diabetes has a foot wound with exposed tendon, palpable pedal pulses, and no systemic signs of infection. Which consult sequence is best?

options: Schedule routine dialysis for tomorrow morning
Give oral potassium binders and observe
Discharge with instructions to attend the next outpatient session
Urgent nephrology consult for emergent dialysis coordination plus dietitian teaching on potassium restriction and adherence barriers
rationale: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes in a missed-dialysis ESRD patient is a medical emergency requiring urgent nephrology-coordinated dialysis, not routine scheduling. Binders alone are too slow for peaked T waves, and discharge risks fatal arrhythmia; dietitian and social work follow-up addresses the adherence gap that caused the crisis.
stem: A 62-year-old with ESRD on hemodialysis is admitted with potassium 6.1 mEq/L, peaked T waves, and missed his last 2 dialysis sessions. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Tell the patient to complete the steps in any order without guidance
Coordinate the required clearances in the program's sequence, starting with psychology and nutrition, and track completion so surgery is not delayed
Skip the psychological evaluation to save time
Schedule surgery first and complete clearances afterward
rationale: Bariatric programs require staged clearances because psychological readiness and nutrition behavior change determine candidacy before surgical scheduling; the nurse navigator sequences and tracks them to prevent delays. Skipping the psych evaluation violates program safety standards, and scheduling surgery before clearance risks cancellation.
stem: A 44-year-old is pursuing bariatric surgery. The program requires psychological evaluation, nutrition counseling, and cardiology clearance. The patient is confused about the order of steps. What is the nurse navigator's best action?

options: Proceed to surgery immediately without any coordination
Cancel surgery indefinitely because of the apixaban
Coordinate orthopedics, cardiology, and anesthesia on timing of surgery versus anticoagulant hold, using reversal only if emergent bleeding dictates
Switch to warfarin today and operate tomorrow
rationale: Hip fracture surgery timing on a DOAC requires balancing thromboembolic risk against surgical bleeding, coordinated across orthopedics, cardiology, and anesthesia; routine reversal is not indicated without life-threatening bleeding. Operating immediately on full apixaban risks major bleeding, indefinite cancellation condemns the patient to immobility, and switching to warfarin acutely is impractical and unsafe.
stem: An 80-year-old with a hip fracture takes apixaban daily for atrial fibrillation and last dosed 8 hours ago. The orthopedic surgeon wants to operate within 24 hours. What is the best coordinated plan?
topic: Hip fracture on anticoagulant - team coordination

options: Allow the patient to eat a regular meal to test swallowing
Request speech therapy evaluation for swallow and speaking valve candidacy before any oral intake
Remove the tracheostomy tube since the patient wants to eat
Consult psychiatry for the patient's frustration
rationale: A new tracheostomy alters swallow mechanics and airway protection, so speech therapy must evaluate swallow safety and speaking valve candidacy before oral intake. Removing the tube prematurely risks airway loss, and allowing unassessed oral intake risks aspiration. Frustration is expected and addressed through communication strategies, not psychiatry first.
stem: A 70-year-old with a new tracheostomy after prolonged intubation has the cuff down and asks to eat lunch. The patient is drooling slightly. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Gastroenterology alone, since the pancreas is the problem
Discharge with advice to stop drinking
Pain management only with opioids
Coordinated gastroenterology, addiction medicine, and nutrition consults to address etiology, recurrence risk, and malnutrition
rationale: Recurrent alcohol-related pancreatitis requires treating the underlying alcohol use disorder and malnutrition alongside pancreatic management; addiction medicine and nutrition address the drivers of recurrence. GI alone manages episodes without preventing the next one, and opioids alone risk dependence without addressing cause.
stem: A 44-year-old with recurrent acute pancreatitis related to alcohol use is admitted with a third episode this year and is malnourished. What is the best interprofessional plan?

options: Transition from the insulin drip to basal-bolus subcutaneous insulin with appropriate overlap per protocol, and consult the diabetes educator
Stop insulin entirely once the anion gap closes
Continue the insulin drip until discharge
Switch to sliding-scale insulin alone
rationale: DKA resolution requires overlapping basal insulin before stopping the drip to prevent rebound hyperglycemia and DKA recurrence; diabetes educator input prepares the patient for home management. Stopping insulin entirely is dangerous in type 1 or insulin-requiring diabetes, and sliding scale alone provides no basal coverage.
stem: A 52-year-old with DKA has a closed anion gap on an insulin drip and wants to eat dinner. The team is transitioning off the drip. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Resume apixaban immediately to prevent stroke
Discharge home with observation instructions
Urgent neurosurgery consult with anticoagulant held per protocol, with reversal available if the patient deteriorates
Consult psychiatry for the fall
rationale: A subdural hematoma on anticoagulation requires urgent neurosurgical evaluation; the anticoagulant is held and reversal agents are reserved for deterioration or operative need. Resuming apixaban risks hematoma expansion, and discharge without neurosurgical input is unsafe in an anticoagulated head injury.
stem: A 76-year-old on apixaban fell and has a small subdural hematoma on CT, currently alert with stable neuro checks. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Treat at home with over-the-counter burn cream
Refer to a verified burn center per American Burn Association criteria for partial-thickness burns of 10 percent or greater
Manage as an outpatient without specialty input
Apply ice directly to the burns
rationale: Partial-thickness burns covering 10 percent or more of total body surface area in an adult meet ABA referral criteria for burn center care, which improves grafting decisions and outcomes. Home treatment of this extent risks infection and hypertrophic scarring, and ice causes further tissue injury.
stem: A 35-year-old sustained partial-thickness cooking burns estimated at 12 percent total body surface area. What is the best referral decision?

options: Order an MRI to confirm the diagnosis before calling anyone
Start oral antibiotics and observe overnight
Consult dermatology for a rash evaluation in the morning
Activate an emergent surgical consult for suspected necrotizing fasciitis plus infectious disease and ICU coordination, with the nurse escalating immediately
rationale: Pain out of proportion with rapidly progressive erythema, bullae, and hypotension is necrotizing soft tissue infection until proven otherwise, a surgical emergency where delay increases mortality; imaging must not delay surgical evaluation. The nurse's role is immediate escalation and coordination of surgery, ID, and critical care.
stem: A 58-year-old with diabetes has rapidly spreading leg erythema, bullae, pain out of proportion to exam, and blood pressure 88/54. What is the best immediate coordinated action?

options: Hematology plus acute pain service plus social work for an individualized pain plan and care coordination
Opioids only, dosed the same as every prior visit
Discharge without follow-up since pain crises are expected
Psychiatry consult alone for drug-seeking concerns
rationale: Frequent sickle cell pain crises benefit from hematology-directed disease management, an individualized pain plan from the pain service to ensure consistent ED treatment, and social work for barriers like transportation. Uniform opioid dosing ignores individualized plans, and labeling the patient drug-seeking without evaluation perpetuates inequitable care.
stem: A 28-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with a vaso-occlusive pain crisis, the fifth ED visit this year, and reports prior visits involved long waits for pain medication. What is the best coordinated plan?
topic: Sickle cell pain crisis - team approach

options: Stop tacrolimus immediately to fight the infection
Treat with over-the-counter antipyretics and observe
Notify the transplant team and request infectious disease input, continuing immunosuppression unless the transplant team directs otherwise
Consult nephrology instead of the transplant team
rationale: Fever in a transplant recipient is a transplant emergency; the transplant team must direct any immunosuppression changes because abrupt cessation risks rejection, while infectious disease guides workup for opportunistic and typical pathogens. Stopping tacrolimus independently or observing risks graft loss and sepsis.
stem: A 62-year-old kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus presents with fever 38.9 C and malaise. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Orthopedics alone, since the tibia is the main injury
Coordinated orthopedics, trauma surgery, pain management, and early physical and occupational therapy
Bedrest for 2 weeks before any therapy
Discharge home with crutches and no follow-up
rationale: Multi-trauma with competing injuries needs coordinated surgical planning so fixation timing and pain control support early mobilization; PT and OT prevent deconditioning and address ADLs. Orthopedics alone misses the rib fractures and pulmonary risk, and prolonged bedrest invites atelectasis, VTE, and deconditioning.
stem: A 45-year-old after a motorcycle crash has multiple rib fractures and a tibial shaft fracture, is hemodynamically stable, and reports severe pain. What is the best interprofessional plan?

options: No further workup is needed after one provoked event
Lifelong anticoagulation without any evaluation
Genetic testing ordered by the nurse independently
Hematology consult for hypercoagulable workup and long-term anticoagulation planning
rationale: Unprovoked or recurrent VTE in a young patient warrants hematology-guided hypercoagulable evaluation to inform duration of anticoagulation and family screening. Committing to lifelong anticoagulation or forgoing workup without specialist input is premature, and nurses do not independently order genetic testing.
stem: A 38-year-old with an unprovoked pulmonary embolism on a heparin infusion asks how long blood thinners will be needed. There is no clear provoking factor. What is the best consultative step?

options: Wound ostomy nurse for pouching and staged teaching plus psych liaison and social work for coping and support resources
Force the patient to look at the stoma immediately
Delay all teaching until the patient asks
Discharge without any ostomy teaching
rationale: New ostomy adjustment requires expert WOCN teaching delivered in stages matched to readiness, with psych liaison and social work addressing grief, body image, and support needs. Forcing confrontation increases trauma, and discharging without teaching risks leaks, skin breakdown, and readmission.
stem: A 55-year-old with a new colostomy is withdrawn and refuses to look at the stoma on post-op day 2. What is the best coordinated plan?
topic: New ostomy - psychosocial and WOCN support

options: Schedule ICD implantation without further discussion
Reassure the patient that the rhythm is benign
Electrophysiology consult for sudden death risk stratification and ICD candidacy, with nurse-provided education on the device decision
Increase beta-blocker independently to suppress the rhythm
rationale: HFrEF with EF 20 percent and NSVT meets criteria for electrophysiology evaluation for primary prevention ICD; the nurse supports informed decision-making through education, not independent medication changes. Implantation without specialist stratification bypasses shared decision-making, and reassurance minimizes a potentially lethal arrhythmia risk.
stem: A 64-year-old with HFrEF (EF 20%) has nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on telemetry and asks about a defibrillator. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Ignore the alcohol history since the bleed is the priority
Addiction medicine consult with thiamine replacement and CIWA-driven withdrawal management coordinated with GI bleed care
Give a large benzodiazepine dose without assessment
Discharge once the bleeding stops
rationale: Alcohol withdrawal can be fatal and must be managed concurrently with the GI bleed using CIWA-driven therapy, thiamine to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and addiction medicine for the underlying disorder. Unassessed sedation is unsafe, and ignoring withdrawal risks seizures that complicate bleed management.
stem: A 52-year-old admitted with a GI bleed has a history of heavy alcohol use, tremor, and a rising CIWA score. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Ignore the rhythm since the patient feels well
Perform bedside cardioversion
Increase the patient's home metoprolol independently
Notify the surgeon and request a cardiology consult for postoperative atrial fibrillation management including rate control and anticoagulation decisions
rationale: New postoperative AF after CABG requires prompt notification and cardiology input for rate versus rhythm strategy and stroke-risk-based anticoagulation decisions. Bedside cardioversion without orders and sedation is unsafe, and independent beta-blocker titration in a fresh post-op patient risks hypotension and graft issues.
stem: A 66-year-old is post-op day 2 after CABG and develops new atrial fibrillation with heart rate 130, blood pressure 118/72. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Qualified medical interpreter plus pharmacist teach-back on warfarin in the patient's language plus community health worker referral for follow-up support
English-only written instructions since numbers are universal
Family member interpretation of the warfarin teaching
No teaching; the clinic will explain it later
rationale: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index with diet and drug interactions, so safe initiation demands professional interpreter-mediated teaching, pharmacist teach-back, and community follow-up support. Family interpretation introduces dangerous errors, and deferring teaching leaves the patient unprotected during the highest-risk first week.
stem: A 68-year-old with limited English proficiency and low health literacy is starting warfarin for atrial fibrillation and discharges tomorrow. What is the best coordinated discharge teaching plan?
topic: Health literacy - interpreter and CHW referral

options: Wait until discharge to involve the case manager
Limit the assessment to insurance verification
Complete a comprehensive assessment within 24 hours for high-risk patients, screening medical, functional, psychosocial, and financial needs to build the discharge plan
Focus only on the admitting diagnosis
rationale: Early comprehensive case management assessment identifies discharge barriers, functional deficits, and psychosocial risks while there is still time to arrange services; waiting until discharge compresses planning into avoidable days. Insurance verification alone misses the clinical and social factors that drive readmissions.
stem: A 74-year-old living alone is admitted with heart failure exacerbation and has a history of falls and missed medications. When and how should case management first engage?

options: Confirm the admission meets medical necessity criteria using evidence-based guidelines such as InterQual or MCG, and document severity of illness and intensity of service
Approve all admissions regardless of clinical criteria
Deny the stay based on diagnosis alone
Delay review until after discharge
rationale: Utilization review applies objective criteria to severity of illness and intensity of service to justify the admission level of care and support payment. Diagnosis alone does not establish necessity, and delaying review until after discharge forfeits the chance to correct status or authorize continued stay prospectively.
stem: A 58-year-old is admitted with cellulitis, afebrile, with mild erythema improving on oral antibiotics. The utilization review nurse questions inpatient medical necessity. What is the UR nurse's proper role?

options: Begin discharge planning on the day of discharge
Leave discharge planning entirely to the physician
Assume the family will arrange everything
Begin discharge planning at admission with an estimated discharge date, identifying anticipated needs and barriers early
rationale: Discharge planning that starts at admission with a target date allows time to arrange home health, DME, and follow-up, reducing avoidable days and readmissions. Day-of-discharge planning compresses complex arrangements into hours, and assuming family capacity without assessment risks unsafe discharges.
stem: A 70-year-old admitted with pneumonia lives alone and will likely need home oxygen and home health. What discharge planning approach best manages length of stay?

options: The terms are interchangeable and status does not matter
Observation is an outpatient status for patients needing short-term evaluation to determine if inpatient admission is warranted, with different billing and cost-sharing implications
Observation always converts to inpatient after 24 hours
Inpatient status requires ICU-level care
rationale: Observation is an outpatient billing status for evaluation and management, typically under 48 hours, while inpatient requires an expectation of a stay spanning two midnights; status affects patient cost-sharing and SNF qualifying days. The terms are not interchangeable, and conversion depends on clinical criteria, not the clock alone.
stem: A 66-year-old with chest pain is placed in observation after negative initial workup. The family asks why the patient is not admitted. How should the nurse explain observation status?

options: Send the patient to any facility without authorization
Assume Medicare Advantage plans never require authorization
Verify benefits and obtain prior authorization for the skilled nursing facility stay, confirming qualifying criteria and network status
Have the patient pay cash for the SNF stay
rationale: Most Medicare Advantage and commercial plans require prior authorization for SNF placement and apply qualifying criteria; verifying benefits and network status before transfer prevents denials and surprise bills. Sending the patient without authorization risks claim denial, and cash pay is unnecessary when coverage exists.
stem: A 78-year-old with a Medicare Advantage plan needs SNF placement after hip fracture surgery. What is the case manager's best action regarding authorization?

options: Question duplicate daily labs that do not change management and promote diagnostic stewardship
Order additional daily labs to be thorough
Repeat all labs because the night shift results might be wrong
Avoid reviewing lab orders since that is solely the physician's role
rationale: Resource stewardship includes questioning low-value repeat testing that does not change management, reducing cost, blood loss, and false positives. Ordering extra labs to be thorough increases iatrogenic anemia and expense, and nurses play a legitimate role in stewardship conversations with the team.
stem: A stable 60-year-old has had a daily CBC and basic metabolic panel for 6 days with no changes in management. What is the best resource stewardship action?

options: No community resources exist for this situation
Recommend a private-pay companion service only
Advise nursing home placement immediately
Refer to the Area Agency on Aging for options counseling, home-delivered meals, transportation, and caregiver support programs
rationale: The Area Agency on Aging is the designated community hub connecting older adults to meals, transportation, respite, and benefits counseling, often at low or no cost. Jumping to nursing home placement bypasses less restrictive options, and private-pay companionship alone does not address meals, transport, or caregiver burden.
stem: An 82-year-old living alone with early dementia needs meals, transportation to appointments, and caregiver respite for her daughter. Which community resource best coordinates these needs?
topic: Community resources - Area Agency on Aging

options: No follow-up is needed if the patient feels better
Schedule the first primary care or cardiology follow-up within 7 days of discharge with reconciled medications
Wait 6 weeks for follow-up
Follow up only if symptoms return
rationale: Early post-discharge follow-up within 7 days allows medication reconciliation, weight and symptom review, and titration before decompensation, and is a core readmission-reduction strategy. Waiting weeks or until symptoms return misses the vulnerable transition window when most preventable readmissions occur.
stem: A 68-year-old with heart failure is being discharged after diuresis. Which follow-up plan best reduces readmission risk?

options: Accept the denial without any review
Immediately discharge the patient
Request a peer-to-peer review between the attending physician and the payer's medical director to discuss medical necessity
File a lawsuit against the insurer
rationale: Peer-to-peer review gives the attending a direct clinical dialogue with the payer's medical director to present severity, failed outpatient management, or complicating factors that criteria screens may miss. Accepting the denial without challenge forfeits legitimate revenue and may force an unsafe discharge, while litigation is premature and disproportionate.
stem: An insurer denies continued inpatient stay for a 64-year-old with pneumonia and hypoxemia requiring 4L oxygen, stating criteria are not met. What is the case manager's best next step?

options: Evaluate whether the patient meets intensive rehabilitation facility criteria of needing multiple therapy disciplines with physician oversight, versus SNF criteria, and present options honoring patient choice
Send all stroke patients to SNF by default
Choose the facility closest to the hospital regardless of capability
Let the insurer decide without clinical input
rationale: IRF admission requires the ability to tolerate intensive therapy with close physician supervision, while SNF suits less intensive needs; the case manager matches criteria to the patient and honors informed choice among qualified options. Defaulting to SNF or proximity ignores rehabilitation potential, and abdicating to the insurer skips clinical advocacy.
stem: A 70-year-old after stroke needs rehabilitation. The family asks about the difference between acute rehab and a skilled nursing facility. What is the case manager's best approach?

options: Tell the patient to buy equipment without guidance
Order DME after discharge and let the vendor sort it out
Assume the supplier will handle all paperwork
Assess the specific equipment need, verify coverage and supplier requirements, and coordinate delivery before discharge with patient training
rationale: DME requires matching the prescription to coverage rules, using contracted suppliers, and ensuring delivery and training before the patient goes home; coordination prevents gaps in oxygen, wound, or mobility support. Post-discharge ordering leaves the patient without essential equipment, and unguided purchasing risks non-covered, unsafe devices.
stem: A 72-year-old discharging on home oxygen and a walker needs durable medical equipment. What is the case manager's best coordination approach?

options: No referral is ever needed in an HMO
The patient can see any specialist without authorization
Obtain the primary care referral and authorization required by the HMO before scheduling the specialist visit
Bill the specialist visit as emergency to bypass the referral
rationale: HMO plans typically require a PCP referral and prior authorization for specialist care; obtaining it before the visit prevents claim denial and patient liability. Mischaracterizing a routine visit as emergency to bypass rules is fraudulent, and assuming open access ignores plan design.
stem: A 55-year-old with an HMO plan needs an outpatient cardiology visit after discharge. What must the care team ensure?

options: Tell the patient to skip the medication if it is expensive
Switch to a less effective drug without discussion
Connect the patient with manufacturer patient assistance programs, foundation grants, or 340B pharmacy options through social work or pharmacy
Have the patient borrow medication from a neighbor
rationale: Patient assistance programs, charitable foundations, and 340B pricing legitimately reduce costs for expensive essential medications, coordinated through social work or pharmacy. Skipping doses or borrowing medication is unsafe, and switching efficacy without discussion undermines informed care.
stem: A 60-year-old cannot afford a newly prescribed anticoagulant costing 500 dollars per month and has no drug coverage. What is the best resource intervention?

options: Confirm the patient is homebound and needs skilled nursing or therapy, then refer to a Medicare-certified home health agency
Refer any patient who requests it regardless of criteria
Require 24-hour needs for home health eligibility
Use home health as a substitute for a needed SNF stay
rationale: Medicare home health requires homebound status plus a skilled need such as nursing or therapy, delivered through a certified agency; confirming criteria ensures coverage. Home health is intermittent skilled care, not 24-hour custodial care, and cannot substitute for a SNF when daily skilled needs exceed its scope.
stem: A 76-year-old homebound patient needs wound care and physical therapy after discharge. What determines appropriate home health referral?

options: Hospice requires the patient to stop all medications
Hospice is only for the last 3 days of life
Any patient with a serious illness automatically qualifies
Verify a prognosis of 6 months or less if the disease runs its normal course, with physician certification, and explain the comfort-focused benefit
rationale: Medicare hospice eligibility requires physician certification of a 6-month prognosis, and the benefit focuses on comfort rather than cure; explaining this helps families understand what hospice provides. Hospice does not require stopping all medications, only curative-directed ones, and serious illness alone does not meet criteria.
stem: An 80-year-old with end-stage heart failure has worsening symptoms despite optimal therapy. The family asks about hospice. What should the nurse explain about eligibility?

options: They are identical services with different names
Palliative care can be provided alongside curative treatment at any stage, while hospice requires forgoing curative treatment with a 6-month prognosis
Palliative care is only for cancer patients
Hospice must be chosen before palliative care
rationale: Palliative care is appropriate alongside curative therapy from diagnosis onward, whereas hospice is a specific Medicare benefit requiring a 6-month prognosis and a comfort-focused plan. Conflating them delays symptom support for patients still pursuing treatment, and palliative care serves all serious illnesses.
stem: A 62-year-old with advanced COPD still pursuing disease-directed therapy asks about the difference between palliative care and hospice. What is the best explanation?

options: Review cases only after discharge for billing purposes
Deny care to reduce costs
Conduct concurrent review during the stay, applying criteria to support appropriate level of care and identify discharge barriers in real time
Avoid communicating with the care team
rationale: Concurrent review during hospitalization allows the UR nurse to validate medical necessity, address status issues, and surface discharge barriers while the patient is still admitted. Retrospective-only review cannot influence the current stay, and UR's role is appropriate utilization, not denying needed care.
stem: What best describes the utilization review nurse's role during a patient's hospitalization?

options: Connect the patient with primary care access, same-day clinic options, or urgent care alternatives and address barriers to follow-up
Discourage any ED use in the future
Provide no guidance since ED use is a patient right
Recommend the ED for all future concerns
rationale: Frequent avoidable ED visits often reflect poor access to primary or urgent care; connecting the patient to timely alternatives and addressing barriers like transportation reduces low-value ED use. Discouraging all ED use risks delayed emergency care, while endorsing the ED for everything perpetuates the pattern.
stem: A 45-year-old with hypertension has visited the ED 6 times this year for medication refills and blood pressure checks. What is the best care coordination intervention?

options: Ignore the issue since it is not medical
Tell the patient to eat less to save money
Prescribe a different diet that costs more
Screen for food insecurity and refer to community food resources, medically tailored meal programs, or SNAP enrollment assistance
rationale: Food insecurity directly undermines diabetes and heart failure management; screening and referral to food banks, medically tailored meals, or SNAP addresses a root cause of poor outcomes. Ignoring it or advising the patient to eat less worsens glycemic control and is clinically inappropriate.
stem: A 58-year-old with diabetes and heart failure reports sometimes skipping meals because food money runs out. A1c is 9.4 percent. What is the best intervention?

options: Tell the patient to pay for rides out of pocket
Cancel follow-up appointments
Arrange non-emergency medical transportation through the Medicaid benefit or community ride programs
Have the nurse drive the patient
rationale: Medicaid covers non-emergency medical transportation for eligible beneficiaries, and community programs fill gaps; arranging rides preserves follow-up adherence. Canceling appointments guarantees readmission risk, and staff personally transporting patients violates boundaries and liability standards.
stem: A 64-year-old on Medicaid misses dialysis and clinic appointments due to lack of transportation. What is the best resource solution?

options: Continue the same cycle of admissions without changes
Assign a dedicated case manager or complex care program to coordinate services, reconcile medications, and address housing and behavioral health needs
Restrict the patient from the ED
Discharge faster each time
rationale: High utilizers typically have interacting medical, behavioral, and social needs that episodic care cannot resolve; intensive case management with a consistent coordinator reduces admissions by addressing root causes. Restricting access is unsafe and faster discharges without support accelerate the cycle.
stem: A 52-year-old with COPD, depression, and unstable housing has had 8 admissions this year. What care model best breaks the cycle?

options: Verify insurance coverage and benefits at admission to identify authorization needs, network status, and potential cost barriers
Wait until discharge to check insurance
Assume all insurance works the same
Avoid discussing coverage with the patient
rationale: Early insurance verification reveals prior authorization requirements, network limitations, and benefit exclusions while there is time to adapt the plan and counsel the patient. Waiting until discharge produces surprise bills and denied claims, and avoiding the conversation leaves the patient unprepared.
stem: A 60-year-old with a new commercial insurance plan is admitted. What is the case manager's best initial insurance-related action?

options: Hide the network status from the patient
Guarantee the same cost as in-network care
Disclose the out-of-network status, estimate potential costs, and help the patient choose an in-network alternative or document informed choice
Refuse to provide any care
rationale: Patients have the right to know network status and cost implications before receiving non-emergent out-of-network care; the case manager facilitates informed choice or an in-network alternative. Concealing the status exposes the patient to surprise billing, and refusing care is inappropriate when alternatives exist.
stem: A 57-year-old is referred to an out-of-network specialist for a non-urgent procedure. What is the case manager's best action?

options: Only the physician needs to know the patient's wishes
Advance directives are only for terminal patients
Facilitate advance directive and POLST completion with the patient and family, and ensure documents are accessible across care settings
Wait until the patient loses capacity to discuss wishes
rationale: Advance care planning belongs upstream while the patient can participate; the case manager ensures advance directives and POLST are completed, witnessed properly, and transmitted to receiving providers. Waiting until incapacity forces surrogates to guess, and limiting planning to terminal patients misses the opportunity for all seriously ill adults.
stem: A 72-year-old with advanced heart failure is being discharged to a SNF. No advance directive or POLST exists. What is the case manager's best action?

options: Allow the family to make all decisions indefinitely without legal authority
Have the nurse sign as decision-maker
Initiate a social work referral for guardianship or surrogate decision-maker evaluation through appropriate legal channels
Discharge the patient to make his own decisions
rationale: An incapacitated patient without a surrogate needs a legally authorized decision-maker; social work coordinates evaluation for guardianship or state surrogate processes. Family members cannot assume authority without legal standing in many states, and discharging an incapacitated unbefriended patient is unsafe.
stem: A 68-year-old with advanced dementia and no family is incapacitated and needs a discharge decision. No advance directive exists. What is the best action?

options: Report the concern to adult protective services and notify the care team per mandatory reporting obligations, while ensuring the patient's immediate safety
Ignore the bruising since the patient did not complain
Confront the caregiver aggressively
Wait for more definitive proof before acting
rationale: Health care workers are mandatory reporters; suspected elder abuse or neglect must be reported to APS promptly, and the team must ensure safety planning. Waiting for proof endangers the patient, and aggressive confrontation can escalate harm and compromise investigation.
stem: A 79-year-old with bruises in various stages of healing is fearful around her caregiver son. The nurse suspects neglect. What is the best action?

options: Tell the patient to go home and work it out
Require the patient to press charges before offering help
Document nothing to protect privacy
Provide a safe private screening, offer community domestic violence resources including shelter hotlines and safety planning, and connect with social work
rationale: Domestic violence intervention centers on safety planning, confidential resources, and social work support without coercing legal action; private screening protects the patient from retaliation. Requiring charges before help deters disclosure, and failing to document misses care continuity and legal protections.
stem: A 42-year-old admitted with injuries gives inconsistent explanations and appears fearful of her partner who stays at the bedside constantly. What is the best nursing action?

options: Discharge without any substance use follow-up
Refer to community medication-assisted treatment programs and peer recovery supports with a scheduled intake before discharge
Recommend willpower alone
Require abstinence before any referral
rationale: Medication-assisted treatment with buprenorphine or methadone plus peer recovery support is evidence-based for opioid use disorder; scheduling intake before discharge bridges the high-risk transition. Willpower-only advice ignores effective treatment, and requiring abstinence before referral withholds care from those who need it most.
stem: A 36-year-old with opioid use disorder is admitted with endocarditis and wants help with recovery. What is the best community linkage?

options: Provide crisis resources including the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, ensure a safety assessment, and arrange urgent behavioral health follow-up with social work
Reassure the patient and discharge without referrals
Tell the patient to call only if things get worse
Document the statement without any action
rationale: A passive death wish with a plan requires immediate safety assessment, crisis resources like 988, and urgent behavioral health linkage coordinated with social work. Reassurance alone or deferring action in a patient with a plan is unsafe, and documentation without intervention fails the duty to protect.
stem: A 54-year-old with chronic pain and depression states he would be better off dead and describes a plan. He is medically stable for discharge. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Tell the patient to change dressings at home without guidance
Refer to any clinic regardless of wound expertise
Coordinate referral to an outpatient wound clinic with the treatment plan, supply needs, and follow-up timing communicated
Wait until the wound worsens to refer
rationale: Complex wounds need continuity with a specialty wound clinic; transmitting the plan, supply list, and follow-up interval prevents gaps that cause deterioration. Generic clinic referral without wound expertise or waiting for worsening invites infection and readmission.
stem: A 64-year-old with a complex venous leg ulcer is discharging and needs ongoing specialized wound care. What is the best referral coordination?

options: Assume the outpatient unit will accept the patient automatically
Delay discharge until a chair is confirmed
Coordinate with the outpatient dialysis unit and nephrology to secure a dialysis chair and schedule, transmitting records before discharge
Discharge without communicating with the dialysis unit
rationale: ESRD patients cannot safely discharge without a confirmed outpatient dialysis slot; the case manager coordinates the chair, schedule, and records transfer with nephrology. Assuming automatic acceptance or discharging without communication risks missed treatments and hyperkalemia.
stem: A 58-year-old with ESRD admitted with pneumonia is medically ready for discharge but missed outpatient dialysis during the stay. What is the case manager's priority?

options: Bedrest for 6 weeks after discharge
No exercise is safe after a heart attack
Unsupervised strenuous exercise immediately
Refer to cardiac rehabilitation for supervised exercise, education, and risk factor modification
rationale: Cardiac rehab provides monitored exercise progression, education, and psychosocial support that reduce mortality and readmissions after MI and heart failure. Prolonged bedrest causes deconditioning, and unsupervised strenuous exercise early after MI is unsafe.
stem: A 62-year-old post-MI patient asks what exercise is safe after discharge. What is the best referral?

options: Refer to pulmonary rehabilitation for exercise training, breathing strategies, and self-management education
Advise the patient to avoid all exertion
Prescribe oxygen without evaluation
No referral is needed since inhalers are sufficient
rationale: Pulmonary rehab improves exercise tolerance, dyspnea, and quality of life in COPD through supervised training and self-management education. Avoiding exertion accelerates deconditioning, and inhalers alone do not restore functional capacity.
stem: A 68-year-old with severe COPD is dyspneic with minimal activity despite optimal inhalers. What is the best referral?

options: Hand the patient a diet pamphlet
Tell the patient to figure out insulin on their own
Refer to a Diabetes Self-Management Education and Support program for structured curriculum and ongoing support
No education is needed for type 2 diabetes
rationale: Accredited DSMES programs deliver structured curriculum on monitoring, medications, nutrition, and complication prevention with proven A1c reduction. A pamphlet alone does not build self-management skills, and forgoing education in a patient with A1c 10.1 percent guarantees poor outcomes.
stem: A 50-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (A1c 10.1 percent) is overwhelmed by new medications and monitoring. What is the best community referral?

options: No further therapy is needed after inpatient rehab
Refer to outpatient stroke rehabilitation for continued PT, OT, and speech therapy with coordinated goals
Wait 6 months before any outpatient therapy
Home exercises alone without professional guidance
rationale: Stroke recovery continues for months; outpatient rehab sustains gains across mobility, ADLs, and communication with coordinated goals. Stopping therapy at discharge wastes the recovery window, and unguided home exercises lack progression and safety oversight.
stem: A 66-year-old stroke patient completed inpatient rehabilitation and is discharging home with residual hemiparesis and aphasia. What is the best next referral?

options: Prescribe a walker without training
Recommend staying home to avoid falls
Restrict all activity
Refer to community fall prevention programs such as Matter of Balance plus home physical therapy for strength and balance training
rationale: Evidence-based community fall prevention programs combined with PT for strength and balance directly target modifiable fall risk. Activity restriction causes deconditioning that increases fall risk, and a walker without training may be used unsafely.
stem: A 78-year-old with 3 falls in 6 months is fearful of walking. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Connect the family with respite care options, caregiver support groups, and the Area Agency on Aging for relief resources
Tell the daughter to keep going without help
Recommend immediate nursing home placement
No resources exist for caregivers
rationale: Caregiver burnout predicts patient institutionalization and poor outcomes; respite care, support groups, and aging-network resources sustain the caregiving arrangement. Dismissing burnout or defaulting to placement ignores less restrictive supports that preserve the dyad.
stem: The daughter caring for her 84-year-old mother with dementia reports exhaustion and crying daily. What is the best resource intervention?

options: Tell the patient the bill must be paid in full immediately
Send the account to collections without discussion
Refer to hospital financial counseling for charity care, payment plans, and coverage enrollment screening
Avoid discussing the bill with the patient
rationale: Financial counselors can screen for charity care eligibility, negotiate payment plans, and enroll patients in coverage, reducing medical debt and preserving access. Immediate full payment demands on an uninsured patient are unrealistic, and avoiding the conversation forfeits available assistance.
stem: A 48-year-old uninsured patient is anxious about a large hospital bill after an admission for pneumonia. What is the best referral?

options: Medicare covers everything with no cost-sharing
Medicare Part A covers inpatient hospital stays, Part B covers outpatient and physician services, and Part D covers prescription drugs, each with distinct cost-sharing
Only Part D matters for hospitalized patients
Medicare Advantage is identical to original Medicare in all respects
rationale: Understanding Parts A, B, and D helps the case manager anticipate coverage, cost-sharing, and authorization needs across the care continuum. Medicare does not cover everything, and Part D is irrelevant to the inpatient stay itself while critical for discharge medications.
stem: A 67-year-old newly eligible for Medicare asks what the different parts cover as discharge planning begins. What is the best explanation?

options: Medicaid is only for children
The patient must be destitute to qualify
Medicaid never covers long-term care
Refer to Medicaid eligibility screening since the patient may qualify based on income and assets, with rules varying by state including expansion status
rationale: Many low-income adults qualify for Medicaid under expansion or aged-blind-disabled pathways, and eligibility screening connects them to coverage for ongoing care. Misinformation about destitution or categorical limits deters applications, while screening is the correct gateway action.
stem: A 58-year-old uninsured patient with chronic illness and low income needs ongoing care after discharge. What is the best coverage action?

options: Apply the two-midnight rule: inpatient admission is generally appropriate when the expectation is that care will span at least two midnights, and document the expectation
Admit all chest pain patients as inpatient regardless of expected stay
Keep every patient in observation indefinitely
Base status solely on the time of arrival
rationale: The two-midnight benchmark guides inpatient versus outpatient status based on the physician's expectation of required hospital care spanning two midnights, supported by documentation. Blanket inpatient admission or indefinite observation ignores medical necessity, and arrival time alone does not determine status.
stem: A 64-year-old with unstable angina is expected to need 3 days of hospital care including cardiac catheterization. What status determination approach is correct?

options: Tell the patient the drug is unavailable
Substitute a different drug without discussion
Work with pharmacy and the prescriber on the prior authorization, including medical necessity documentation and formulary alternatives if denied
Have the patient pay cash without exploring options
rationale: Prior authorization requires clinical documentation of medical necessity, failed alternatives, or contraindications, coordinated among pharmacy, prescriber, and case management. Silent substitution bypasses informed consent, and cash pay without exploring coverage wastes the patient's resources.
stem: A 66-year-old is prescribed an expensive anticoagulant that requires prior authorization. Discharge is tomorrow. What is the best coordinated action?

options: Step therapy means the patient must try surgery first
The insurer can never require step therapy
Explain that the plan requires trying a preferred lower-cost medication first, and help the prescriber document medical necessity if an exception is warranted
Tell the patient to ignore the requirement
rationale: Step therapy protocols require trial of preferred agents before covering alternatives; the team supports exceptions with documentation of contraindication, intolerance, or expected failure. Ignoring the requirement guarantees denial, and mischaracterizing it as surgery-first confuses the patient.
stem: A patient's new prescription is denied with a note requiring step therapy. The patient is upset. What is the best explanation and action?

options: All drugs cost the same under insurance
The pharmacy decides tiers arbitrarily
Tiering is illegal
Explain that formulary tiers determine patient cost-sharing, with lower tiers costing less, and work with pharmacy on tier exceptions or therapeutic alternatives
rationale: Formulary tiers structure cost-sharing to steer toward cost-effective options; understanding tiers lets the team pursue tier exceptions or alternatives when a higher-tier drug is clinically necessary. Claiming uniform costs or arbitrary tiering misleads the patient about real financial exposure.
stem: A 60-year-old is shocked that a discharge medication costs 300 dollars while a similar one costs 10 dollars. What is the best explanation?

options: Continue concurrent review, updating clinical information to support ongoing medical necessity and actively resolving discharge barriers
Stop all review once the patient is admitted
Discharge the patient when criteria lapse regardless of clinical stability
Avoid telling the care team about authorization limits
rationale: Continued stay review keeps the clinical picture current for the payer, supports authorization for each additional day, and drives barrier resolution. Discharging solely because criteria lapse, while the patient remains unstable, is unsafe, and hiding authorization limits from the team prevents planning.
stem: A 72-year-old remains hospitalized on day 5 with persistent hypoxemia and the payer requests continued stay review. What is the UR nurse's best action?

options: Physically prevent the patient from leaving
Have security escort the patient out immediately

Engage the patient with nonjudgmental discussion of concerns, involve the provider and case management to address barriers, assess decision-making capacity, and document the discussion and follow-up plan
Refuse to provide any discharge instructions
rationale: AMA discharges require exploring the patient's reasons, addressing modifiable barriers, confirming capacity, and providing harm-reduction instructions and follow-up; this approach reduces return visits. Physical prevention is false imprisonment, and withholding instructions abandons the patient.
stem: A 50-year-old with cellulitis demands to leave against medical advice because of childcare concerns. What is the best coordinated response?

options: Send the patient to the facility the hospital prefers
Let the payer choose without patient input
Present appropriate post-acute options with quality information and honor the patient's informed choice among qualified providers
Withhold options to simplify the decision
rationale: CMS conditions of participation require presenting post-acute options and respecting patient choice; the case manager provides quality data and logistical facts to support informed selection. Steering to a preferred facility or withholding options violates patient rights and choice requirements.
stem: A 74-year-old needs SNF placement and asks how to choose among several facilities. What is the case manager's obligation?

options: The 3-day rule applies to observation days
Any single overnight qualifies the patient for SNF coverage
SNF coverage never requires a prior hospital stay
Confirm a qualifying 3-day inpatient stay, noting that observation days do not count, before assuring SNF coverage under traditional Medicare
rationale: Traditional Medicare SNF coverage requires 3 consecutive inpatient midnights, excluding observation time; verifying qualifying status prevents coverage denials. Counting observation days or assuming single overnights qualify leads to unexpected patient liability.
stem: A 76-year-old spent 2 days in observation and 2 days as inpatient, and now needs SNF care. What must the case manager verify for traditional Medicare coverage?

options: Provide the Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice explaining observation status and cost-sharing implications when observation exceeds 24 hours
No notice is required for observation stays
Give the notice only at discharge
Observation status has no financial impact
rationale: The MOON is a CMS-required notice for observation stays exceeding 24 hours, informing beneficiaries of outpatient status and potential cost-sharing including SNF implications. Omitting it violates federal requirements and leaves patients unaware of financial exposure.
stem: A 70-year-old has been in observation for 30 hours. What notice is required?

options: The patient must be discharged immediately
Bill as inpatient without any process
Use Condition Code 44 to change inpatient to outpatient status with physician concurrence and proper documentation when inpatient criteria are not met
Ignore the status error
rationale: Condition Code 44 allows compliant reclassification from inpatient to outpatient when the UR committee and physician agree inpatient criteria were never met, with required documentation and notice. Billing inpatient without medical necessity invites improper payment liability, and immediate discharge may be unsafe.
stem: Utilization review determines a patient admitted as inpatient never met inpatient criteria on day 1. What is the compliant correction process?

options: No notice is needed when coverage ends
The patient can be billed without warning
Issue the Hospital-Issued Notice of Non-coverage when the hospital believes Medicare will no longer cover the inpatient stay, informing the patient of appeal rights
Discharge the patient without discussion
rationale: The HINN notifies beneficiaries when the hospital believes continued stay is not covered, triggering appeal rights including expedited QIO review. Billing or discharging without notice denies due process protections Medicare guarantees.
stem: A 68-year-old's continued hospital stay is deemed no longer medically necessary under Medicare. What notice must be issued?

options: The ABN is only for emergency services
Verbal warning is sufficient
The patient cannot be billed under any circumstances
Issue an Advance Beneficiary Notice before providing a service Medicare may not cover, so the patient can decide whether to proceed and accept liability
rationale: The ABN is the CMS-required written notice given before potentially non-covered services, allowing informed financial consent. Verbal warnings do not satisfy the requirement, and without a valid ABN the provider generally cannot bill the beneficiary.
stem: A 64-year-old wants a screening service during admission that Medicare likely will not cover. What is required before proceeding?

options: Complete a discharge planning evaluation addressing post-discharge needs, arrange services, and provide clear instructions with follow-up, as required by CMS conditions of participation
Discharge planning is optional
Only arrange services the patient requests
Provide instructions verbally without documentation
rationale: CMS conditions of participation mandate discharge planning evaluations, arrangement of post-discharge services, and clear instructions; this is a regulatory requirement, not optional. Verbal-only instructions without documentation fail both safety and compliance standards.
stem: What are the hospital's core discharge planning obligations under CMS conditions of participation?

options: No follow-up contact is needed after discharge
The patient must return to the ED for follow-up
Provide transitional care management with patient contact within 2 business days and a face-to-face visit within 7 or 14 days depending on complexity, with medication reconciliation
Bill for a routine office visit only
rationale: TCM services require timely post-discharge contact, a face-to-face visit within 7 days for high complexity or 14 days for moderate complexity, and medication reconciliation to prevent errors. No contact or ED-only follow-up misses the evidence-based transition window.
stem: A 72-year-old with multiple chronic conditions is discharged after heart failure exacerbation. Which transitional care approach best supports the transition?

options: Medication lists never change during hospitalization
The patient can rely on memory alone
Reconcile admission, inpatient, and discharge medication lists at every transition, resolving discrepancies with pharmacy and the prescriber
Only reconcile controlled substances
rationale: Medication discrepancies at transitions cause a large share of post-discharge adverse events; comprehensive reconciliation across all transitions with pharmacy collaboration catches omissions, duplications, and dosing errors. Limiting reconciliation to controlled substances misses the most common harmful discrepancies.
stem: A 78-year-old on 10 medications is transferring from hospital to SNF. What medication safety process is most important?

options: Send records without any direct communication
Assume the PCP will read the discharge summary eventually
Have the patient explain everything to the PCP
Perform a warm handoff with direct clinician-to-clinician communication of the care plan, pending results, and follow-up needs
rationale: Warm handoffs with direct communication ensure the receiving provider understands active issues, pending tests, and the follow-up plan, reducing errors and readmissions. Passive record-sending or relying on the patient to relay complex plans creates dangerous gaps.
stem: A 66-year-old with new diabetes and heart failure is discharging to primary care follow-up. What communication best ensures continuity?

options: Refer to a community health worker who can provide culturally tailored navigation, appointment support, and barrier assessment
Community health workers have no role in care coordination
Only physicians can coordinate community care
CHWs should replace all clinical follow-up
rationale: Community health workers bridge clinical care and community realities through trusted, culturally aligned navigation and barrier resolution. They complement rather than replace clinical follow-up, and restricting coordination to physicians ignores their proven effectiveness.
stem: A 58-year-old with limited English, missed appointments, and distrust of the health system needs ongoing chronic disease follow-up. What linkage best supports engagement?

options: Discharge to the street with wound care supplies
Keep the patient admitted indefinitely
Require the patient to find housing before treatment
Coordinate medical respite placement for continued wound care and recovery with case management and social work
rationale: Medical respite provides homeless patients a safe place to heal with clinical support, improving wound outcomes and reducing readmissions. Street discharge with supplies is unsafe for wound vac management, and indefinite admission is poor stewardship.
stem: A 46-year-old homeless patient needs 3 more weeks of wound vac therapy after discharge. What is the best placement?

options: Deny all care based on immigration status
Refer only to the ED for future needs
Connect with a Federally Qualified Health Center for sliding-scale primary care and hospital financial counseling for charity care screening
Tell the patient no resources exist
rationale: FQHCs provide primary care regardless of immigration status on a sliding scale, and hospital financial counseling screens for charity care; emergency care remains available under EMTALA. Denying care or claiming no resources exist abandons a patient with treatable conditions.
stem: A 40-year-old undocumented patient with hypertension and diabetes needs ongoing primary care after discharge. What is the best resource plan?

options: Use the patient's young child as interpreter
Rely on gestures and hope for understanding
Delay all teaching until an English-speaking relative visits
Use qualified medical interpreters and translated materials for all teaching, documenting language needs in the care plan
rationale: Qualified interpreters and translated materials are required for safe, effective teaching; using children as interpreters is unethical and error-prone. Documenting language needs ensures every discipline provides accessible communication throughout the stay.
stem: A 62-year-old who speaks only Vietnamese needs complex discharge teaching on wound care and medications. What is the best approach?

options: Use teach-back to confirm understanding, documenting the patient's explanation in their own words
Ask if the patient understands and accept a yes
Provide written materials only
Assume understanding based on education level
rationale: Teach-back verifies actual comprehension by having the patient explain in their own words, catching misunderstandings before discharge. Accepting a yes or relying on written materials alone overestimates understanding, especially with low health literacy.
stem: A 70-year-old with low health literacy is learning a new insulin regimen. Which teaching verification method is best?

options: Telehealth is never appropriate for follow-up
Require all visits to be in person
Offer telehealth follow-up visits where clinically appropriate to reduce transportation and access barriers
Use telehealth only for emergencies
rationale: Telehealth follow-up for stable chronic conditions reduces transportation, time, and cost barriers while maintaining continuity. Restricting it to emergencies or requiring all in-person visits ignores its proven role in access expansion.
stem: A 64-year-old in a rural area misses follow-up appointments due to a 90-minute drive. What access solution best supports continuity?

options: Remote monitoring has no role in chronic disease
Require daily in-person visits instead
Enroll in remote patient monitoring for daily weights, blood pressure, or glucose with clinician review and escalation protocols
Give the patient a device without any monitoring plan
rationale: RPM with structured clinician review detects early deterioration in heart failure, hypertension, and diabetes, enabling timely intervention. Devices without monitoring plans create false security, and daily in-person visits are impractical.
stem: A 68-year-old with heart failure and hypertension lives alone far from clinic. What technology-supported approach best enables early detection of decline?

options: Bundled payments reward higher volume of services
Providers are paid separately for every service
Bundles apply only to outpatient care
Explain that bundled payments provide a single payment for an episode of care, incentivizing coordination and efficiency across providers
rationale: Bundled payments align incentives across the episode by paying a target price for all related services, rewarding coordination and waste reduction. They do not reward volume, and misunderstanding them as fee-for-service misses their care-redesign purpose.
stem: A 70-year-old asks why the hospital is so focused on coordinating the joint replacement episode. What payment concept best explains the emphasis?

options: Describe the accountable care organization model where providers share responsibility for quality and total cost of care for a defined population
ACOs penalize all hospital admissions
ACOs only affect physicians
No explanation is needed
rationale: ACOs hold provider networks jointly accountable for quality and spending, driving the care coordination, prevention, and transition work the patient experiences. Describing admission penalties alone mischaracterizes the model, which rewards value rather than punishing necessary care.
stem: A 66-year-old notices the clinic emphasizing prevention and care coordination and asks why. What best explains the ACO context?

options: CCM is only for hospitalized patients
No coordination is needed between visits
Enroll in chronic care management services providing structured between-visit coordination, care plan maintenance, and 24-hour access for eligible patients with multiple chronic conditions
CCM replaces the primary care physician
rationale: CCM reimburses structured non-face-to-face coordination for patients with multiple chronic conditions, filling the between-visit gap with care plan oversight and access. It supplements rather than replaces the PCP, and limiting it to inpatients misses its outpatient purpose.
stem: A 74-year-old with diabetes, heart failure, and CKD has frequent between-visit questions and medication issues. What service best provides structured ongoing coordination?

options: Dual eligibles cannot have both coverages
Medicare always covers everything so Medicaid is irrelevant
Coordinate benefits recognizing Medicare as primary and Medicaid as secondary, and screen for programs that help with premiums and cost-sharing
Tell the patient to drop one coverage
rationale: For dual eligibles, Medicare pays first and Medicaid covers cost-sharing and additional benefits; coordination plus screening for Medicare Savings Programs maximizes coverage. Dropping coverage or ignoring Medicaid's secondary role leaves benefits unused.
stem: A 70-year-old has both Medicare and Medicaid and is confused about which pays for hospital and drug costs. What is the best coordination?

options: PACE is only for wealthy seniors
PACE requires nursing home placement
The patient must give up their primary care doctor without discussion
Evaluate PACE eligibility for comprehensive community-based care including medical, social, and long-term services for nursing-home-eligible older adults who wish to remain home
rationale: PACE integrates medical, social, and long-term services for nursing-home-eligible adults who prefer community living, with an interdisciplinary team. It does not require institutionalization, and evaluation should precede any assumptions about the primary care relationship.
stem: An 80-year-old who qualifies for nursing home level of care wants to remain at home. What program best integrates medical and long-term services?

options: Coordinate VA benefits and referrals for eligible veterans, verifying enrollment and service-connected priorities
Veterans cannot use VA and community care together
VA benefits are only for active-duty members
No coordination is needed
rationale: Eligible veterans can access VA services and community care under programs like the MISSION Act; verifying enrollment and coordinating referrals prevents duplication and gaps. Excluding veterans from VA coordination or claiming active-duty-only eligibility is incorrect.
stem: A 68-year-old veteran needs specialty follow-up after discharge. What is the best benefits coordination?

options: Keep the patient hospitalized for all IV antibiotics
Switch to an oral antibiotic that is ineffective for the organism
Discharge without any antibiotics
Coordinate home infusion services with infectious disease, pharmacy, and home health for eligible patients needing ongoing IV therapy
rationale: Home infusion with ID, pharmacy, and nursing oversight safely delivers OPAT for stable patients, reducing hospital days. Hospitalizing for the full course wastes resources, and ineffective oral substitution risks treatment failure.
stem: A 58-year-old with osteomyelitis needs 4 more weeks of IV antibiotics and is otherwise stable. What is the best plan?

options: Remove the PICC immediately without a plan
Leave the PICC in indefinitely without follow-up
Have the patient manage the PICC alone
Coordinate PICC placement timing with the infusion plan, confirm home health nursing for line care, and arrange timely removal when therapy ends
rationale: PICC lines require coordinated insertion timing, skilled nursing for maintenance and dressing changes, and planned removal to prevent infection and thrombosis. Indefinite retention or solo patient management invites complications, and premature removal disrupts therapy.
stem: A 62-year-old needs 6 weeks of IV antibiotics via PICC after discharge. What is the best line coordination plan?

options: Start home TPN without any coordination
Discharge with oral diet alone despite malabsorption
Coordinate home TPN through a specialty pharmacy and home infusion nursing, with dietitian monitoring and lab surveillance
TPN can never be given at home
rationale: Home TPN requires specialty pharmacy compounding, trained infusion nursing, dietitian oversight, and lab monitoring for metabolic complications. Uncoordinated initiation risks sepsis and metabolic crisis, while oral diet alone in severe malabsorption guarantees decline.
stem: A 54-year-old with short bowel syndrome needs ongoing parenteral nutrition after discharge. What is the best coordination?

options: Verify the enteral formula and supply needs, confirm DME coverage and supplier, and ensure delivery and caregiver training before discharge
Order supplies after discharge and hope they arrive
Tell the family to buy formula at a grocery store
No training is needed for tube feeding
rationale: Enteral feeding at home requires confirmed formula coverage, a contracted DME supplier, timely delivery, and hands-on caregiver training to prevent misconnections and aspiration. Post-discharge ordering creates dangerous gaps, and retail formula may not match the prescription.
stem: A 70-year-old discharging with a PEG tube needs ongoing enteral feeding. What is the best DME coordination?

options: Tell the patient to reuse supplies indefinitely
Order supplies without verifying coverage
Arrange ostomy supply needs through a covered DME supplier before discharge, with the WOCN confirming the correct products
No supplies are needed after discharge
rationale: Ostomy patients need a reliable supply of the specific pouching products fitted by the WOCN, obtained through a covered supplier to ensure continuity. Reusing supplies causes leaks and skin breakdown, and unverified ordering risks non-covered products.
stem: A 60-year-old with a new ileostomy is discharging and needs ongoing ostomy supplies. What is the best plan?

options: Tell the patient to buy any wheelchair online
Order the most expensive power chair for every patient
Deny mobility equipment to save costs
Assess mobility needs with physical therapy, obtain the required face-to-face evaluation and documentation, and coordinate prior authorization with a contracted supplier
rationale: Wheelchair coverage requires PT assessment, a face-to-face examination, detailed medical necessity documentation, and prior authorization through a contracted supplier. Unprescribed online purchases may be unsafe and non-covered, while blanket denials abandon mobility needs.
stem: A 72-year-old with progressive weakness needs a wheelchair for discharge. What is the best authorization process?

options: Prescribe home oxygen for comfort without criteria
Deny oxygen to all COPD patients
Qualify home oxygen using ABG or oximetry criteria per coverage rules, with documentation of medical necessity and retesting as required
Order oxygen without any testing
rationale: Home oxygen coverage requires documented hypoxemia by ABG or oximetry under specified conditions, with proper certification and follow-up testing. Prescribing without criteria wastes resources and exposes patients to unnecessary therapy, while blanket denial harms those who qualify.
stem: A 68-year-old with COPD and resting SpO2 86 percent needs home oxygen. What is the correct qualification process?

options: Coordinate CPAP setup with DME, adherence monitoring, and follow-up to address mask fit and tolerance issues
Prescribe CPAP without any follow-up
Tell the patient CPAP is optional
No education is needed for CPAP use
rationale: CPAP success depends on proper setup, mask fitting, adherence monitoring, and troubleshooting; DME coordination with clinical follow-up addresses the tolerance issues that cause abandonment. Prescribing without support leads to closet storage, not treatment.
stem: A 58-year-old with severe OSA is prescribed CPAP but previously abandoned it due to mask discomfort. What is the best coordination?

options: Hospice provides only one level of care
Patients must choose a single setting forever
Explain the four levels of hospice care including routine home, continuous home, inpatient respite, and general inpatient, matched to changing needs
Hospice cannot manage crises at home
rationale: Hospice offers routine home care, continuous home care for crises, inpatient respite for caregiver relief, and general inpatient care for uncontrolled symptoms; matching level to need is core case management. Describing a single rigid level misleads families about available support.
stem: An 82-year-old on hospice has escalating symptoms the family cannot manage at home. What should the nurse explain about hospice options?

options: Bereavement support ends at the time of death
Only the patient receives hospice services
Families must seek counseling independently
Connect the family with hospice bereavement services, which continue for at least a year after death, plus community grief resources
rationale: The Medicare hospice benefit includes bereavement support for families for at least 13 months after death, supplemented by community grief programs. Ending support at death abandons grieving families during the highest-risk period.
stem: The family of a patient who died on hospice is struggling with grief. What ongoing support should the nurse arrange?

options: The nurse should decide about donation independently
Donation is never discussed in hospitals
Make a timely referral to the organ procurement organization and allow trained OPO staff to approach the family about donation options
Ask the family to decide without any information
