rationale: Federal regulations require timely OPO notification for imminent deaths, and trained OPO coordinators conduct donation discussions to ensure sensitivity and informed consent. Nurses should not independently solicit donation, and skipping the referral violates regulatory requirements.
stem: A 45-year-old with catastrophic brain injury is progressing to brain death. What is the nurse's best action regarding organ donation?

options: Notify the medical examiner or coroner per jurisdictional requirements for deaths that are unexpected, unexplained, or involve trauma, and follow facility policy
All deaths require coroner investigation
No notification is ever needed
The family decides whether to notify
rationale: Medical examiner and coroner statutes mandate reporting of specific death categories such as trauma, unexpected, or unattended deaths; the nurse follows facility policy and jurisdictional law. Universal or zero reporting both violate legal requirements, and families do not control this determination.
stem: A 52-year-old dies unexpectedly 12 hours after admission for chest pain. What is the nurse's obligation?

options: Quality ratings are meaningless
Choose based on distance only
Use CMS Care Compare star ratings and quality measures along with patient preferences to inform facility choice
The hospital must choose for the patient
rationale: CMS star ratings and quality measures provide objective data on staffing, outcomes, and inspections that, combined with patient preferences, support informed choice. Distance-only selection or hospital-directed placement ignores quality and violates patient choice rights.
stem: A 76-year-old needs SNF placement and the family asks how to compare facilities. What guidance best supports their choice?

options: The patient must use the nearest facility
Out-of-area placement is never allowed
Deny the request without discussion
Explore the request, verify benefit coverage and network implications, and coordinate records transfer and follow-up with the distant facility
rationale: Patients may choose out-of-area SNFs to be near family; the case manager verifies coverage, addresses network and cost implications, and ensures records and follow-up transfer. Mandatory nearest-facility rules violate choice rights, and blanket denial ignores legitimate family support benefits.
stem: A 74-year-old wants SNF placement near her daughter in another state. What is the case manager's best response?

options: Cancel all travel for dialysis patients
Dialysis cannot be arranged away from home
Coordinate transient dialysis with the destination unit in advance, transmitting records and the treatment prescription
Have the patient skip treatments during travel
rationale: Transient dialysis units accommodate travelers with advance scheduling and records transfer; coordination ensures continuity of the prescription. Skipping treatments risks hyperkalemia and volume overload, and prohibiting travel is unnecessary and paternalistic.
stem: A 60-year-old on hemodialysis plans a 2-week trip to visit family. What is the best coordination?

options: Connect with oncology navigation for treatment coordination, barrier assessment, and supportive resource linkage
Navigation is only for surgical patients
The patient must coordinate everything alone
No support services exist for cancer patients
rationale: Oncology navigators guide patients through complex treatment timelines, assess barriers like transportation and cost, and link to support resources, improving adherence and outcomes. Leaving patients to self-coordinate through fragmented cancer care increases delays and distress.
stem: A 58-year-old newly diagnosed with colon cancer is overwhelmed by referrals to surgery, oncology, and genetics. What is the best support?

options: Clinical trials are never appropriate
Enroll the patient without discussion
Refer to clinical trial navigation or the treating oncologist to discuss trial eligibility as a care option with informed consent
Trials are only for patients with no other options
rationale: Clinical trials are a legitimate care option at many stages; navigation or oncologist discussion with informed consent respects autonomy and expands options. Enrolling without discussion violates consent, and restricting trials to last-resort cases misrepresents their role.
stem: A 62-year-old with advanced lung cancer asks about experimental treatments. What is the best response?

options: Genetic counseling is never indicated
Order genetic testing independently
Tell the family testing is unnecessary
Refer to genetic counseling for risk assessment, testing guidance, and family implications before testing decisions
rationale: Genetic counselors provide pre-test risk assessment, informed consent, and interpretation of implications for relatives, which direct-to-test ordering bypasses. Independent nurse ordering of genetic tests exceeds scope and skips essential counseling.
stem: A 45-year-old with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer asks about genetic testing. What is the best referral?

options: Tell the patient quitting is solely willpower
No resources exist for smoking cessation
Refer to the state quitline and community cessation programs, coordinating pharmacotherapy with the prescriber
Recommend switching to vaping without guidance
rationale: Quitlines provide free evidence-based counseling and often nicotine replacement, and combining behavioral support with pharmacotherapy doubles quit rates. Willpower-only advice ignores effective treatment, and unguided vaping substitution is not evidence-based cessation care.
stem: A 60-year-old with COPD who smokes a pack daily wants to quit. What is the best resource linkage?

options: Refer to food pharmacies, medically tailored meal programs, or SNAP enrollment assistance through social work or community partners
Tell the patient to eat whatever is cheapest
Ignore nutrition since medications matter more
Prescribe supplements without addressing food access
rationale: Medically tailored meals and food pharmacies address the nutritional foundation of heart failure and diabetes management, while SNAP enrollment provides ongoing support. Supplements without food access or ignoring nutrition undermines disease control.
stem: A 62-year-old with heart failure and diabetes cannot afford the recommended low-sodium diet. What is the best intervention?

options: Housing is not a health issue
Tell the patient to find housing alone
Connect with housing navigation services, medical-legal partnerships, or community housing resources to address the health-harming housing instability
Discharge without addressing housing
rationale: Housing instability directly drives readmissions through medication storage problems, wound contamination, and missed follow-up; housing navigation and medical-legal partnerships address root causes. Dismissing housing as non-medical ignores its documented health impact.
stem: A 50-year-old facing eviction has poorly controlled diabetes and a chronic foot ulcer. What is the best care coordination action?

options: Legal problems are outside the scope of health care
Tell the patient to hire a private attorney
Ignore the benefits denial
Refer to a medical-legal partnership where attorneys address health-harming legal needs such as benefits denials and housing conditions
rationale: Medical-legal partnerships embed attorneys in care teams to resolve benefits denials, unsafe housing, and other legal barriers that drive poor health. Ignoring legal barriers or expecting patients to hire private counsel abandons solvable problems.
stem: A 55-year-old was denied disability benefits and faces utility shutoff, worsening his chronic conditions. What resource best addresses these legal needs?

options: Tell the patient to go without heat
No assistance programs exist
Refer to LIHEAP and community utility assistance programs before shutoff occurs
Wait until utilities are disconnected to act
rationale: LIHEAP provides federally funded heating and cooling assistance, and early referral before shutoff preserves health and avoids reconnection crises. Waiting until disconnection endangers patients dependent on powered medical devices.
stem: A 70-year-old on a fixed income cannot afford winter heating and uses home oxygen. What is the best resource?

options: Screen for Lifeline phone program eligibility and other communication assistance so the patient can receive appointment reminders and telehealth
Assume the patient does not need a phone
Provide no communication support
Require the patient to buy an expensive plan
rationale: The Lifeline program discounts phone service for eligible low-income patients, enabling appointment reminders, telehealth, and care coordination contact. Assuming no need or requiring expensive plans excludes patients from basic communication access.
stem: A 66-year-old without reliable phone service misses appointment reminders and cannot do telehealth visits. What resource helps?

options: Adult day programs are only for children
No daytime supervision options exist
Recommend immediate nursing home placement
Refer to adult day programs for supervised daytime care, socialization, and caregiver respite
rationale: Adult day programs provide supervised activities, meals, and health monitoring during work hours, supporting both the patient and the working caregiver. Defaulting to nursing home placement bypasses this less restrictive option.
stem: An 80-year-old with moderate dementia needs daytime supervision while her daughter works. What is the best community option?

options: No support exists for dementia families
Tell the family to manage alone
Recommend nursing home placement immediately
Connect with the Alzheimer's Association for education, support groups, respite resources, and 24-hour helpline
rationale: The Alzheimer's Association provides evidence-based caregiver education, support groups, respite guidance, and a 24-hour helpline that reduce caregiver burden and delay institutionalization. Telling families to manage alone ignores proven supports.
stem: The family of a 78-year-old newly diagnosed with Alzheimer disease feels overwhelmed. What is the best community linkage?

options: No peer support is available after stroke
Tell the patient recovery ends at discharge
Refer to stroke support groups and community reintegration programs for peer support and ongoing encouragement
Discourage community participation
rationale: Stroke support groups provide peer encouragement, practical adaptation tips, and community reintegration that sustain motivation beyond formal rehab. Declaring recovery over at discharge contradicts neuroplasticity evidence and abandons psychosocial recovery.
stem: A 64-year-old stroke survivor feels isolated and depressed 3 months after discharge. What is the best community referral?

options: Connect with American Cancer Society resources for transportation, lodging, support groups, and financial guidance
No cancer support resources exist
The patient must manage treatment logistics alone
Only the oncology team can provide support
rationale: The American Cancer Society offers transportation, lodging during treatment, support groups, and financial navigation that complement clinical care. Claiming no resources exist or restricting support to the oncology team ignores substantial community assets.
stem: A 58-year-old starting daily radiation lives 60 miles from the cancer center and worries about transportation and costs. What is the best linkage?

options: The patient can never work again
No employment resources exist
Refer to vocational rehabilitation services for assessment, training, and workplace accommodation planning
Tell the patient to find any job immediately
rationale: Vocational rehabilitation provides individualized assessment, skills training, and accommodation planning that support safe return to work after major illness. Declaring permanent work disability prematurely or pushing immediate unplanned employment risks health and job loss.
stem: A 52-year-old recovering from a major cardiac event wants to return to work but has lifting restrictions. What is the best resource?

options: Penalties apply to individual nurses
Readmissions never affect payment
Hospitals are penalized for all readmissions
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program adjusts payment based on excess 30-day readmissions for targeted conditions, driving investment in transitions of care
rationale: HRRP reduces Medicare payments for hospitals with excess 30-day readmissions in measures like heart failure, MI, and pneumonia, which is why hospitals invest in discharge planning and follow-up. Penalties target hospitals, not individual nurses, and not all readmissions count.
stem: A nursing student asks why the hospital emphasizes heart failure discharge planning. What payment policy best explains the focus?

options: Patients have no appeal rights
The discharge is final with no recourse
Inform the patient of the right to expedited review by the Quality Improvement Organization when disagreeing with the discharge decision
Tell the patient to call the police
rationale: Medicare beneficiaries facing discharge they believe is premature can request immediate QIO review, which provides an independent determination while protecting coverage during appeal. Denying appeal rights or declaring the discharge final violates beneficiary protections.
stem: A 72-year-old Medicare patient believes discharge is premature and wants to challenge the decision. What right should the nurse explain?

options: Coordinate workers' compensation coverage verification and communication with the employer's carrier and case manager per jurisdictional rules
Workers' compensation never applies to hospital care
Bill the patient's regular insurance first without question
Ignore the work-related nature of the injury
rationale: Work-related injuries fall under workers' compensation, requiring carrier verification and coordination distinct from regular health insurance billing. Billing regular insurance first or ignoring the work-related designation creates payment errors and compliance issues.
stem: A 48-year-old injured on the job needs surgery. What coverage coordination is required?

options: Swing beds are only for pediatric patients
No rural hospital options exist
Evaluate swing bed availability in a critical access hospital for skilled-level care when SNF access is limited
Transfer the patient 200 miles to the nearest SNF
rationale: Swing beds allow critical access hospitals to provide skilled nursing-level care in rural areas lacking SNF beds, keeping patients near home. Forcing long transfers when swing bed capacity exists disrupts family support and continuity.
stem: A 78-year-old in a rural area needs skilled nursing care but the nearest SNF is 200 miles away. What option best serves the patient?

options: LTACHs provide the same care as SNFs
Any patient can go to an LTACH
LTACHs are for short outpatient visits
Evaluate long-term acute care hospital criteria for patients needing extended hospital-level care averaging 25 days, such as prolonged ventilation or complex wound management
rationale: LTACHs serve medically complex patients requiring extended hospital-level care, distinct from SNF skilled care; appropriate referral matches prolonged needs like ventilator weaning. Equating LTACHs with SNFs or using them for short stays misapplies the benefit.
stem: A 64-year-old ventilator-dependent patient needs weeks of weaning after a prolonged ICU stay. What post-acute setting best fits?

options: Subacute care is identical to acute care
No step-down options exist
Coordinate subacute placement for patients needing skilled care below hospital intensity but above routine SNF care, matching services to need
Send all complex patients to LTACH
rationale: Subacute units bridge hospital and SNF intensity for patients needing skilled nursing with moderate medical complexity; matching intensity to need optimizes outcomes and cost. Defaulting all complex patients to LTACH overuses the highest-cost setting.
stem: A 70-year-old needs IV antibiotics and complex wound care but is otherwise stable. What level of post-acute care best fits?

options: Provide caregiver training on medications, wound care, warning signs, and emergency contacts with teach-back before discharge
No training is needed for family caregivers
Give written instructions only without demonstration
Assume the caregiver already knows everything
rationale: Structured caregiver training with demonstration and teach-back prepares families for complex home care tasks and recognizes warning signs, reducing errors and readmissions. Written-only instructions without practice leave caregivers unprepared for hands-on care.
stem: A 76-year-old with a complex wound and 8 medications is discharging to his wife's care. What best prepares the caregiver?

options: POLST is only valid in the hospital
A new POLST is never needed
Transcribe the POLST orders into the receiving facility's orders and confirm the form accompanies the patient across settings
POLST can be ignored during transitions
rationale: POLST contains actionable medical orders that must transfer with the patient and be transcribed into receiving facility orders to remain effective. Treating POLST as hospital-only or ignoring it during transitions risks unwanted resuscitation or withheld comfort measures.
stem: An 84-year-old with a POLST indicating comfort-focused measures and DNR is transferring to a SNF. What ensures the orders remain effective?

options: The patient must manage benefits alone
Benefits can be redirected without process
Family members can automatically take over
Refer to the Social Security Administration for representative payee evaluation when the patient cannot manage benefits, following proper application procedures
rationale: When cognitive impairment prevents benefit management, a representative payee can be appointed through SSA's formal evaluation and application process to protect funds. Informal family takeover without authorization lacks legal standing and oversight.
stem: A 72-year-old with advancing dementia cannot manage his Social Security benefits and bills are going unpaid. What is the proper process?

options: Discharge to the street with the wound vac
Keep the patient admitted until the wound closes
Discontinue the wound vac as too complex
Coordinate a portable wound vac with medical respite placement and home health nursing for dressing oversight
rationale: Portable wound vacs with respite placement and nursing oversight allow continued negative pressure therapy in homeless patients, balancing healing needs with realistic settings. Street discharge with a device requiring power and sterile technique is unsafe, and indefinite admission is poor stewardship.
stem: A 50-year-old homeless patient needs 2 more weeks of wound vac therapy. What is the best coordinated plan?

options: Verify clinical stability, safe home environment, ability to manage the line, and home health nursing availability before approving home IV antibiotics
Approve home IV antibiotics for every patient who asks
Deny home IV therapy to all patients
No assessment is needed before home infusion
rationale: Safe OPAT requires assessing stability, home safety, line management capability, and nursing support; unselected approval risks line infections and treatment failure. Blanket denial keeps stable patients hospitalized unnecessarily, wasting resources.
stem: A 60-year-old with cellulitis requests home IV antibiotics. What assessment determines appropriateness?

options: Keep the patient in an inpatient bed until transport arrives
Delay discharge until the next day
Discharge the patient to the waiting room alone
Coordinate the discharge lounge for patients awaiting transportation or final arrangements, freeing the inpatient bed while ensuring supervision and comfort
rationale: Discharge lounges safely hold discharged patients awaiting rides or prescriptions, improving bed turnover and reducing avoidable inpatient days. Holding patients in inpatient beds for logistics wastes capacity, while unsupervised waiting room discharge is unsafe for frail patients.
stem: A 74-year-old is medically cleared for discharge but the ride arrives in 4 hours. What best manages the bed and the patient?
